backups.overview: Abernathy Peak is the high point of Abernathy Ridge, between the Twisp River and Wolf Creek drainages in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. The more heavily traveled standard route climbs from Scatter Lake on the south side (class 2); the North Ridge described here is a quieter, more sustained class 2-3 alternative reached from the North Creek/Twisp River side, following an old mine trail onto the ridge crest before scrambling to the summit.
backups.beta: Rather than the popular Scatter Lake approach, this line reaches Abernathy from the north, joining a broad ridge at a roughly 7,680+ ft saddle about 0.6 mile north of the summit, then scrambles the crest — weaving around or over gendarmes — to the top. Route-finding is loose and 'pick-your-own-adventure' in spots; parties report it as noticeably harder and slower than the standard route.
backups.turnaround: Loose rock, exposed class 3-4 steps, and a long, largely trail-less descent mean parties should set a firm turnaround time that leaves ample daylight for a slower-than-expected reverse scramble, especially in poor visibility or if unfamiliar with route-finding on open ridges.
backups.rappels: None — unroped scramble; no rappels reported by parties ascending or descending.
backups.permit: No wilderness permit is required to hike or camp in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.

backups.detailed_rack: No roped rock rack is carried on this route. Cross-referenced trip reports consistently describe the non-standard North Ridge (via the Wolf Creek/Gardner Meadows trail and an old, largely-vanished mine boot path) as an unroped Class 2-3 scramble: talus and scree to Gardner Meadows, then an unmaintained path/cairns to a 7,680+ ft saddle 0.6 mi north of the summit, then a 'pick-your-own-adventure' scramble along the ridge crest with 'a few class 3 moves' on a spur ridge. No party describes placing cams, nuts, or using a rope.

map/compass or GPS — the old mine boot path is faint to nonexistent above Gardner Meadows, marked only by occasional cairns and cut logs
extra water — long ridge approach (11 mi to Gardner Meadows) with few reliable water sources higher up

backups.pro_needs: None placed — this is unprotected scrambling, not protected rock climbing. Hazard is loose rock/footing (talus, scree, old mining debris) rather than lack of gear placements; a helmet is the relevant safety item, not a rack.
backups.approach: From the North Creek Trailhead (officially the Gilbert Trailhead; ~3,660 ft, reached via Twisp River Road/FR-44 roughly 22-25 miles west of Twisp), pick up North Creek Trail #413. The first ~50 feet of tread is shared with the Twisp Pass Trail — bear right (north) to stay on North Creek Trail. The lower ~1.9 miles cross the 2018 Gilbert Fire zone: hot, shadeless standing burnt timber with no direct access to North Creek for water, so carry enough to get through this stretch. Around mile 1.9 the trail re-enters live forest and shade returns; at about mile 2.4 a roughly 6-ft boulder beside the trail gives a good view toward Reynolds Peak. At approximately mile 2, watch for an unsigned, faint mine trail splitting off the main tread and crossing North Creek — the crossing is a rustic log arrangement (about four 6-inch-diameter logs forming an 8-ft span), reported as somewhat springy and slick, and sometimes partly submerged during early-season high water (a horse ford exists nearby as an alternative). Once across, the old mine trail — a remnant of early-1900s prospecting in this basin — climbs east, fading in and out through forest and then open talus/scree as it gains the flank of Abernathy's North Ridge. Expect roughly another 1.5-2 miles and close to 2,000 ft of additional gain, on ground that starts as reasonably solid talus but grows progressively looser and scree-covered higher up, to reach a broad 7,680+ ft saddle about 0.6 mile north of the summit. Water is unreliable above the North Creek crossing, so top off there. The upper approach faces south and is essentially snow-free by early July in a normal year; a late-spring ascent on firmer, axe/crampon-friendly snow can actually make the loose talus band easier and safer to travel, at the cost of needing snow gear.
backups.descent_text: Abernathy Peak's North Ridge is a scramble, not a technical roped climb, and no fixed rappel anchors exist on this route — descend by reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb/scramble the class 3 ridge crest north back to the 7,680+ ft saddle (the route's crux terrain, with a couple of noticeably 'intense' exposed spots — face in and downclimb deliberately here, since the same loose, eroded rock that's manageable going up is more consequential coming down). From the saddle, pick your way back down the loose scree and talus — solid footing near the saddle gives way to looser scree lower down, similar in character to the neighboring, more-traveled Scatter Lake route where parties commonly plunge-step the scree comfortably once clear of the rockier upper band. Continue down to the mine trail and the North Creek crossing, then rejoin North Creek Trail #413 for the hike back to the trailhead. This is a 0-rappel walk-off/downclimb in normal summer conditions — no rope, rack, or anchors needed. Parties who ascended on firm early-season snow should be ready to descend the upper slopes via glissade or a controlled snow descent with an ice axe instead of scree, and should watch for rockfall from parties above given the generally loose rock on this route.
backups.bail: Retreat down the ridge to the approach.

pitch_detail.notes: Ridge-crest scramble from the ~7,680 ft saddle (0.6 mi north of the summit) to the top, weaving around or over gendarmes; loose rock and unmarked route-finding.

itinerary.cal: North Creek Trail/mine-trail terrain can hold snow into early-mid summer at the saddle; most parties climb it July-October.

days.note: From the North Creek Trail trailhead on Twisp River Road, hike ~2 miles of trail, cross the creek onto the old mine trail, and climb ~1.5-2 miles up to the 7,680+ ft saddle just north of the summit. From the saddle, scramble south along the ridge crest (Class 2-3, a few loose/exposed steps and old mine tailings) to the 8,321 ft summit, then reverse the entire route to descend.

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends in Mid-July through September, especially when paired with the popular Scatter Lake day hike
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low - Abernathy is a Bulger 100 peak (~98th of 100) so it draws dedicated peak-baggers, but the long approach (11+ mi RT via Scatter Lake, or 11 mi one-way via Wolf Creek/Gardner Meadows) and remote Twisp River access keep numbers small; realistically a couple dozen parties or fewer per season

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong - typical day is 10-12+ miles round trip with roughly 4500-5500 ft of gain (Scatter Lake approach is ~11 mi RT / 5200 ft; Wolf Creek/Gardner Meadows approach is longer at ~11 mi one-way to the saddle)
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day-pack (roughly 15-20 lb) is sufficient in the dry summer window - no glacier or snow travel gear required, but bring layers for afternoon thunderstorms

partner_requirements.approachTime: 5-6+ hours to reach the base of the North Ridge (roughly 4.2 mi to Scatter Lake plus scrambling beyond, or ~11 mi to Gardner Meadows via Wolf Creek Trail before the ridge itself)

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September - this is a dry-rock/talus scramble that needs the snow off both the approach trail and the ridge

July.reason: Prime window opens as the route dries out; early July can still hold isolated snow patches on the ridge, late July is typically clear

June.reason: Lingering snow on the ridge and approach trail is likely ('snow-covered; trails snowbound' in spring); road/trailhead access may also still be affected by late snowpack

August.reason: Peak dry-season conditions ('hot and dry east-side conditions'); best combination of trail/ridge dryness and long daylight

October.reason: Early season snow and shortening daylight increase risk; not part of the best-season window

September.reason: Stable weather continues but days shorten; early storms are possible later in the month

weather.typical: Drier continental NE Cascades climate typical of the Sawtooth/Methow area; hot, dry east-side summer conditions
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer - start before dawn (as already recommended) to be off the ridge before storms build

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate to locally high on the ridge crest - short Class 3 steps and gendarmes have real fall exposure, and parties report bypassing some towers by dropping off the crest rather than climbing directly over them; loose rock raises rockfall risk to any party members below on the ridge; the long, remote approach (5-6+ hrs one-way) amplifies the consequence of an injury given self-rescue/evacuation would be lengthy

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer talus/rock scramble; NWAC does not maintain a forecast zone specifically covering the Twisp River/Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness area (nearest NWAC zone, East Slopes North/Washington Pass, is oriented toward the North Cascades Highway corridor, not confirmed to extend to this drainage)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; route is entirely talus, scree, and rock ridge scrambling

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the North Creek Trailhead (officially the Gilbert Trailhead; ~3,660 ft, reached via Twisp River Road/FR-44 roughly 22-25 miles west of Twisp), pick up North Creek Trail #413.

backups.rope_note: Unroped Class 2-3 scramble on established boot path/scree to a saddle then along the ridge crest; steep snow or loose rock possible early season, carry an ice axe if snow persists, but no rope or rack needed for the ridge itself.

approach_variants.name: Gardner Meadows to the north ridge
approach_variants.notes: This is the side every recorded ascent of the north ridge has come from. Maps show an old trail running west from Gardner Meadows toward a mine at a small tarn on the peak's northeast side, but there is very little evidence of it leaving the meadows and it is effectively abandoned: parties bushwhack along its rough line, picking up occasional cairns and cut logs, and the tread only firms up nearer the tarn. Expect the trail to peter out past the campsites and the going to become a matter of climbing over, around and under downed timber. Keep above the lake below the ridge rather than dropping to it. The north side can also be entered from the North Creek valley on the far side of the range, but that way is undescribed, so the marks below are written for this approach rather than that one.
approach_variants.season: The upper slopes face south and are normally clear from about early July. Earlier in the season, firmer snow makes the loose upper talus easier to travel at the cost of carrying an axe and crampons.
hazards: The mapped trail is abandoned and largely invisible leaving the meadows
Heavy deadfall low down, with long stretches of climbing over and under log jams
No maintained tread and no reliable cairns; the boot path that does exist is short and intermittent
Loose class 2 and 3 boulders and scree on the crest, with route choice left entirely to the party
Water is limited to the stream near the tarn — nothing dependable above it
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE DRIED-UP TARN WITH CABIN REMNANTS IS THE PROOF, AND THE OLD MINE ON THE CREST CONFIRMS IT. Working west from the meadows, the tread becomes distinct only as you near a small dried-up tarn on the peak's northeast side, known to some as Nasty Pond. Beside it are the remnants of a small cabin and an old pot sitting on a fire pit. That wreckage is the marker — there is no sign, no cairn at the turn, and no maintained trail — and a good stream just below it is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge rising directly to the main north ridge; expect a few class 3 moves on it. Once on the crest you pick up a short stretch of boot path running through old mining evidence, with metal cables and other equipment lying on the rocks, and that hardware is the confirmation you are on the historic line rather than a game trail. The path disappears past the mine and the rest is pick-your-own-line class 2 and 3 through boulders and scree to the top. Coming down, the scree slope back to the pond is generally preferred over reversing the spur ridge.

backups.overview: The Southeast Ridge of Argonaut gives a longer and slightly more technical line to the summit than the northeast ridge, climbing the rocky crest over a series of steps and towers on excellent Stuart Range granite. With sustained moderate climbing, real exposure, and a remote setting, it rewards parties willing to make the long approach into this quieter corner of the range. Route-finding among the towers is part of the challenge and the fun.
backups.beta: Climbs the southeast ridge in about eight pitches up to 5.6 to the southeast spire, a false summit and the lowest of Argonaut's three summits, then carries on to the true summit on the west spire. The lower pitches are blocky and awkward, carry a lot of lichen and are somewhat hard to protect. The line includes two single-rope rappels, or one double-rope rappel, into the notch. The main summit needs a short, non-exposed Class 4 move to its highest block after Class 3 ridge traversing. The Colchuck Col side is the better way to the base; the Ingalls Creek side means a long, strenuous bushwhack.
backups.turnaround: With the long approach and a multi-step ridge, fix a turnaround in the early afternoon. If you are behind schedule among the towers, the safest decision is often to rappel and retreat rather than push into deteriorating weather.
backups.rappels: Two single-rope rappels, or one double-rope rappel, back into the notch
backups.permit: Free self-issued USFS wilderness permit at the trailhead — no quota, no lottery. This Teanaway-side (Beverly Creek/Ingalls Creek) approach lies outside the Enchantment Permit Area, whose zones are reached from the Icicle Creek side.
backups.comms: No reliable cell service. Satellite communication essential for emergencies (Iridium phone or iPhone 14+ satellite messaging).
backups.descent: Reverse the ridge with rappels, or descend toward the basin and approach drainage.
obj_haz: Lichen-covered, hard-to-protect blocky rock on the lower pitches
Long, strenuous bushwhack on the Ingalls Creek approach option
Route-finding between the SE spire (false summit) and the true summit

backups.detailed_rack: Single set of nuts and cams from finger-size through ~3in covers the ridge's crack and corner systems; nothing larger is reported as needed. Rappel anchors are natural (slung horns, blocks, small trees), so bring cordelette/webbing to back up or replace tat if worn.

light rock rack rather than a heavy trad rack

Sling horns to protect and move fast over the crest.
Pre-plan rappel stations for a quick retreat.
Watch the sky; the ridge is fully exposed.

backups.pro_needs: Protection is moderate and intermittent on 4th-to-low-5th ridge terrain; parties report finding rappel anchors along the ridge as hoped, implying stations are already equipped and spaced for single-strand rope lengths. A distinct winter/mixed variant (East Ridge to a crossover into the NE Couloir) exists and is far more serious, requiring rock pro placed to protect wind-slab traverses plus ice tools/crampons — that is NOT the standard 5.6 summer rock route and should not be conflated with it.
backups.approach: Start at the Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112 (roughly 3,650 ft). At about 0.5 mile, bear left onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike/Beverly Creek Trail) — do not miss this junction, as a wrong-fork error onto the Bean Creek Trail is a commonly reported mistake. Continue to roughly 3.1 miles and turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek Trail), climbing to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles (roughly 5,900-6,000 ft), which opens up the first real views of Argonaut, Colchuck, and Dragontail. From the pass, descend the well-maintained trail on the far side to the south shore of Ingalls Creek at about 6 miles (roughly 4,200-4,250 ft); ford the creek (wading or a footlog depending on the season/year) to reach flat camping at the Fourth Creek/Ingalls Creek confluence. From camp, leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb generally north into the gentle, heather-and-slab Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side, working up open basin terrain toward the broad saddle between Argonaut and Colchuck (the Argonaut-Colchuck col, about 7,700 ft), which most parties use to access the upper East Ridge. From the basin/col area, angle up snow or blocky rock to a notch on the ridge crest just west of a distinctive lone gendarme — this notch is where the roped, belayed climbing on the East Ridge (6 pitches) begins. Hazards: the Ingalls Creek ford can be a real obstacle in early season or after rain; the basin approach involves loose talus and, in shoulder season, hard snow that may warrant an axe and crampons; this is a long, remote approach (partial day just to reach the base) so plan for a car-camp or bivy.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the East Ridge: downclimb and scramble back through the gendarme and knife-edge sections to the notch just west of the lone gendarme where the roped climbing began. From the notch, parties either make two single-rope rappels or one longer double-rope rappel (two ropes tied together, or twin/half ropes) down steep snow to the glacier/snow slopes below rather than downclimbing the exposed step -- both are standard, established options, not just one. Anchors on this route are natural — slung horns, blocks, or small trees — supplemented by whatever tat/fixed slings a prior party left; there is no bolted station, so carry extra webcord and be ready to build or back up an anchor. Once down to the snow/talus below the notch, downclimb into the basin and reverse the long approach: back down through Porcupine Creek basin, re-ford Ingalls Creek, and climb back out over Fourth Creek Pass to the trailhead. Given the length of this descent, start it with a comfortable margin of daylight.
backups.bail: The ridge can be retreated from with rappels off horns and blocks at several points, giving a reasonable escape if weather turns, though the long walk out remains a constant.

pitch_detail.notes: From the Argonaut-Colchuck col (~7,700ft) gain the east ridge crest over low-angle blocks and broken granite steps, easing into the climb before the terrain steepens.
Surmount a compact, steeper granite tower via face moves and thin gear placements; this is the route's technical crux and the most sustained pitch on the ridge.
Weave over and around a series of towers along the crest, alternating short exposed steps with easier ledge traverses; belay from a horn where the ridge narrows.
Moderate climbing and scrambling up blocky granite toward the upper mountain, with route-finding between minor gendarmes rather than sustained difficulty.
Continue past another gendarme on the upper ridge, staying near the crest on exposed but moderate granite before the angle relents toward the summit spires.
Class 3-4 ridge traverse to the base of the summit block, finishing with a short nonexposed scramble past the block's small cave feature to the true summit.

itinerary.cal: Ingalls Creek must be forded (no bridge) and the approach trail is brushy into early summer — most parties go July-September once the creek drops and snow gullies consolidate.

days.note: From the Beverly Creek/Ingalls Creek trailhead system, hike and ford Ingalls Creek, then climb steep, vegetated slopes toward the basin below Argonaut and the Colchuck-Argonaut col. Expect real bushwhacking and slow going in the upper section.

access.fees: Free — no fee for a day climb or an overnight camp here; this approach (Ingalls Creek Trail or Longs Pass/Ingalls Way from the Teanaway) sits entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area lottery boundary, so the paid Enchantments lottery ($6 application + $5/person/night) does not apply.
access.notes: Do not confuse this approach with the actual Enchantment Permit Area lottery (Stuart/Colchuck/Snow Lakes/Eightmile/Core zones, reached via the Stuart Lake or Snow Lakes trailheads) — Argonaut Peak's standard approaches are separate, non-quota Alpine Lakes Wilderness trailheads.
access.rules: Standard USFS Alpine Lakes Wilderness group-size limit of 12 (people + stock). Bear-resistant food storage mandatory forest-wide.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead — no lottery, no reservation needed, even for an overnight camp.
access.closures: Beverly Creek/Fourth Creek Pass (FR-9737-112, Beverly Turnpike Trailhead) and several nearby Teanaway trails (Longs Pass, Ingalls Way, Standup Creek, etc.) were closed under a USFS order effective May 20-Dec 31, 2026 following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — confirm current status with the Cle Elum Ranger District before planning a Teanaway-side approach.

fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/bivy pack weight for the approach, plus a full trad rack, rope, and rock shoes for 6 pitches of climbing

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long: multi-hour trailhead approach to a basin camp, then ~2 hrs from bivy to the east end of the ridge; nearly always done as a 2-day trip with a bivy
requiredSkills: Confident 5.6 trad leading with gear placements on somewhat loose rock
Efficient multi-pitch systems (belay transitions, rope management) to keep an 8-pitch day moving
Route-finding among towers on an undefined ridge crest
Rappelling / downclimbing competence for the descent
Self-sufficiency in remote, no-cell-service terrain with no easy bail options
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Solid alpine rock climber — this is a full Grade II, 5.6, 8-pitch outing requiring genuine multi-pitch trad experience, not just scrambling

July.reason: Early-month snow can still linger on the approach and lower ridge; conditions firm up to the best-season window by mid-month

August.reason: Peak dry-granite conditions ('best with dry granite and a melted-out approach')

September.reason: Stable, cool weather, but shorter days add pressure to a route already timed at ~10 hours round trip from bivy

weather.typical: Warm, dry summer alpine weather once the route is in season
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a recurring hazard here, and this route's fully exposed open ridge and longer 6-pitch climbing time raise the stakes of getting caught out

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High: sustained exposure across 6 pitches of moderate 5.6 climbing over towers with real fall consequences, compounded by loose rock on the towers and complex route-finding in terrain with no quick retreat and no cell coverage

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer rock route (the area falls within NWAC's Cascade East Central zone, but that zone's forecasts run in winter, not during this route's July-September season)

gaps: Corrected 2026-07-15: previously named 'East Ridge' at Grade III/6 pitches with no corroborating source; renamed to the real, documented Southeast Ridge route (Grade II, 5.6, 8 pitches) per Mountaineers.org and SummitPost. The record's own itinerary.sourceNote cited 'SummitPost Argonaut Peak route page (East Ridge descent/rappel notes)' — but SummitPost has no East Ridge entry, only Southeast Ridge, confirming this was a mislabeling of real Southeast Ridge research.

Pitch-by-pitch breakdown for pitches 7-8 (to reach the sourced 8-pitch count) not found in any available source; existing 6-pitch breakdown may need renumbering/expansion once a topo or trip report with pitch-level detail is located.
Route tops out on the SE spire (a false summit) before continuing to the true summit — a real, distinctive feature worth confirming is reflected in the overview.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112 (~3,650 ft) off the North Fork Teanaway River Road, via Trail #1391 up Beverly Creek

backups.rope_note: Descent (and the standard connector use of this ridge) is done via established single-strand rappel stations — trip reports repeatedly describe finding rap anchors on the ridge and executing single-rope raps, not full-length double-rope raps. A single 60m rope is standard; double ropes are only clearly justified for the harder winter East Ridge/NE Couloir mixed variant, not the summer 5.6 rock route.
backups.corrections: If the prior auto-generated text implied a double/half-rope requirement or a large rack, that overstates it: real trip reports (NW Arete descents via this ridge, a 2024 winter TR) consistently describe single-strand rappels off pre-existing stations and a light-to-moderate rack (nuts, cams to ~3in). No source supports needing doubled ropes for the standard summer ascent/descent.

rappel_detail.notes: First rappel down steep terrain toward the snow/talus below the notch, off a pre-placed sling on a rock.
Second rappel from a small tree, continuing down to the snow slopes; parties then traverse a snow-covered ledge toward the east gully.

backups.rappel_count_note: Reported as two 30 m rappels, off a slung rock and a small tree. A count of four rappels belongs to a different descent line and does not apply to this one.

approach_variants.name: Beverly Turnpike TH over Fourth Creek Pass to Porcupine Creek basin
approach_variants.notes:
Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112, around 3,650 ft. At about half a mile bear LEFT onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike / Beverly Creek). Taking the Bean Creek fork instead is the commonly reported error and costs a lot of the day.

At roughly 3.1 miles turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek) and climb to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles and 5,900-6,000 ft, which opens the first real view of Argonaut, Colchuck and Dragontail. Descend the far side to the south bank of Ingalls Creek at about six miles and 4,200-4,250 ft, and ford — wading or a footlog depending on the season. Flat camping at the Fourth Creek / Ingalls Creek confluence.

From there leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb north into the Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side: gentle heather and slab, open basin travel, working up toward the broad saddle between Argonaut and Colchuck at about 7,700 ft. Porcupine Creek basin also holds bivy sites.

Be aware this whole Teanaway-side trail network has been under a Forest Service closure order following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — confirm current status with the Cle Elum Ranger District before planning on it.

Note this trailhead is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area lottery boundary: a free self-issue wilderness permit covers you, even for an overnight.
hazards: Wrong-fork error onto Bean Creek Trail near the start
Ingalls Creek ford is a genuine obstacle in early season or after rain
Loose talus in the basin; hard snow in shoulder season warranting axe and crampons
Long, remote approach — a partial day just to reach the base, so plan a car-camp or bivy
Teanaway-side trail closures following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — verify before committing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the roped climbing is a NOTCH on the ridge crest, and the feature that identifies it is a single conspicuous GENDARME standing alone on the ridge. The notch you want is immediately WEST of that lone gendarme. Not east of it, not the next notch along — west, with the gendarme on your east side as you stand in it.

Getting there: from the Porcupine Creek basin or the Argonaut-Colchuck col area at about 7,700 ft, angle up snow or blocky rock to gain the crest. The southeast ridge can be crossed lower at a notch around 6,750 ft, so a notch on its own does not tell you much — the gendarme does.

In cloud, work the crest until you meet a free-standing tower, then take the gap on its west side. If you are already on knife-edge ground with exposure, you have gone past the start and are on the route.

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
bivy.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
bivy.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

bivy.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
bivy.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
bivy.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

backups.name: Southwest Ridge (Hemlock Pass)
backups.fa: 1926 - Anderson, Best, Maxwell, Shorrock, West, Wunderling (first ascent of Bryant Peak)
hazards: loose scree
lingering snow early season
loose, exposed summit block with rockfall from parties above
backups.overview: Bryant Peak (5,801 ft) sits on the ridge between Chair Peak and The Tooth above the Source Lake and Snow Lake basins in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, about 0.65 miles southeast of Chair Peak. Originally named Hemlock Peak, it was renamed in 1925 for Sidney V. Bryant; the peak was first climbed in 1926. It's a popular, moderate scramble often paired with Chair Peak and/or The Tooth on the Alpental skyline traverse. The standard summer line comes up the southwest side from Hemlock Pass, reached by the Denny Creek trail, and is often paired with nearby Hemlock Peak.
backups.beta: From Hemlock Pass the route follows the ridgeline toward Bryant Peak, angling right behind trees to a brushy notch, then climbs roughly 170 ft to a meadow at the base of a talus slope that covers about three-quarters of the peak's base. The final scramble goes up rock on the left (or, when snow-free, around the exposed north side) to the summit; the rock is loose and helmets are recommended.
backups.turnaround: Turn around with enough daylight and margin to reverse the loose, exposed summit scramble before deteriorating weather, wet rock, or fatigue increase fall and rockfall risk.
backups.comms: No confirmed cell coverage data found for this specific route; the broader Snoqualmie Pass/I-90 corridor has patchy but sometimes usable cell signal on ridges and summits, unreliable in valleys and basins.
obj_haz: avalanche

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead (I-90 Exit 52)
waypoints.note: The Denny Creek Trail -> Hemlock Pass -> ridge -> SE talus field approach is the one used for this Southeast Slopes route.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 to Exit 52, then follow Alpental Road to its end. Park at the Alpental day-use trailhead, at roughly 3,100 to 3,120 feet.

waypoints.name: Source Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Signed junction on Snow Lake Trail #1013; leave the main trail here and head toward Source Lake basin.

waypoints.name: Source Lake basin stream crossing
waypoints.note: Climbers' path fords the outlet stream draining Source Lake basin around 4,100 ft; last reliable water before the ascent gully, cairns mark the crossing.

waypoints.name: Gully 'secret passage' below the cliffs
waypoints.note: An easy-to-miss rock passage at ~4,780 ft where the route leaves the open streambed gully and climbs NE along cliff bands into the upper basin.

waypoints.name: Thumbtack (rock tower), upper basin
waypoints.note: Prominent free-standing rock tower marking the talus basin between Bryant and Chair Peak; from here the route corkscrews southwest toward the Bryant-Chair gully.

waypoints.name: Bryant-Chair Peak gully / talus shoulder
waypoints.note: Steep, loose gully between the two peaks gains a talus shoulder on Bryant's ridge; helmets recommended, rockfall risk from parties above.

waypoints.name: Summit block traverse
waypoints.note: Route stays left (south) of the talus field and traverses the south side of the west shoulder before the final scramble; exposed with loose rock, though holds are generally good.

sectionBreakdown.note: This is done in a single long day car-to-car — no camping. Hike the Denny Creek Trail to Hemlock Pass, then follow the ridge and talus slopes on the standard route to the class 2-3…

what_to_bring: helmet (loose rock on the summit block)
pro_tips: Often part of a skyline traverse
Pair with Chair Peak or the Tooth
Nearby Hemlock Peak is a short add-on from the same ridge
A quieter NE/east line goes from Source Lake through Great Scott Basin to Bryant Col
watch_out: loose footing
snow early season
the first high point on the summit block may be a false summit — a short exposed traverse is needed to reach the true top
backups.best_season: Late July through September — the gully and upper slopes often hold snow into July. A separate, more technical winter/early-season ascent (ice axe and crampons required, significant avalanche hazard) is popular but distinct from the summer scramble.
backups.approach: From I-90 Exit 47, take Denny Creek Road (FR 58) about 3 miles, past Denny Creek Campground, then turn left onto FR 5830 to the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft). Follow the Denny Creek Trail (#1014, the Melakwa Lake trail) up the valley past waterfalls, then up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft above the car. At the crest of the pass turn right and follow the ridge on a bearing of about 33°, skirting cliff bands mainly on the left, to a plateau and meadow on the ridge. Early in the season, while snow still covers the brush, a brushy notch behind trees on the right leads about 170 ft up and then northeast to a meadow at the foot of the talus field that wraps about three-quarters of the peak's base; later in the season that line is choked with brush, so stay on the ridge and go straight up it to the summit block. The final scramble is loose rock on the left, or when snow-free around the exposed north side; helmets are recommended. The round trip is about 9 miles with roughly 3,600 ft of gain for Bryant alone; adding nearby Hemlock Peak makes it about 9.5 miles and 3,900 ft.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappels and no fixed anchors. Reverse the ascent: downclimb the loose Class 3 summit block carefully, facing in where it is steep, then return across the talus and down the ridge to Hemlock Pass, keeping to the ascent line around the cliff bands rather than cutting down the fall line. From the pass, follow the Denny Creek Trail back down to the trailhead. The steep gully between Bryant and Chair Peak on the Source Lake side is a separate line and an avalanche path in winter and spring; it is not a descent from this route.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward on this route: reverse course down the talus to Hemlock Pass and the Denny Creek Trail at essentially any point below the final summit rock step.

itinerary.cal: Best late June through September once the Denny Creek Trail and upper snowfields have melted out; earlier-season ascents involve more snow travel and require an ice axe.

days.note: This is done in a single long day car-to-car — no camping. Hike the Denny Creek Trail to Hemlock Pass, then follow the ridge and talus slopes on the standard route to the class 2-3 summit block, and reverse the same line to descend. Helmets recommended for loose rock and minor exposure near the top.
days.title: Car-to-car scramble

schedule.label: Leave Denny Creek Trailhead
schedule.detail: Start at ~2,300 ft; trailhead lot fills early on summer weekends.

schedule.label: Reach Hemlock Pass
schedule.detail: About 4 miles up Denny Creek Trail No. 1014, gaining roughly 2,300 ft.

schedule.label: Base of the summit talus field
schedule.detail: From the pass, follow the ridge on a 33° bearing, skirting cliff bands, to the meadow below Bryant's talus slopes.

schedule.label: Summit Bryant Peak
schedule.detail: Final class 2-3 scramble, typically around the north side of the summit block; rock is loose.

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Reverse the ascent line back through the talus, ridge, and Hemlock Pass.

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Most parties finish the full round trip in 8-10 hours car-to-car.

days.objective: Summit Bryant Peak via Denny Creek Trail and Hemlock Pass, then return

itinerary.totalNote: A single long day car-to-car: about 9 miles round trip with roughly 3,600 ft of gain/loss for Bryant alone (about 9.5 miles and 3,900 ft with Hemlock Peak added), typically 8-10 hours total; no camping involved.

access.fees: $5/day or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass; America the Beautiful/Interagency passes are also accepted.
access.notes: Climbable roughly June–October; heavy winter snowfall and frequent avalanche control closures on I-90 affect access the rest of the year.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; wilderness group-size limits apply
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk (fill out, carry your copy, deposit the stub) — no quota or advance reservation required here (unlike the Enchantments core).
access.landManager: Alpine Lakes Wilderness (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest)
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Snoqualmie Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass ($30/yr) or America the Beautiful pass, or a $5/day pass at developed trailheads.

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry it with you.

road.name: Denny Creek Road (FR 58) and FR 5830
road.driveNote: From I-90 Exit 47, take Denny Creek Road (FR 58) about 3 miles, past Denny Creek Campground, then turn left onto FR 5830 and continue to the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft). The lot fills early on summer weekends — arrive before mid-morning.

climate.typical: Wet maritime climate; clearest mid- to late summer.

emergency.notes: Popular, heavily trafficked trailhead; cell coverage is spotty on the ridge and summit block — a satellite messenger/SOS device is worth carrying.
emergency.rangerStation: Snoqualmie Ranger District – North Bend Office, 902 SE North Bend Way, Bldg 1, North Bend, WA 98045; (425) 888-1421 (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest)
emergency.nearestHospital: Snoqualmie Valley Hospital, 9801 Frontier Ave SE, Snoqualmie, WA — a Level 5 (rural critical-access) trauma center roughly 20 minutes from the trailhead; more serious trauma is typically transferred to Harborview Medical Center in Seattle.

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends in August, especially when linked into the Chair Peak-Tooth skyline traverse; Mountaineers scramble course outings add periodic weekday/weekend groups
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Roughly 15-30 parties per season - a moderate-traffic Snoqualmie Pass scramble, busier than a remote alpine objective but well below trade routes like Mount Si or Granite Mountain

fitnessSpec.hiking: Sustained off-trail alpine approach with meaningful elevation gain over rugged talus and heather - solid aerobic fitness needed
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day pack (helmet, layers, water, basic first aid) - no technical rack required for the standard line

partner_requirements.approachTime: Full day out of the Denny Creek trailhead: about 4 miles of trail to Hemlock Pass, then off-trail ridge and talus to the summit
requiredSkills: Class 2-3 scrambling and routefinding on scree/talus
loose-rock hazard awareness (helmet recommended)
basic navigation off-trail
comfort with early-season snow if climbing at the shoulder of the July window
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Comfortable on off-trail Class 2-3 terrain with loose rock; prior scrambling experience recommended before attempting the summit block

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August is the core optimal month, with the Mid-July through September window giving a reliable dry-scramble margin either side

July.reason: Season opens mid-July; early-month climbs can still encounter residual snow patches before the route fully melts out

June.reason: Lingering snow on approach and summit slopes; not within the documented season

August.reason: In season - driest, most stable conditions in a Best summer

September.reason: Fall is a Good window; scree and rock are dry, though days shorten and early snow becomes possible late in the month

weather.typical: Wet maritime pattern - summer offers the best stability but conditions can turn quickly
weather.probability: Afternoon convective buildups are common in the Cascades in July-August; check a point forecast before committing to the summit block

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Class 2-3 exposure with loose scree underfoot; the final summit block is the main fall-exposure crux, with rockfall/footing hazard more significant than sustained cliff exposure. Snow lingering into early season adds slip/postholing risk before full melt-out

avalanche.zone: Snoqualmie Pass (NWAC forecast zone) - used as the nearest regional proxy; this route is climbed dry-season and is not typically avalanche-forecasted

gaps: Elevation/prominence for Bryant Peak varies by source (elevation 5,790–5,801 ft; prominence roughly 321–346 ft) — no single authoritative survey confirmed, so area figures were left unchanged.

No confirmed technical/scramble class rating from a published guidebook (e.g. Beckey's Cascade Alpine Guide) was found; Class 2-3 reflects online trip-report/Mountaineers consensus, not a verified guidebook grade.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead (~3,100 ft), at the end of Alpental Road off I-90 Exit 52

backups.rope_note: Class 2-3 scramble via Hemlock Pass with talus and a rock scramble finish; some exposure and rockfall potential (helmet recommended) but no rope used in trip reports.
backups.corrections: None — reconfirmed via SummitPost, Mountaineers, and WTA sources.

approach_variants.name: Denny Creek Trail to Hemlock Pass, then the ridge
approach_variants.notes: The standard summer approach. From the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft), reached from I-90 Exit 47 by Denny Creek Road and FR 5830, follow the Denny Creek Trail #1014 toward Melakwa Lake past waterfalls and up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft of gain. Leave the trail at the pass for the ridge on the right.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September for a dry scramble; earlier the ridge and talus hold snow and an axe is needed
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall on the summit block
Lingering snow on the ridge and talus early in the season
Brush in the notch below the talus once the snow has gone
Exposure on the north side of the summit block
approach_variants.baseFinding: HEMLOCK PASS IS WHERE THE TRAIL STOPS CLIMBING. At its crest, before the trail drops toward Melakwa Lake, turn right onto the ridge and hold a bearing of about 33°, skirting the cliff bands mainly on their left. The check that you are on line is a plateau and meadow on the ridge, then a talus field wrapping most of the peak's base with the summit block above. Negative marker: if you are descending toward a lake, you stayed on the trail past the pass.

approach_variants.name: Alpental, Source Lake and Great Scott Basin to the Bryant-Chair gully
approach_variants.notes: A steeper alternative from the Alpental side, better known as a winter and spring snow climb than as a summer scramble. From the Alpental day-use trailhead at about 3,120 ft, take the Snow Lake Trail #1013 through old avalanche brush and second growth. At roughly 1.8 miles and 720 ft of gain, a boot path splits LEFT (southwest) toward Source Lake while the main trail continues right toward Snow Lake Col. Drop briefly to cross Source Lake's outlet creek — the last dependable water — and follow the use trail along the lake's north and east shore into the open basin below The Tooth and Chair Peak. From there the tread becomes intermittent boot-track over boulders and heather benches, climbing southwest into Great Scott Basin under The Tooth's east face. Contour left (south) beneath the broken cliff bands on Bryant's east side and cross a talus field to the foot of the gully.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July to September once the gully has melted out; earlier the gully holds snow and needs an axe and crampons
hazards: The gully is an active avalanche path in winter and spring; avoid it in unstable snow or soon after a storm
Loose scree, with the centre and left of the gully markedly worse than the right
The gully funnels rockfall from parties above
Lingering early-season snow, requiring axe and crampons
Exposed and loose class 3 on the north side of the summit block when the block is dry
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE THUMBTACK IS THE LANDMARK YOU WALK PAST, AND THE GULLY IS THE ONE IMMEDIATELY BEYOND IT. Contouring south beneath Bryant's east side you cross a talus field below the rock spire known locally as the Thumbtack. The mouth of the route's gully is at the far side of that talus. Spire behind you, steep scree-and-talus gully splitting the face in front of you.

WHAT THE GULLY IS, IN OTHER WORDS: this is the same drainage backcountry skiers call the Bryant Couloir or the wonder gully. If your winter partner knows the ski line, they know the route.

THE FOOTING TEST TELLS YOU WHERE TO BE WITHIN IT: climb favouring the FAR CLIMBERS' RIGHT side of the gully, which is noticeably firmer than the loose centre and left. A party grinding up loose ground in the middle is in the correct gully and in the wrong part of it.

WHERE IT DELIVERS YOU: the gully tops out on the BRYANT-CHAIR CONNECTING RIDGE, not on a summit. From there you work SOUTH over blocky ridge and talus to the base of the summit block. A gully that finishes on a summit is not this one.

AND THE LAST STEP CHANGES CHARACTER WITH THE SNOW, which is worth knowing before you commit: with snow on the block the final scramble is easy class 3 with little real exposure. Dry, the only reasonable line goes round the NORTH — climbers' left — side on exposed and distinctly loose class 3. Test every hold.

climbing_route.label: Ridge from Hemlock Pass
climbing_route.notes: From the crest of Hemlock Pass turn right and follow the ridge on a bearing of about 33°, skirting cliff bands mainly on the left, to a plateau and meadow on the ridge. Early in the season a brushy notch behind trees on the right leads about 170 ft up and then northeast to a meadow; once the snow is gone that notch is choked with brush, so stay on the ridge.

climbing_route.label: Talus to the summit block
climbing_route.notes: A talus field wraps about three-quarters of the peak's base; cross it, or follow the ridge above the plateau, to the base of the summit block.

climbing_route.label: Summit block
climbing_route.notes: Scramble up loose rock on the left, or when snow-free around the exposed north side. The first high point may be a false summit, with a short exposed traverse to the true top. Loose holds and rockfall are the main hazard; helmets recommended. Summit 5,801 ft.

backups.name: West Ridge / Walrus Glacier
hazards: Walrus Glacier crevasses
loose summit rock
long approach
backups.overview: Clark Mountain (8,602 ft) is the highest summit of the Dakobed Range, rising about 8 miles southeast of Glacier Peak at the head of the Boulder Creek/White River, Napeequa, and Chiwawa drainages within the Glacier Peak Wilderness. The mountain's south and west sides are open, rugged scree and heather slopes, while its glaciated north and east flanks carry the small Clark (Walrus) Glacier and the Richardson Glacier. Luahna Peak, about a mile northwest along the connecting ridge, is a common add-on for strong parties. Two standard lines are climbed: a non-glacier scree/Class 3 scramble up the south side, and the more scenic Walrus Glacier route approached from Boulder Pass, often called one of the most esthetic non-technical glacier climbs in the eastern Cascades.
backups.beta: Most parties camp at Boulder Basin and climb Clark as a two-day (sometimes three-day) trip. From camp, drop over Boulder Pass to a bench on Clark's eastern arm, gain the Walrus Glacier, and ascend a moderately steep chute on the glacier's left (south) margin, stepping over narrow crevasses and crossing at least one snow-bridge, to a short summit scramble. A glacier-free alternative (the 'Southeast Route') avoids the glacier via a gully out of the south basin but is not the line documented here.
backups.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before committing to the glacier chute — softening snow bridges over crevasses later in the day, deteriorating visibility/flat light (both reported as common on this glacier), and a rising afternoon flow at the unbridged Boulder Creek ford all argue for an early start and a conservative decision to retreat if conditions or weather sour.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at many trailheads.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage is reported in Boulder Basin or on Clark Mountain itself; the remoteness of the Glacier Peak Wilderness and the multi-day nature of the approach make a satellite communicator (e.g., inReach) advisable — Chelan County Sheriff's Office/SAR has responded to inReach-triggered rescues in this general area.
backups.descent: Reverse the south-side scree/Class 3 route, or reverse the Boulder Pass/Walrus Glacier line while the glacier is still firm; parties continuing on to Luahna Peak descend Clark's west side via a steep, loose ('choss'-filled) gully rather than returning the same way.
obj_haz: crevasses on the Walrus/Clark Glacier
unbridged, multi-channel ford of Boulder Creek
loose rock on the summit scramble
route-finding in flat light/low cloud
fresh-snow-covered crevasses early season

waypoints.name: White River Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 6400 past Coles Corner/WA-207; $5 day-use fee or NW Forest Pass, self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk, vault toilet, no potable water.
waypoints.directions: From US-2 at Coles Corner take WA-207 about ten miles up past Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road / FS-6400 another ten miles to the road end. Pavement gives out partway along; the gravel that follows is rough but not rutted, and the trailhead has a large gravelled lot shared with the Indian Creek, Mount David and PCT approaches.

waypoints.name: Boulder Creek Trail #1562 junction
waypoints.note: White River Trail's first 4 miles are flat, brushy, and often overgrown; bear right (east) off White River Trail #1507 onto the unmaintained Boulder Creek Trail #1562.
waypoints.directions: Head south on White River Trail #1507 along the valley floor. Four miles of nearly flat walking with almost no gain, brushy in places and notoriously mosquito-heavy from early to mid summer. Bear right (east) at the junction onto Boulder Creek Trail #1562, which is unmaintained above this point.

waypoints.name: Boulder Creek ford
waypoints.note: Unbridged, knee-to-thigh-deep crossing at the top of Boulder Basin depending on snowmelt; swap to sandals, current is swift early season.
waypoints.directions: Boulder Creek Trail climbs steadily through forest for about four and a half miles into Boulder Creek Basin. The creek is unbridged and must be forded; early in the season it runs cold and knee- to thigh-deep and often braids into two or three separate channels, which is easier to read but wetter than a single crossing. Sandals are worth carrying for it.

waypoints.name: Boulder Basin camp
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp used as the standard base for a Clark summit day; the unmaintained climbers' path to Boulder Pass/Walrus Glacier splits off climbers-left just past the campsites and can vanish into brush.
waypoints.directions: A short walk past the ford puts you in the open basin, where established camps are spread between roughly 4,900 and 5,300 ft — around 8.5 miles and 3,000 ft from the car. Water is reliable here and essentially absent above it, so this is where you fill for the summit day. Given the scale of the outing most parties base here rather than attempt it car-to-car.

waypoints.name: Boulder Pass
waypoints.note: Scenic saddle with airy views over both the White and Napeequa drainages; the non-glacier south-side scramble and the Walrus Glacier line to the summit diverge from here.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at camp and climb open heather and talus north toward the pass, picking up the climbers' path that breaks off climbers-left just past the campsites. It is a direct fall-line push and takes most parties around an hour and a half. Slopes in the basin below the pass hold wet-slide avalanche debris into early summer.

waypoints.name: Walrus (Clark) Glacier rope-up / crevasse zone
waypoints.note: Rope up here east of Boulder Pass before stepping onto the ~0.3 sq mi Walrus Glacier; stay on the left (south) margin, several narrow crevasses and one large crevasse crossed on a snowbridge.
waypoints.directions: Drop over the far side of the pass on steep snow to a bench around 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm, then traverse east across the basin beneath Peak 7242, crossing its northeast ridge at about that same height. Turn back west from there, roughly half an hour, to the toe of the glacier — it is labelled Clark Glacier on some maps. Rope up here with crampons and axe: the non-glacier south-side line diverges back at the pass, so stepping onto the ice is the committing choice.

waypoints.name: Clark Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit of the Dakobed Range's high point, 8 mi southeast of Glacier Peak; final approach is a short scramble over summit rocks above the glacier or south-side scree.
waypoints.directions: Take the moderately steep chute on the glacier's left (south) margin, stepping over several narrow crevasses and crossing one larger one on a snow bridge whose condition changes through the season and through the day. Above the ice a short Class 3 scramble over the summit rocks, with a soft 45-50 degree snow traverse below the top, gains the true summit.

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed; this is a glacier scramble rather than a roped rock climb. Bring a standard glacier-travel kit — ice axe, crampons, a rope for the team, and a basic crevasse-rescue rack (a few ice screws, prusik cords or mechanical ascenders, a pulley, and slings/carabiners) for the Walrus Glacier crossing, where narrow crevasses and at least one snow-bridge are typically encountered.
what_to_bring: trekking poles for Boulder Creek fords
pro_tips: Carry glacier gear for the Walrus/Clark Glacier crossing and rope up around 6,700-7,000 ft on its northeast side
Cross the glacier early in the day while snow bridges are firm
Camp at Boulder Basin or Boulder Pass to shorten summit day given the long approach
Ford Boulder Creek earlier in the day before afternoon snowmelt raises its flow
watch_out: hidden crevasses on the Walrus/Clark Glacier
loose rock and choss on the south ridge and the west gully used toward Luahna Peak
cold, swift, sometimes thigh-deep Boulder Creek crossings
exposed summit block in afternoon thunderstorms
backups.pro_needs: Glacier-travel and crevasse-rescue gear rather than rock protection: a rope, crevasse-rescue hardware, ice axe, and crampons for the glacier chute. No fixed or removable rock protection is typically placed on the Class 3 scrambling sections above the glacier.
backups.approach: Start at the White River Trailhead (~2,300 ft, end of White River Road/FR-6400). Follow White River Trail #1507 south along the flat valley floor for about 4 miles - easy grade but notoriously buggy/mosquito-heavy in early-to-mid summer - to its junction with Boulder Creek Trail #1562. Turn onto Boulder Creek Trail and climb roughly 4.5 miles through forest into Boulder Creek Basin, fording Boulder Creek (unbridged) around 4,000 ft; in early season this crossing is cold and knee-to-thigh deep and sometimes braids into two or three separate channels. Established camps sit in the open basin between about 4,900 and 5,300 ft (roughly 8.5 miles and ~3,000 ft of gain from the car), and given the scale of this outing (~22-23 miles round trip, 6,200-6,500+ ft one-way gain to the summit) most parties treat this as a base camp rather than a car-to-car day. From camp, leave the maintained trail and climb open heather/talus north toward Boulder Pass (~6,300 ft) - a direct fall-line push from about 5,800 ft takes roughly 1.5 hours. Two lines diverge from the pass area: for the glacier line, traverse east across the basin under Peak 7242, crossing its NE ridge near 6,700 ft, then turn west (~30 min) to reach the toe of the Walrus Glacier (marked 'Clark Glacier' on some maps) and rope up for crevassed glacier travel, crampons and axe required. For the West Ridge/south-basin line, stay climber's-left, gain the south ridge of Pt. 8373 on open heather, and locate what published notes call 'the one and only easy gully' near 7,200-7,300 ft breaching the summit rock band; contour broken rock and lingering snow to the final south/west ridge and a short class 3 scramble to the summit. Water is reliable along the White River and in Boulder Creek Basin but essentially absent above camp - fill up before the push. Key hazards: the unbridged Boulder Creek ford, heavy mosquitoes on the valley approach, wet-slide/avalanche-prone slopes on the basin traverse into early summer, and genuine route-finding difficulty picking the correct gully/ridge above the basin - parties have gotten cliffed out searching for it.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line back to Boulder Creek Basin camp, then out via Boulder Creek Trail #1562 and White River Trail #1507 to the trailhead. If you climbed via the Walrus Glacier, descend the same glacier line back down to the 6,700 ft bench and over Boulder Pass, staying roped through the crevassed sections and unroping once back on stable moraine/talus below the ice. If you climbed/are descending the West Ridge or south-basin (non-glacier) line, downclimb the same class 3-4 gully and ridge terrain you ascended back to the heather slopes above camp. One specific account of this line (a Dakobed/'Tacobell' traverse trip report) describes a short, exposed step low on Clark's west side near the ridge crest where a rope for a single short rappel would be reassuring but is 'not critical for the more agile' - i.e. an optional, roughly single-pitch downclimb rather than a mandatory technical descent; no fixed/bolted anchor is reported at this spot, so a rope-down here would use a natural anchor (horn, gear, or a sling around rock). Watch for lingering wet-snow avalanche debris on the basin traverse below Boulder Pass in early/mid-summer, and re-ford Boulder Creek on the way out. This is fundamentally a long walk-off/scramble descent, not a rappel-dependent one.
backups.bail: This is a non-technical route with no fixed rappel stations, so retreat at any point is simply reversing the ascent line back down the glacier chute to Boulder Pass and out the Boulder Creek Trail. The main complication for a bail is timing the unbridged Boulder Creek ford, which rises later in the day with snowmelt.

pitch_detail.notes: White River Trail to the Boulder Creek Trail junction, about 4 miles, mostly forest.
Climb from Boulder Basin camp northeast to roughly 6,300-ft Boulder Pass, then descend steep snow on the far side to a ~6,700-ft bench on Clark's eastern arm.
Ascend a moderately steep chute on the glacier's left (south) margin, stepping over narrow crevasses and crossing a snow-bridge over one larger crevasse.
Short scramble over the summit rocks above the upper glacier snowfield to the true summit.

itinerary.cal: Boulder Creek fords and lingering snow on the glacier approach are easiest from mid-July through August; the road to White River Trailhead is normally clear by late May but the glacier itself is best climbed before it opens up too much in late summer.

days.note: From the White River Trailhead (2,300 ft), hike the White River Trail about 4 miles, then turn up the Boulder Creek/Boulder Pass Trail, fording Boulder Creek where it braids into several shallow channels. Camp in the basin anywhere from about 4,900 to 5,300 ft with a view of Clark Mountain's south side.

crowds.estimatePerSeason: unknown exact count - qualitatively 'popular' among Seattle-area alpine scramblers (a known Mountaineers club objective), but the ~23 mile round trip and remote Boulder Pass/Little Giant Pass approach filter out casual traffic; likely well under 50 total parties per season

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very high - roughly 23 miles round trip with on the order of 6,500 ft of cumulative gain; most parties split it into a 2-day overnight rather than a single push

requiredSkills: glacier travel and crevasse rescue
off-trail routefinding through brush, heather, slabs and morainal debris
basic snow travel with ice axe/crampons
Class 2-3 scrambling comfort, including loose rock near the summit

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through September, with August the most reliable month

July.reason: Only the back half of July is typically viable; earlier in the month lingering snow on the approach and less-consolidated glacier bridges are more likely in a transitional season of firm mornings

August.reason: Best window - glacier is firm in the morning and the approach is typically snow-free

September.reason: Still climbable, but crevasses opening more in fall means the reliable window narrows; watch for early-season snowfall late in the month

weather.typical: Transitional climate between the wetter Cascade crest and drier east side, with firm mornings on the glacier
weather.probability: Afternoon convective buildup/thunderstorms are common across the Cascades in August

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate - Class 2-3 scrambling with loose rock near the summit combined with glacier crossing; a fall near crevasses or on the loose summit rock could be serious, though the route lacks sustained high-angle exposure

avalanche.zone: No NWAC forecast zone precisely covers the Chiwawa/Napeequa/Glacier Peak Wilderness area; nearest reference zones are Stevens Pass and East Slopes Central, but NWAC does not issue forecasts during this route's July-September climbing season

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the White River Trailhead (~2,300 ft) at the end of White River Road / FR-6400 above Lake Wenatchee

backups.rope_type: 30-40m glacier rope (crevasse hazard), unroped for the final rock scramble
backups.rope_note: Route crosses the Walrus (Clark) Glacier before a Class 3 rock finish to the summit. Rope up for glacier travel; standard crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks) recommended. Rock finish from the ~8000' col is typically done unroped.
backups.corrections: None — glacier-crossing requirement confirmed across multiple independent trip reports (Mountaineers, Mazamas, trailcatjim).

approach_variants.name: Boulder Creek and the sheepherder's trail to the south basin — the non-glacier line
approach_variants.notes: Start at the White River trailhead at the end of White River Road, FR 6400, at about 2,300 ft; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed. Walk the White River trail #1507 about four flat miles — one party gained all of three hundred feet in a little over an hour — to the Boulder Creek trail #1562 junction. Turn east up Boulder Creek. At about the 5,000 ft level, roughly four and a half miles up this trail, pick up an old sheepherder's trail heading west and follow it to around 5,600 to 5,700 ft. Note that published mileages on this stretch do not reconcile cleanly between sources, so navigate by elevation and by the basin rather than by a mile count. There is a faint path that contours, crosses the creek and climbs the west side of Boulder Creek, firming up into decent tread as it gains the slope. Leave the sheepherder's trail in the basin above Boulder Creek around 5,700 ft and climb open heather north-north-west to the southern ridge running off Clark's south-east peak, Point 8373. Car to summit is given as about eleven and a half miles one way with roughly 6,500 ft of gain, and essentially every party camps in the Boulder Creek basin rather than trying it in a day.
hazards: Getting cliffed out on the spur while looking for a gully that is really a ledge
Unbridged Boulder Creek crossing, cold and thigh-deep early season and sometimes braided
Losing the sheepherder's trail — it is notoriously hard to find from the White River trail
Heavy mosquitoes on the valley walk
No water above the Boulder Creek basin
approach_variants.baseFinding: EVERYTHING TURNS ON ONE FEATURE AND IT IS MISDESCRIBED BY ITS OWN NAME. Published descriptions call it the one and only easy gully breaching the ridge — the way down off the spur into Clark's south basin — and it leaves the crest at about 7,200 to 7,300 ft. The correction, from a climber who found it: it is Class 2, and it FEELS MORE LIKE A SLOPING LEDGE THAN A GULLY. Parties hunting for a defined cleft walk past it and get cliffed out. Two accounts both put it at 7,200 ft and both anchor it to the south spur of Point 8373, so the elevation is the reliable half of the identification and the word gully is the unreliable half. The positional cue that puts you in the right place to look: there is a flattish section of the spur at 7,200 ft that is reached easily on scree and grass. Stand on that flat and you can see the south slope of Clark, which looks easy — and it is. The difficulty is purely in getting DOWN to it, which is what the ledge is for. Drop a couple of hundred feet down that ledge, then contour the upper south basin on broken rock and patches of permanent snow to the final south ridge and a short Class 3 scramble to the top. A note on names before you cross-reference anything: the Walrus Glacier is shown as the Clark Glacier on maps. They are one feature with two names.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Pass and the Walrus Glacier — the glacier line
approach_variants.notes:
Approach identically to Boulder Basin: White River trail #1507 four miles to the Boulder Creek trail #1562, then up into the open basin at roughly 5,300 ft, about five to six hours and three thousand feet from the car. That basin is the camp.

From camp, climb north-east to Boulder Pass at about 6,300 to 6,330 ft. Drop down steep snow on the far side, then climb to a bench at about 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm.

THE BENCH IS WHERE YOU ROPE UP. Do it there, before you go anywhere, because of what comes next.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jun-Sep, on the earlier side while the crevasses are still bridged
hazards: Crevasses and snowbridges on the lower Walrus Glacier
Steep snow on the far side of Boulder Pass
No view of the glacier until you have committed around the eastern arm
Unbridged Boulder Creek ford lower down
The 7,200 ft south-basin gully is a landmark for a different route and will mislead you here
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU CANNOT SEE THE WALRUS GLACIER UNTIL YOU ARE COMMITTED TO IT. From the 6,700 ft bench you wrap around Clark's eastern arm, and only then does the glacier come into view for the first time. That is why the bench is the roping-up point rather than the glacier's edge — there is no convenient stopping place once you are round the corner.

The entry is specific and it is not the middle of the toe: go up a moderately steep chute on the LEFT, SOUTHERN margin of the glacier. Expect to step over several narrow crevasses and, in at least one recorded year, to cross a snowbridge over a large one.

Once on the gentle upper glacier the summit wedge is visible in the distance and the navigation problem is over. The finish skirts the upper south face of that wedge on a steep snowfield and ends with a short scramble onto the summit rocks — about six hours from camp.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and this one matters because it would send you to the wrong landmark entirely: the famous one-and-only-easy-gully at 7,200 ft belongs to the SOUTH BASIN route, not to this one. If you are on the Walrus you never touch it. A published page titled for the Walrus Glacier in fact describes the south-basin line in its turn-by-turn, so read carefully which route a description is actually walking.

climbing_route.label: The one and only easy gully through the summit rock band
climbing_route.notes: Stay climber's-left and gain the south ridge of Pt. 8373 on open heather, then locate what published notes call 'the one and only easy gully' near 7,200-7,300 ft breaching the summit rock band. Genuine route-finding difficulty picking the correct gully/ridge above the basin — parties have gotten cliffed out searching for it.

climbing_route.label: Broken rock and lingering snow to the final ridge
climbing_route.notes: Contour broken rock and lingering snow to reach the final south/west ridge.

climbing_route.label: Final south/west ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: A short class 3 scramble along the final south/west ridge finishes on the summit.

bivy.name: Boulder Basin camp
Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
bivy.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

backups.name: Southwest Scramble
backups.fa: Fred Beckey and Ralph Widrig, September 20, 1948
backups.season: Late June-early October is snow-free; trips in April-June commonly need an ice axe (and sometimes snowshoes/skis) for Aasgard Pass and the upper basin
gear: crampons or microspikes for Aasgard Pass snow in June/early July
hazards: loose granite blocks and talus
route-finding among the summit's high points
afternoon thunderstorms
lingering snow on shaded benches early season
Aasgard Pass: ~2,000 ft of steep, loose scree/talus in under a mile; a serious fall/SAR hotspot
hidden meltwater channel and collapsing snow bridges on Aasgard Pass in late spring/early summer (at least one fatality reported)
backups.overview: Enchantment Peak (8,538 ft) is the granite high point of the Core Enchantments, rising on the ridge between Prusik Peak (NE) and Dragontail Peak/Aasgard Pass (SW), within the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. The peak actually has two summits about 1,500 ft apart and of nearly equal height: the NE summit is the traditionally recognized true high point — a short, fun class 3 scramble to a roughly 6x6 ft flat block — while the SW summit is a narrow ~1-ft-wide, 6-ft-long granite fin reached only by an exposed class 4 (some say low 5th class) scramble that most parties skip. The 'Southwest Scramble' route described here approaches the NE summit from the southwest via the Core basin/Aasgard Pass side, not the technical SW pinnacle.
backups.beta: From a high camp in the Core Enchantment Zone (commonly near Inspiration/Sprite/Perfection Lakes), climbers cross to Prusik Pass and work west and then up the southwest/south flank of the peak. The going is a straightforward talus/rock walk-up with occasional hands-on 2nd-to-3rd-class scrambling and no sustained technical difficulty until a short, airy 3rd-class (some parties call it 3rd/4th) summit block. The higher NE summit is a compact, flat ~6x6 ft platform; a separate, more serious SW summit lies about 1,500 ft away and involves sustained 4th-class-to-low-5th climbing on a narrow fin — most parties do not attempt it.
backups.turnaround: The route is short, so weather rather than difficulty sets the schedule. Aim to be off the open upper slopes before afternoon storms build, which they often do over the Enchantments on summer afternoons.
backups.rock_grade: Class 2-3, with a short, loose 3rd-class gully below the summit plateau (an exposed 4th-class (some say low 5th) option exists onto the more exposed SW sub-summit but is not required for the true high point)
backups.face: Southwest ridge/plateau above Aasgard Pass and Tranquil Lake — the opposite side of the peak from the Prusik Pass east ridge
backups.permit: Enchantment permit area: overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need the free self-issued day-use permit at the trailhead.
backups.comms: No reliable cell service in the Core Enchantment Zone or on the peak; coverage reportedly only returns near the Snow Lakes trailhead on the opposite side of the range. A satellite communicator (e.g., Garmin inReach) is commonly recommended given the lack of any short bail-out from the core basin.
backups.descent: Retrace the class 2-3 scramble down the southwest slopes into the Core basin, then reverse the approach: back up and over Aasgard Pass (very steep and exposed on the descent — many parties down-climb facing in on the upper section) and down through the Colchuck Lake basin to the Stuart Lake Trailhead. Snow bridges and a hidden meltwater channel on Aasgard Pass have collapsed underfoot in past seasons, so descending parties should stay alert for undermined snow, especially in early-to-mid summer.
obj_haz: loose/choss rock in the summit gully (helmet recommended)
exposure on the SW sub-summit's narrow fin if that side-trip is attempted
steep, loose talus/boulder field on Aasgard Pass above Colchuck Lake
afternoon thunderstorms building over the open basin
lingering snow/ice on the pass and gully into early summer
