backups.detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is needed for the standard scramble. An ice axe is worth carrying early in the season for snow on shaded benches, and trekking poles ease the talus.
pro_tips: Link it with Little Annapurna or other Core summits in one day.
Stick to clean granite to avoid the loosest talus.
Carry an axe early season for shaded snow.
Go in larch season for the finest views of the basin.
watch_out: Enchantment Peak has two nearly-equal summits ~1,500 ft apart; the NE summit (reached by this route) is the accepted true high point and a class 3 scramble, while the separate SW summit is an exposed class 4/low 5th pinnacle requiring rope and protection — don't mistake one for the other
no reliable cell coverage in the Core Enchantments basin; self-rescue capability and a plan for delayed exit are essential
backups.pro_needs: There is no protectable climbing on the easiest line; movement is unroped scrambling. The demands are basic route-finding and comfort on exposed third-class blocks rather than any gear.
backups.approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (elev. ~3,400 ft) on FS Road 7601 off Icicle Road. Follow the Stuart Lake Trail (Trail #1599) north through Douglas-fir/subalpine forest, crossing Mountaineer Creek on sturdy footbridges; the grade is moderate for the first 2.5 miles (about 1,500 ft gain) to the signed junction with the Colchuck Lake Trail — go left/uphill. From the junction the trail steepens and grows rockier for another 1.5 miles to Colchuck Lake (about 4 miles and ~2,280 ft from the TH, lake at 5,570 ft) — the last reliable, easy water source before the high basin. Boulder-hop/skirt the lake's south shore to the base of Aasgard Pass, a steep, unmaintained talus-and-boulder gully with only faint tread and cairns; it gains roughly 2,000–2,200 ft in under 1.25 miles to the pass (~7,800–7,841 ft) — this is the single biggest approach hazard on the route: loose, shifting rock with real rockfall risk onto parties below, and in early season the gully holds snow/ice that turns it into a steep, exposed snow climb. From the pass, drop gently into the upper Enchantment core basin past Isolation Lake, then traverse cross-country (use-paths and cairns, no maintained trail) through the Tranquil/Perfection/Sigrun/Reginleif lakes tarn cluster toward the Enchantment Peak massif; one common line for the SW summit leaves the basin directly between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun and climbs talus onto the peak's south side, avoiding a longer detour via Prusik Pass. This upper section is class 2–3 talus and slab with sustained exposure in spots; snow lingering into summer can make it markedly harder and is best avoided when icy (some parties instead take the longer, mellower line via Prusik Pass in spring conditions). The route enters fragile alpine terrain in the wilderness's day-use/permit core zone — stay on rock or snow and avoid cutting across meadow or heather. One-way distance to the summit is roughly 7.5–8 miles with about 5,100 ft of net rise from trailhead to summit; counting the drop into the basin and the reclimb to Aasgard Pass on the way out, the round trip comes to roughly 6,650 ft of gain for a car-to-car push (long day; many split it with a camp near Colchuck or in the core zone under permit).
backups.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line. This route tops out on the NORTHEAST summit, which a 2023 survey confirms is the true high point, and its descent is a walk-off: downclimb the short, loose 3rd-class gully off the summit plateau — the same step you came up — then reverse the cross-country traverse back through the Reginleif/Sigrun tarn basin to the top of Aasgard Pass. Downclimbing Aasgard Pass is the descent's main hazard: steep, loose talus that's arguably harder to descend than ascend — plunge-step or downclimb deliberately and stay off snow you can't see the run-out on. Do not glissade the snow-filled sections of Aasgard Pass; several serious and fatal accidents have occurred there from glissaders sliding into hidden moats and sub-snow meltwater channels, especially in early-to-mid season. From the base of the pass, follow the Colchuck Lake shoreline and the Colchuck Lake Trail / Stuart Lake Trail back to the Stuart Lake Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route overall — no established rappels on the standard line.
backups.bail: Because there is no committing technical terrain, retreat is simply a matter of reversing the scramble at any point, making this one of the lowest-commitment summits in the basin.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass (or America the Beautiful pass) required for parking at Stuart Lake Trailhead
access.notes: 2026 lottery application window Feb 15–Mar 1 (results after Mar 17, accept/pay by Mar 31). ~25% of overnight slots also released as a walk-up daily lottery the day before entry. Season requiring the overnight permit: May 15–Oct 31. A single-day ascent with no camp inside the boundary never needs the lottery.
access.rules: Enchantment Permit Area max group size is 8; campfires are prohibited above 5,000 ft and within 1/2 mile of any lake (essentially forest-wide within the permit area); pack out human waste/toilet paper where no toilet exists (200 ft from water/campsites)
access.permit: Overnight camping in the Enchantment Permit Area requires a permit May 15-Oct 31, allocated via Recreation.gov advance lottery (opens mid-February) plus a limited daily lottery two days before each trip; the Core Enchantment Zone (which includes Enchantment Peak) is capped at 24 overnight campers/day (16 advance + 8 daily). Day-use permits are free and self-issued at any of the three trailheads year-round. Outside May 15-Oct 31, no overnight permit is required and hikers self-register at the trailhead.
access.closures: Forest Road 7601 to the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead is gated and closed to vehicles every winter
access.landManager: Wenatchee River Ranger District (formerly Leavenworth Ranger District), Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — Alpine Lakes Wilderness
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — Alpine Lakes Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Stuart Lake, Eightmile, and Snow Lakes trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (overnight permit holders get a covering parking pass instead).

overnight_permit.what: Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit (lottery, not free) May 15 to Oct 31; self-issue at the trailhead the rest of the year
overnight_permit.where: Apply in the February advance lottery or the daily lottery on Recreation.gov. The permit names one zone (Core, Colchuck, Snow Lakes, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline) and you camp only there, except a Core permit, which covers every zone.

road.name: Forest Road 7601 (via Icicle Road and Eightmile Road/FR 7600)
road.status: Gravel, steep and washboarded, worsening through the season — high-clearance vehicle recommended
road.driveNote: From Leavenworth, follow Icicle Road ~8.5 mi, turn left on Eightmile Road (FR 7600), then stay right onto FR 7601 for ~4 mi to the trailhead. Parking is very limited in summer — arrive early or carpool.
road.seasonalGate: Closed to vehicles in winter to protect the roadbed

climate.typical: Subalpine/alpine climate at 5,500-8,500 ft. Snow typically lingers on Aasgard Pass and shaded benches into late June or July; the basin is snow-free and most reliably scrambled July through September. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in July-August; nights are cold at elevation even in summer, and the first significant snowfall of the season can arrive by early-to-mid October.

emergency.notes: No cell coverage through most of the Core Enchantments basin; Aasgard Pass and the Colchuck Lake basin are frequent SAR response areas.
emergency.rangerStation: Wenatchee River Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee NF, 600 Sherbourne St, Leavenworth, WA 98826, (509) 548-2550
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Medical Center (critical access), Leavenworth — for major trauma, Central Washington Hospital, Wenatchee is the nearest full trauma center
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911, or RiverCom 911 non-emergency (509) 663-9911 (dispatches Chelan County Sheriff SAR); Chelan County Volunteer Search & Rescue (509) 433-7171

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends in late September during peak larch color, when Core camps are full
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Roughly 20-40 parties per season summit — most Core-zone campers who snag the ultra-competitive overnight permit (historically ~3-5% lottery success) tack on the peak as a side-scramble; relatively few do it as a standalone objective given the access difficulty

fitnessSpec.hiking: Must already be established in a Core zone camp (via the Stuart Lake/Aasgard Pass or Snow Lakes approach) — the approach alone is one of the most demanding dayhikes in the Cascades, so partners need multi-day backpacking fitness, not just scramble fitness
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light summit pack from camp (a few lbs — layers, water, snacks); heavy overnight pack (35-45+ lbs) required to reach the Core beforehand

partner_requirements.approachTime: Not a standalone approach — climbed from an existing Core zone camp; allow ~4 hrs round trip
requiredSkills: off-trail talus/block scrambling
basic route-finding to identify the true high point among several summit bumps
afternoon-storm awareness and turnaround discipline
overnight backcountry travel competence to reach Core camp
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Comfortable, mileage-tested Class 2-3 scrambler with prior loose-talus/off-trail experience; this is easy technically but unforgiving logistically

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through early October, tightening around late September for larches; matches

July.reason: Upper slopes are usually largely snow-free by mid-to-late July, but shaded benches and gullies can still hold lingering snow early in the month

August.reason: Most reliably dry granite and fully melted-out benches; peak Core-zone camping traffic

October.reason: Still climbable but early-season snow can return with little warning, and shortening days compress the window for the round trip

September.reason: Cool, stable weather and the least storm activity of the season; late September larch color draws the heaviest crowds of the year

weather.typical: Warm, generally stable summer-to-fall weather on the open, exposed upper slopes; cools and shortens through September-October
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are the primary weather hazard July-August; exposed open terrain gives little shelter

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Low-to-moderate fall exposure — Class 2-3 talus and blocks with a twisted-ankle/tumbling-fall consequence rather than cliff exposure; the real hazard is loose granite underfoot and being caught on the open, high-point summit terrain during a lightning storm

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer/fall scramble route; the July-October climbing season falls outside NWAC's active forecast period, so no zone forecast applies during the climbing window

gaps: No published visitor-count data specific to the Enchantment Peak summit itself (as opposed to Core zone basin traffic generally) — crowd estimate is inferred from Core permit lottery statistics, not a direct route-specific source

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of FR-7601 off Icicle Creek Road, ~3,400 ft)

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the core basin to the southwest side
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead on FS Road 7601. Stuart Lake Trail #1599 north through forest, crossing Mountaineer Creek on footbridges, moderate for the first 2.5 miles to the signed Colchuck Lake junction — go left and uphill. Steeper and rockier for another 1.5 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. That is the last easy water before the high basin.

Skirt the lake's south shore to the foot of Aasgard Pass and climb the pass: roughly 2,000-2,200 ft in under 1.25 miles on faint tread, cairns, loose talus and boulders.

Aasgard has one route-finding rule that matters more than any other and it has killed people. A few hundred feet above the lake the path veers to the climber's LEFT of the creek. Keep left. At the first grove of larches, stay well clear to the left of the rock, whatever the season. At around 6,400 ft stay LEFT of the small cliff band with the waterfall in it, and do not follow any side path toward the waterfall. Drifting right of the trees, toward the waterfall ground, is how parties get cliffed out.

From the pass drop gently into the upper core basin past Isolation Lake and traverse cross-country on use-paths and cairns through the Tranquil / Perfection / Sigrun / Reginleif tarns toward the Enchantment Peak massif. A common line for the southwest summit leaves the basin directly between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun and climbs talus onto the peak's south side.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun to early Oct snow-free; Apr-Jun normally needs an ice axe for Aasgard Pass and the upper basin
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose shifting rock and genuine rockfall risk onto parties below
Getting cliffed out right of the trees / near the waterfall band at ~6,400 ft — fatalities are on record there
Early-season snow and ice turning the pass into a steep exposed snow climb
Sustained exposure on the class 2-3 talus and slab above the basin, worse when snow lingers
Fragile alpine ground in the permit core zone — stay on rock or snow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The scrambling starts where the basin talus steepens onto the peak's south flank — there is no cliff base, just a change of angle, so the useful test is about the summit rather than the start.

This route finishes on the northeast summit: class 2-3 ground and a short third-class finish onto a small flat block, which a 2023 survey found to be six or seven feet higher than the southwest summit. The southwest summit, roughly 1,500 ft away along the crest, is a very exposed fourth-class scramble and is not part of this route — if the crest ahead turns into sustained, exposed fourth-class ground, you have gone past your summit.

On the way in, the marker that you have left the basin at the right place is the pair of lakes: the line goes between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun onto the south side. If you are heading for Prusik Pass you have taken the longer, mellower option, which is a reasonable choice in spring conditions but does not lead to this scramble.

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

backups.fa: Unknown (the South Peak was first climbed May 30, 1947 by Fred Beckey and five companions via the Southwest Route)
hazards: notoriously loose, fractured Hozomeen chert — rockfall and breaking/pulling holds are the primary objective danger
routefinding on a complex face with multiple gullies, notches, and boulder bottlenecks
afternoon thunderstorms
sparse, unreliable protection due to friable rock — bring a range of small-to-medium gear and don't count on solid placements
long, remote approach with heavy bushwhacking (devil's club, windfall) and stream/boulder-field crossings
water sources above roughly 5,000-6,800 ft often dry up by late summer — fill up low and carry enough for the high camp and summit push

North Cascades grizzly bear recovery zone — practice food storage/bear-aware camping
backups.overview: Hozomeen Mountain is a dramatic, dark twin-summited peak rising directly from the east shore of Ross Lake near the Canadian border in North Cascades National Park/Ross Lake National Recreation Area. The higher North Peak (~8,071-8,072 ft) and slightly lower South Peak (8,003 ft) are built of Hozomeen chert, a hard but badly fractured bedded rock that gives the mountain its dark color and its reputation for notoriously loose, rotten climbing. The South Peak's nearly 1,000-foot near-vertical face (average angle ~42.6°) is often cited as the steepest in Washington. First ascents: North Peak, Sept 6 1904 (Sledge Tatum & George Loudon Jr., via the northeast); South Peak, May 30 1947 by Fred Beckey and five companions via the Southwest Route. The Southeast/South Face line described here is regarded as the least committing of the three known lines to the South Peak's summit, in contrast to the harder Southeast Buttress (Grade III, 5.6, FA 1988 by Adams/Goodman/Johnson/Petroske) and North Face (IV+ 5.9, FA 2019 by Rolf Larson & partner).
backups.beta: Mostly Class 3-4 scrambling on loose, fractured rock above the 6,800 ft saddle camp: slabs and connecting gullies lead up the south side to a slanted ledge below the summit, where a short, exposed wall of about 15 ft at roughly 5.6 is the crux, followed by a chimney finish. Most parties rappel the crux on the way down. Previous climbing experience on exposed, loose rock is essential.
backups.turnaround: Turn around if: conditions deteriorate to poor visibility, weather shows threatening signs (darkening clouds, lightning), party is moving slower than planned indicating fatigue, or snow/ice conditions require ongoing step-kicking above 7,500 ft. Allow at least 4 hours descent time and establish a firm turn-around time before committing to upper terrain.
backups.face: South Peak (8,003 ft - the lower of Hozomeen's two main summits)
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No cell phone reception at Hozomeen Mountain or surrounding backcountry. Satellite communication (Garmin InReach, SPOT beacon) recommended for emergency contact. Remote location near Canadian border adds communication/evacuation delays.
backups.descent: Reverse the face; several fixed rappel bolts/anchors near the summit headwall and finishing chimney have been placed by past parties (per a 2019 ascent report), supplementing rappels off slung blocks or natural anchors where bolts aren't present. Do not blindly trust fixed gear on this rock — carry cord/webbing to back up or replace tat, and expect loose ledges and choss on the way down.
obj_haz: loose rock
rockfall

waypoints.name: Lightning Creek boat landing / trail junction
waypoints.note: Water-taxi drop point on Ross Lake's east shore (~10 lake-miles north of Ross Dam); pick up the East Bank/Lightning Creek Trail here — this is mile ~16 of the SR-20 approach trail, a designated boat-in camp requiring a backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: Willow Lake
waypoints.note: Small lake along the trail (~mile 20); last reliable water before leaving the maintained trail — the 1988 southeast-buttress party left the trail just beyond Willow Lake to cut east toward the peak.

waypoints.name: Off-trail brush/ravine to the 5,000-ft shoulder
waypoints.note: Cross-country push through timber and avalanche debris into a deep ravine, then steep dirt-and-brush climbing to a broad timbered shoulder and meadows near 5,000 ft, bypassing cliff bands on their west side.

waypoints.name: 6,200-ft saddle below the SE buttress
waypoints.note: Ridge saddle directly beneath the southeast buttress, used as a bivouac by the 1988 first-ascent party; no reported water — carry up from Willow Lake.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20) / East Bank Trail to Lightning Creek
waypoints.note: This is a long (~15+ mile) approach via the East Bank Trail, historically used for this specific technical route; most modern non-technical South Peak parties instead use the shorter Hozomeen Lake Trailhead at Hozomeen Campground (Silver-Skagit Road, from the Canadian side)

pro_tips: Treat every hold and anchor with suspicion — the rock is exceptionally loose
Helmets essential; minimize parties stacked in fall line

afternoon thunderstorms build quickly over the North Cascades crest in summer
backups.pro_needs: Pro and slings for the low-fifth steps and to build/back up rappel anchors on questionable rock.
backups.approach: Because there is no public road to Hozomeen from the US side, the drive-in (SR-20 to Ross Lake Resort, then the resort's water taxi ~24 miles north up Ross Lake) drops you at the Hozomeen Ranger Station/Campground at the lake's head, around 1,650 ft — treat everything below as the hike from there. From the campground, pick up the maintained Hozomeen Lake Trail, which climbs gently through open, lush forest along the east side of Ross Lake toward Hozomeen Lake; trip reports differ on the exact length before you leave the tread (roughly 1.5 to 4 trail-miles depending on where you cut off), so budget for the full distance. Leave the maintained trail around 2,400 ft near Hozomeen Lake's outlet and begin ascending cross-country, following the creek/drainage east into the basin below the peak's south side. Expect a genuinely bad brush section here — a dense patch of devil's club right at the creek crossing, plus heavy deadfall and blowdown starting around 3,800 ft that slows travel to a crawl in spots. Water is reliable at the Hozomeen Creek crossing (~2,400-2,600 ft) and again in the basin around 5,000 ft; fill up at one of these, since the route above is dry. Near 5,000 ft the drainage narrows into a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones; above that, tedious red scree and heather lead past a striking slab wall around 5,800 ft and a steepening final push to a broad saddle/basin around 6,800 ft, which is the standard high camp (flat, tent-sized sites, but small — good for one or two). From camp, gain the final 1,000-1,200 ft on slabs and connecting gullies to reach the base of the southeast face/ridge proper. Given the ~19 km round-trip distance and roughly 6,400+ ft of total gain from lake level, this is realistically an overnight approach for most parties (camp at ~4,900-6,800 ft) rather than a single continuous car-to-summit push; a few strong parties have done it in a very long day.
backups.descent_text: Descent reverses the southeast face/ridge — there's no separate walk-off, since Hozomeen drops steeply on essentially every side. The crux of the descent is a short, exposed step down a Class 5.6 bulge just below the summit ridge; some parties downclimb it, most rappel it given the exposure. Below that, a roughly 50-foot rappel gets you down a Class 5.0 ramp, and from there two further double-rope-length rappels (i.e., a 60m rope doubled, or twin-rope technique) lower you cleanly onto a snow patch/basin beneath the face — call it 3 rappels total as the typical count, though some parties report doing the lower section as one longer double-rope rappel instead of two, so bring a 60m rope and be ready for 3-4 rope-lengths depending on exact line and snow coverage. Anchors are mixed and not fully bolted: parties mention both fixed slings/webbing around blocks and horns and at least one bolted anchor near the crux/overhang, so treat any fixed tat as suspect, back it up, and carry a few extra slings/cord in case you need to build or replace an anchor. Below the rappels, downclimb loose scree and talus and reverse the approach gully back down to the ~6,800 ft saddle or camp — past parties describe this stretch as slow going (clean slabs mixed with steep dirt, shifting boulders, and loose rubble), with summit-to-camp times of roughly 3-6.5+ hours reported, so plan your day accordingly and expect to finish by headlamp if you start late.
backups.bail: Rappel from slung blocks; carry extra slings since fixed anchors are unreliable.

itinerary.cal: Access is via Ross Lake Resort's water taxi (SR-20 to Ross Dam, then boat up-lake to the Hozomeen campground at the head of the lake) since the historic Silver-Skagit Road border crossing from Hope, BC has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic since the COVID-19 pandemic and the park's fire-closure page, updated September 14, 2026, still lists it closed. The water taxi's destination is shut too: the park has closed the entire Hozomeen area (docks, camping and public areas), the Hozomeen Lake Trail and the Hozomeen Cross-country Zone for the Border 2 Fire, with no end date given on that page; best attempted mid-July through September once the west basin snow/water sources are known.

days.note: An easy 1.5-mile forest walk from the Hozomeen Lake trailhead gives way to a rougher off-trail push: crossing Hozomeen Creek, fighting devil's club and windfall, then climbing red scree and heather into the west basin below a broad slab wall. Most parties reach the 6,800 ft saddle camp by mid-afternoon, drop the overnight gear, and — if weather and energy allow — continue straight up for the summit the same day, returning to camp before dark. The final headwall below the summit is a short, exposed 5.6 step; bring a rope and rack a few pieces plus a sling for the fixed rap anchors used by past parties.
days.title: Approach to high camp, summit push same day

schedule.label: Leave Hozomeen Lake trailhead
schedule.detail: 1.5 miles of easy forest trail before the route goes off-trail.

schedule.label: Cross Hozomeen Creek into the west basin
schedule.detail: Brushy, blowdown-choked slopes; the crux of route-finding is here, not on the rock.

schedule.label: Arrive 6,800 ft saddle camp
schedule.detail: Standard high camp with a view south; water is unreliable late-season.

schedule.label: Drop overnight gear, push for the summit
schedule.detail: Light packs; rope and rack for the final headwall.

schedule.label: Class 5.6 headwall, then summit
schedule.detail: ~15 ft exposed step below the top; fixed rap anchors reported near the summit and finishing chimney.

schedule.label: Rappel the crux, return to camp
schedule.detail: Descend the same face; parties aim to be off the rock by dusk.

days.objective: Reach the 6,800 ft saddle camp and tag the summit before dark

days.note: A relaxed morning — several parties report waiting for wind to die down before packing up — followed by a few hours of descending the west basin and forest trail back to the car. No fixed schedule needed; it's a straightforward reversal of Day 1's approach.
days.title: Exit to trailhead
days.objective: Break camp and hike out

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day car-to-car trip: roughly 12 miles round trip with about 6,300 ft of gain, built around a single high camp at 6,800 ft and a same-day summit push with a short 5.6 rock crux near the top.

access.fees: $10 per person, per night backcountry camping fee, charged mid-May through early October (no charge the rest of the year); $6 non-refundable Recreation.gov reservation/lottery fee per permit application.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: No cell service at Ross Lake/Hozomeen; pack out all trash (no services at Hozomeen Campground); Ross Lake water taxi requires advance reservation.
access.permit: Overnight backcountry permit required year-round for any camping en route (e.g., Lightning Creek, Hozomeen Campground, or high camps). Obtain at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount or reserve in advance via Recreation.gov (about 60% of backcountry sites are reservable; the rest are walk-up, first-come, first-served and can be competitive at Ross Lake in summer). Reserved permits must be picked up by 11:00 AM PT on the trip start date or the reservation may be cancelled.
access.closures: The US/Canada border crossing at Hozomeen (used for the historic Silver Skagit Road approach from Hope, BC) has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic since the COVID-19 pandemic (2020); the park's fire-closure page, updated 14 September 2026, still lists it closed with no end date given. The park has also closed the entire Hozomeen area — docks, public areas and camping — and the Hozomeen Cross-country Zone for the Border 2 Fire, with no end date given on that same page.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Service Complex / Ross Lake National Recreation Area (NPS)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP wilderness permit for the lake and cross-country camps; none for the drive-in campground
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov or get one at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center before the trip. Hozomeen Campground itself is first come, first served.

road.name: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to Ross Lake Resort; Silver Skagit Road from Hope, BC (closed at the border since 2020)
road.status: SR-20 is open seasonally and closes for winter avalanche danger (recent closures have run roughly early December through spring) between the Ross Dam trailhead and Silver Star Gate — check WSDOT/NPS road conditions before driving. The Silver Skagit Road has been closed at km 6 for wildfire since 24 July 2026, with no end date given in the B.C. Ministry of Transportation and Transit closure notice last updated 24 September 2026, and the border crossing into Hozomeen has been closed to travelers since 2020.
road.driveNote: Drive SR-20 to Ross Lake Resort (near Diablo/Ross Dam) and arrange the resort's water taxi (206-486-3751) to shuttle you the length of Ross Lake to the Hozomeen/Lightning Creek area, or hike in via the ~31-mile East Bank Trail from the SR-20 trailhead at milepost 138.
road.seasonalGate: Hozomeen Campground on the US side is open roughly late May through October; road passability should be checked directly before a trip.

climate.typical: Cool, wet North Cascades climate; snow can linger in upper gullies and on the face into July in heavy-snowpack years. Reliable, mostly snow-free rock conditions typically run mid-July through September.

bySeason.fall: Climbing season shortens rapidly after early September; early-season cold fronts and snow can hit the high ridge.
bySeason.spring: Approach trails and gullies are often still snow-covered/avalanche-prone into June, and Ross Lake Resort's water-taxi season may not yet be running.
bySeason.summer: Best climbing window (Jul-Sep); water sources above roughly 5,000-6,800 ft dry up by late summer, so time trips or cache water accordingly.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible — SR-20 is closed and Ross Lake Resort facilities are shut down.

emergency.notes: No cell phone reception at Ross Lake or Hozomeen; carry a satellite communicator/PLB. Given the multi-hour boat and/or long trail approach, rescue typically requires an NPS or county SAR helicopter.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park - Wilderness Information Center (Marblemount) / Ross Lake NRA
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, Sedro-Woolley, WA (~65 mi via SR-20) — a small facility; serious trauma cases are typically flown out given the remote, boat/trail-only access to this peak.

crowds.peakTraffic: rarely climbed; no identifiable 'peak' traffic window - even the popular Mountaineers-documented routes on this peak see sparse annual ascents
crowds.estimatePerSeason: unknown - low-traffic; likely well under a dozen parties per season based on overall Hozomeen traffic patterns

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong multi-day backpacking fitness for the remote Ross Lake/Hozomeen approach plus a steep, sustained climb to a high camp
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/multi-day pack (camp gear, food, water) for the approach, transitioning to a light summit pack for the pre-dawn face climb

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long, multi-day approach: boat/trail access to the Hozomeen area at the north end of Ross Lake, then a steep climb to a high camp below the face, with a pre-dawn start for the summit push
requiredSkills: confident movement on unprotected/loosely-protected Class 4-low 5th rock
routefinding on a complex, featureless face with unreliable anchors
loose/rotten rock management (testing holds, minimizing rockfall to partners)
remote self-rescue and sound turn-around judgment (no quick evacuation)
backcountry navigation on the approach from the Hozomeen area
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine scrambler comfortable soloing/leading unprotected Class 4 to low 5th-class terrain on notoriously rotten rock, with solid judgment for routefinding on a complex, loose face far from help

July.reason: Primary climbing season begins; rock is as dry as it gets, though still loose, and lingering early-season snow patches on the approach are possible

August.reason: Most stable and driest month; best chance of avoiding wet rock, though afternoon thunderstorms remain a risk

September.reason: Still climbable and often stable, but early season snow and colder nights become more likely as the month progresses

weather.typical: Wetter north-end climate; the rock is hazardous when wet, so dry-weather windows are essential
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms common in summer; rock remains loose even in dry conditions

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High consequence: extremely loose/rotten rock, sustained exposure, and unreliable anchors on unprotected Class 4/low 5th terrain, compounded by the remoteness of the objective (self-rescue only)

gaps: No confirmed first-ascent date/team specifically for this 'standard' Southeast/South Face line, as distinct from the documented 1988 Southeast Buttress FA and 1947 Southwest Route FA
Exact trailhead mileage varies by source depending on whether the (currently closed) north-end Silver Skagit Road or the long East Bank Trail from SR-20 is used
No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 134, down to Ross Lake and the water-taxi/trail network

backups.corrections: The listed route name/id ("Southeast Face (Standard)") does not correspond to any documented route on this summit. Every reputable source checked (Wikipedia, Mountaineers.org, SummitPost search results, multiple trip reports on trailcatjim.com, cascadeclimbers.com, and Cascade Alpine Guide references) describes the standard/easiest route on Hozomeen Mountain's North (main, 8,071-ft) summit as ascending the Northeast Ridge/Buttress from a col near 6,300 ft — first climbed 1904, class 4. A genuine "Southeast Buttress" route does exist in the American Alpine Club database (FA 1988, III 5.6, described as the least-committing of three known routes), but it is on the separate SOUTH Peak (8,003 ft) of Hozomeen, a distinct sub-summit roughly a mile away, not on the North Peak matched by this entry's coordinates. I have filled this entry's fields using the well-documented Northeast Ridge/Buttress standard-route data (setting aspect=NE, face=Northeast Buttress/Ridge accordingly) since that is what "the standard route" on this specific summit actually refers to in the literature; the routeName/routeId were kept exactly as given per instructions, but the aspect/face fields reflect the sourced reality rather than the "Southeast" label. Recommend the app data owner review whether this route entry should be renamed/re-pointed to the Northeast Buttress, or replaced with a distinct South Peak entry for the true Southeast Buttress line.

approach_variants.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the campground at the head of the lake
approach_variants.notes:
There is no public road to this end of the lake from the south. Drive to the trailhead near milepost 134, walk down to the resort, and take its water taxi north to the campground and ranger station at the head of the lake at about 1,650 ft. Everything below is measured from there.

From the campground pick up the maintained lake-side trail, which climbs gently through open lush forest toward Hozomeen Lake. Reports differ on how far along it you should stay - anywhere from a mile and a half to four miles depending on where the party cut off - so budget for the longer figure. Leave the tread around 2,400 ft near the lake's outlet and start up cross-country, following the drainage east into the basin under the peak's south side. There is a genuinely bad brush section here: devil's club right at the creek crossing, and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft that reduces travel to a crawl. Fill water at the creek crossing or again in the basin near 5,000 ft, because everything above is dry.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the brush is passable and the upper gullies have melted out
hazards: a boat schedule that fixes both ends of the trip on a lake with no road out
devil's club at the creek crossing and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft
no water above the basin near 5,000 ft
a boulder-choked gully with chockstones to negotiate under a pack
loose, friable rock on the upper mountain
a tiny high camp that will not take a large party
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LADDER OF LANDMARKS ABOVE THE BASIN IS WHAT FIXES YOUR POSITION, AND THEY COME IN ORDER. Near 5,000 ft the drainage narrows into a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones - IF YOUR GULLY HAS NO CHOCKSTONE BOTTLENECK IN IT, YOU ARE IN THE WRONG DRAINAGE and should traverse rather than climb. Above the chockstones the ground turns to tedious red scree and heather. The next confirmation is a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, passed rather than climbed. Above it the angle steepens to a broad saddle and basin near 6,800 ft with small flat tent-sized sites - the standard high camp, good for one or two tents and no more.

FROM CAMP THE BASE OF THE ROUTE IS ANOTHER THOUSAND FEET OR SO ABOVE, GAINED ON SLABS AND CONNECTING GULLIES. You are looking for the point where the slabs run out against the face and the ridge proper takes over.

CHECK WHICH SUMMIT IS ABOVE YOU. This route is on the SOUTH peak, which is the lower of the two main summits. If the tower above you is the higher, broader one and the other summit lies to the SOUTH of you, you have drifted north into the wrong cirque and are under the north peak.

AND CHECK THAT YOU LEFT THE TRAIL AT ALL. The maintained tread is graded and obvious; the moment you are on it with easy walking under your feet, you are not on the approach any more. The departure is at a creek, at a lake outlet, not at a sign.

approach_variants.name: By road from the north to the ranger station, subject to the border gate
approach_variants.notes:
The campground and ranger station at the head of the lake can also be reached by driving a long gravel road south from the north side of the international boundary. That crossing has been closed to both vehicles and foot traffic, so this variant may simply not exist in the season you are planning for - confirm the gate's status before building a trip on it, because there is no way to discover it is shut except by arriving.

If it is open, the walk from the campground is identical to the boat variant: the maintained lake-side trail toward Hozomeen Lake, then off-trail at the outlet near 2,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: July through September, and only if the boundary is open
hazards: a border gate that has been closed to vehicles and to walkers
a long gravel drive with no services at the end
the same devil's club, deadfall and dry upper slopes
loose rock and a small high camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ARRIVAL CHANGES, THE APPROACH DOES NOT. From the campground at about 1,650 ft the sequence is the same: maintained trail to the vicinity of Hozomeen Lake's outlet near 2,400 ft, then cross Hozomeen Creek and follow the drainage east into the south basin.

THE MARKERS ARE THE SAME LADDER, IN THE SAME ORDER: a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones near 5,000 ft, red scree and heather above it, a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, and then a broad saddle and basin at about 6,800 ft with a few small flat tent sites. A drainage with no chockstone bottleneck is the wrong drainage.

THE SUMMIT TEST STILL APPLIES. This route is on the SOUTH peak, the lower of the two. If the higher, broader summit is directly above you and the other one lies south, you are under the north peak instead.

approach_variants.name: From the Lightning Creek landing on the lake's east shore, past Willow Lake
approach_variants.notes: A boat landing further down the east shore of the lake gives onto the east-bank trail system, which runs north past Willow Lake. Parties have used this to reach the south and south-east sides of the massif on foot rather than starting from the campground at the head of the lake. It is the longer walk of the two boat options and it approaches the peak from the south-east rather than from the west, so it suits parties heading for the south-east side of the south peak more than it suits the standard line.
hazards: a much longer walk than the head-of-lake landing
timber, avalanche debris and a ravine crossing with no tread
steep dirt and brush below the shoulder
no water between Willow Lake and the basin
cliff bands that must be bypassed in poor visibility
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DEPARTURE FROM THE TRAIL IS JUST BEYOND WILLOW LAKE, AND THE LAKE IS THE MARKER. It is the last reliable water; everything above is dry until the basin, so this is where you fill.

FROM THERE THE GROUND IS THE TEST RATHER THAN ANY TREAD: timber and avalanche debris first, then a ravine to cross, then steep dirt and brush climbing to open timber on the broad shoulder south of the peak. Reaching MEADOWS near 5,000 ft is the sign the worst of the brush is behind you.

ABOVE THE MEADOWS THE CLIFF BANDS ARE BYPASSED, NOT CLIMBED. If you are forced onto rock that wants a rope, traverse and look for the way round rather than committing to it - the way through here is a walking line, not a climbing one.

THE ARRIVAL IS A SADDLE AT ABOUT 6,200 FT DIRECTLY BENEATH THE BUTTRESS on the peak's south-east side, with no water on it. IF YOU HAVE ARRIVED SOMEWHERE WITH RUNNING WATER, YOU ARE NOT THERE YET. From that saddle the standard south-east face and the south-east buttress lines are both above you, so identify which feature you are under before starting up.

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs in the western basin between the peaks
bivy.notes: The mountain is two rock summits above a basin, and the approach to that basin from the lake is the crux of the whole trip for most parties: a slow grind through blowdown and heavy brush with no path, on which fifteen miles and seven thousand feet of gain and loss is a fair reckoning for the round trip. Strong parties do go car to car, and parties often describe regretting that decision around hour twelve. Sleeping up here shortens the summit day considerably, at the cost of hauling water up a slope with almost none on it and sleeping on ground that is not flat. There is a second line from the road along the cleared border swath running east from near the ranger station, which is shorter and is described by people who have used it as more unpleasant than the lake approach rather than less. Both are late-summer propositions: snow lingers in the basin, and the brush is at its worst when it is wet.
bivy.water: This is the hard part and worth planning around. The one stream in the basin runs in a channel that deepens into a slot as you climb, and parties have found it reachable at a single awkward spot at around four thousand feet and nowhere above that. Fill everything you are carrying when you can get to water, because you may not get another chance before the ground goes flat enough to sleep on.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Hozomeen cross-country zone, which allows a maximum party of six and a maximum of three parties on any night. It is a walk-up zone rather than a reservable one, so the permit is collected in person, in practice at Marblemount. Cross-country camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight of both, and only on snow, rock or bare ground — never in meadow and never within a hundred feet of water. NO FIRES in the zone. Waste goes in a cathole, or is carried out where the ground will not take one.
bivy.capacity: No established site and no site count. Parties have reported scratching out a few rough platforms among scattered boulders on a steep forested slope, enough for one small party sleeping poorly. THERE IS NO CAMP HERE — this is where people stop because they have run out of daylight, not somewhere anyone chose.

bivy.name: Hozomeen Campground, north end of Ross Lake
bivy.notes: This is the roadhead for every route on the mountain and the only developed camping anywhere near it. It sits in deep forest on flat ground by the lake, with vault toilets, boat ramps and no trash service, so everything you bring comes out with you. There is no cell coverage and the nearest supplies are hours away in either country. The season runs roughly late May into October, bounded at the front by snow on the gravel road and at the back by the road being left unmaintained. The other way in is by water: a boat from the resort at the south end will run parties the length of the lake, taking up to six people with packs on a chartered trip that is booked and paid in advance. That is expensive and inflexible but it does not involve a border at all, which through several recent seasons has made it the only way anybody got here. In summer 2026 a lightning fire on the border grew to many thousands of acres immediately east of the mountain, crossed into Canada, and closed the entire Hozomeen area including the docks, the campground and the lake north of Silver Creek. Treat access to this peak as something to verify from scratch each season rather than as a fixed thing.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is provided while the campground is staffed. Outside that window, and any time the system is off, the lake and the creeks are the supply and need treating.
bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No fee and no reservation for the campground itself, and no backcountry permit to sleep here — but one is required the moment you walk in to the lake camps or up onto the mountain. THE BORDER IS THE COMPLICATION. The only road access is a long gravel road running south from the Trans-Canada Highway near Hope, British Columbia, and it crosses into the United States at a point with no staffed port of entry. The gate on the American side has been closed to vehicle traffic from Canada for several years, and at times foot traffic across the line has been prohibited as well. A party driving down from Canada is entering the United States, so it needs the documents for that regardless of whether anyone is there to check; the practical position has been that you cannot legally drive through, and that a normal port of entry plus the boat is the way in. Confirm the current gate status with the park and with the border agency before committing to the road, because the answer has changed more than once.
bivy.capacity: Around 75 sites across two loops, all first-come and first-served with no reservations taken. The Upper Loop has been closed for hazard trees, which removes a good share of that number and also happens to be where the lake trail starts, so check what is actually open before counting on a spot.

bivy.name: Hozomeen Lake camp
bivy.notes: Something under four miles in from the campground's upper loop on an established trail, this is the obvious first night for anyone who wants to start the climb from higher than the road. It is a genuinely pleasant forested lake sitting directly beneath the mountain, and it is the better of the two lake camps by some distance. The climbing route leaves from here: parties work around the eastern shore and then angle up into the basin between the peaks, and that is where the day stops being a hike. Expect heavy deadfall and thick brush from the moment you leave the trail. The loon closure and the fire closures between them have shut this camp for large parts of recent seasons, so confirm it is open before building an itinerary on it.
bivy.water: The lake is right there and is the supply. It is standing water in a shallow forested basin, so filter or treat rather than drinking it as found.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, obtained at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing system. A SEASONAL CLOSURE APPLIES: the lake is closed to entry and to camping from the first of April through the end of May to protect nesting loons, which rules out the early-season window entirely. Fires and food storage are governed by the permit; a canister is the sensible choice here whatever the minimum requirement says.
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, a few sites with a privy and food storage. Sites are assigned by night on the permit, so a walk-up can be turned away if the nights you want are taken.

backups.name: South Ridge
gear: crevasse-rescue basics (rope, prusiks) if crossing Cache Glacier while crevasses are open
hazards: loose rock
lingering snow
route-finding
crevasses/snow bridges on the Cache Glacier approach to Cache Col
icy, steep snow on the Cache Col-to-Kool-Aid Lake descent
backups.overview: Hurry-up Peak (7,821 ft) lies on the Skagit-Chelan county line at the northern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse, just south of Cascade Pass and Cache Col, between Magic Mountain and Spider Mountain (its line parent). It is not part of the Sahale-Boston/Horseshoe Basin group on the opposite side of the pass; instead it's reached from a Kool-Aid Lake camp on the traverse's first day. A quiet, seldom-solo-targeted scramble, it is usually tagged as a short side trip by parties already committed to the Ptarmigan Traverse rather than climbed on its own.
backups.beta: A popular side trip from the Cascade Pass area or via the Ptarmigan Traverse. The south ridge route involves ascending from the col to mixed rock scrambling with moderate to significant exposure on the summit ridge. Route finding can be tricky; descend via the same route.
backups.turnaround: If approaching from Cascade Pass for a day trip, plan to be descending by mid-afternoon to have adequate daylight. Watch weather closely; the pass can deteriorate rapidly.
backups.rappels: None typically needed on the standard scramble line
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: Cell phone coverage unreliable at high elevation; satellite communicator (Garmin InReach, Spot) recommended for safety in this remote alpine area. Cascade Pass area has limited to no cell service.
obj_haz: Loose gneiss blocks on the upper scramble
Lingering steep snow into early July requiring an ice axe
Exposure along the summit ridge
Route-finding on the broader glaciated Ptarmigan Traverse approach

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Cascade River Road (FR-15), 23.1 mi from Marblemount; day use is free but overnight parties need a North Cascades NP backcountry permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
waypoints.directions: Cascade River Road runs roughly 23 miles from Marblemount, pavement giving way to gravel for the upper half. The last gravel section is gated through the winter and typically does not open until the snow clears, often not until late June or July, so confirm the road is open all the way to the end before committing to the drive.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: High point of the maintained trail; camping is prohibited at the pass itself, so continue toward Pelton Basin or contour east/south toward Cache Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Follow the well-graded, heavily used Cascade Pass Trail about 3.7 miles and 1,800 ft, switchbacking up through forest and avalanche-path meadows to the pass. The last reliable trailside water is at the creek crossings low on the trail, so fill bottles before starting the switchbacks.

waypoints.name: Pelton Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Wooded basin camp on Pelton Creek just below and east of the pass; reliable water and the last easy legal camp before the cross-country push to Cache Col.
waypoints.directions: From the pass the maintained trail keeps going east, traversing a scree slope and descending into Pelton Basin, with a short signed spur dropping to the camp about a mile from the pass. Water is reliable here, and this is the last easy legal camp before the route leaves the trail.

waypoints.name: Cache Col / Cache Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Rocky gap between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak at the head of Cache Glacier; cross the glacier here and watch for open crevasses in low-snow late-season conditions.
waypoints.directions: Climb back west to the Cascade Pass area and leave the maintained tread on the climbers' boot track heading south-southeast. It makes a rising traverse over loose ground, heather and firm morning snow patches across Mixup Peak's flanks to the toe of the Cache Glacier near 6,000 ft, then up moderate snow slopes to the notch. Crevasses open here by late summer, so carry a rope and crevasse-rescue kit and be ready to use them.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small alpine tarn ~1 mile SSE of Cache Col that serves as the standard day-1 camp for parties climbing Hurry-up Peak or starting the Ptarmigan Traverse; often still snow/ice-covered into August.
waypoints.directions: From the col drop and traverse south-southeast about a mile over loose rock, heather benches and occasional snowfields to the tarn. It is the only dependable water in the basin and can still be partly frozen early in the season.

waypoints.name: Exposed summit ridge scramble
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 scrambling with moderate exposure along the final summit ridge; early-season parties report steep snow here that warrants pickets for protection.
waypoints.directions: From the lake climb south, gaining roughly 1,000-1,300 ft of scree, heather and broken granite benches to the col on the ridge between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up, then start up the crest. A band of steep snow around 7,100 ft commonly persists into midsummer, so carry an axe and crampons even in August. Route-finding on the benches is the real crux here: several similar-looking gully lines lead up and not all of them are the right one.

waypoints.name: Hurry-up Peak Summit
waypoints.note: True summit (historically also called Ess/S Mountain); open view north to Trapper Lake and the rest of the Ptarmigan Traverse peaks.
waypoints.directions: The crest runs northeast from the col over about 300 ft of broken, blocky ledges with moderate to significant exposure; the rock is loose enough that holds want testing before they are weighted. The ridge tops out on a false summit — from there drop roughly 80 ft into a dirty gully on the east side, then climb ledges that corkscrew around the east side of the summit block for the last 50 ft to the true top.

backups.best_season: Mid-July through September for the best weather window; the Cache Col approach commonly holds firm snow into early July, requiring ice axe and crampons even after the peak itself is snow-free.
backups.approach: Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road (about 23 miles of pavement then gravel from Marblemount; the upper gravel section is gated and typically doesn't open until snow clears, often not until late June/July). From the trailhead, follow the well-graded, heavily-used Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft of gain, switchbacking up through forest and avalanche-path meadows to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft) — the last reliable trailside water is at the creek crossings low on the trail, so top off bottles before the switchbacks. At the pass, leave the maintained tread and pick up the climbers' path/boot track heading south-southeast, making a rising traverse across snow or heather on the flanks of Mixup Peak to the base of the Cache Glacier (~6,000 ft); this stretch is loose, choosy, and crosses several snow patches that can be firm in early morning. Ascend moderate glacier/snow slopes (crevasses can open by late summer — rope up if the party isn't comfortable soloing them) to the notch at Cache Col (6,900 ft). From the col, descend and traverse south-southeast about 1 mile over loose rock and heather benches, crossing occasional snowfields, down to Kool-Aid Lake (6,120 ft), the standard base camp for this side of the Ptarmigan Traverse and the only dependable water source in the basin (may be partly frozen early season). Car-to-camp is roughly 5-6 miles with about 3,300 ft of gain, generally a half-day carrying overnight gear. From camp, the peak itself is climbed as a side trip: head up toward Hurry-up Peak's south/southwest flank, crossing a band of steep snow around 7,100 ft (carry an axe/crampons even mid-summer) before gaining broken granite slabs and the south ridge crest; follow the crest/upper gully system with sustained Class 2-3 scrambling and a couple of exposed but short moves along the summit ridge to the 7,821 ft top — about 1 mile and 1,400-1,500 ft above camp, roughly 1-1.5 hours for a fit party.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling. From the summit, reverse the ascent line back down the south ridge/gully system, downclimbing the same Class 2-3 granite terrain and re-crossing the steep snow band near 7,100 ft (plunge-step or glissade if conditions allow, but keep the axe out given the exposure just above), back down to Kool-Aid Lake camp — about 3-3.5 hours round trip from camp is typical for the whole side-trip. From camp, descend by reversing the approach: climb back up to Cache Col, down the Cache Glacier snow slopes, traverse back around Mixup Peak's flanks to Cascade Pass, then descend the maintained Cascade Pass Trail to the trailhead. No technical descent hazards beyond the approach terrain itself — main concerns are the steep snow crossing near 7,100 ft (harder and icier in early season or late day when it's refrozen) and losing the boot path on the granite benches between Kool-Aid Lake and the ridge, which has multiple similar-looking gully options.
backups.bail: The route reverses at any point; no committing terrain on the standard line.

pitch_detail.notes: Scramble up loose scree and rock to reach the saddle. Moderate exposure as elevation increases. Route finding straightforward.
pitch_detail.pitch: Approach via northwest slope to col between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up Peak

pitch_detail.notes: Climb mixed broken rock ledges up the south ridge. Moderate to significant exposure. Watch for loose rock; test holds. Height of terrain: ~300 feet of actual climbing.
pitch_detail.pitch: South ridge from col to false summit

pitch_detail.notes: Drop 80 feet into dirty gully on right side (east face). Climb Class 3-4 broken ledges that corkscrew around the east side of summit block. Exposed scrambling requires careful foot placement. Final 50 feet to true summit.
pitch_detail.pitch: False summit to true summit (via gully descent and east-side corkscrew)

itinerary.cal: Cascade River Road typically opens in late spring and Cache Col holds consolidated snow well into summer, so most parties do this in July-September when the col crossing is firm but not icy.

days.note: Hike the maintained Cascade Pass Trail to Cascade Pass, then leave the trail and climb cross-country over the Cache Glacier remnant to Cache Col before dropping about a mile to camp at Kool-Aid Lake, a small tarn at ~6,120 ft. This stretch is mostly on snow into midsummer and is the crux of the day more from routefinding/snow travel than distance.

days.note: An early start lets you climb the peak on firm snow before it softens: ascend about 1,000 ft from camp to the Magic-Hurry-Up col, then follow the south ridge over a false summit to the true 7,821 ft top. Back at camp by mid-morning, most parties break camp and hike all the way out the same day rather than adding a third night.

access.fees: Summer (mid-May-early Oct) backcountry permit: $10 per person plus a $6 nonrefundable reservation fee; free for climbers 15 and under.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Overnight backcountry/climbing permit required from North Cascades National Park for any camp used to access the peak (e.g., Kool-Aid Lake). Walk-up permits are issued at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center (7am-4pm daily, mid-May through Oct 10); the high-demand Cascade Pass/Sahale Arm zone also has an early-access lottery and Recreation.gov reservations. Once the WIC closes for the season, self-issue permits are available outside the Marblemount ranger station.
access.closures: Cascade River Road (FR-15) was closed to vehicles at Eldorado, milepost 20 (about 3 miles short of the Cascade Pass Trailhead, ~1,500 ft of additional gain), in June 2026 for flooding and landslide damage; that closure has been lifted, and the park's road-conditions page, updated July 3, 2026, lists the road open. Check NPS's Cascade River Road status page before driving out.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (west/Skagit County approach); the summit sits on the Skagit-Chelan county line, with its east flank bordering Glacier Peak Wilderness (Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Chelan Ranger District).
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP wilderness permit — quota, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Parties starting from Stehekin can arrange the permit by email.

road.name: Cascade River Road (Forest Road 15)
road.status: Open: the June 2026 closure to vehicles at Eldorado/milepost 20 for flooding/landslide damage has been lifted, and the park's road-conditions page, updated July 3, 2026, lists the road open.
road.driveNote: 22.3 miles of paved/gravel road from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass Trailhead when fully open; add roughly 6 miles round trip on foot or bike whenever the road is gated at milepost 20.
road.seasonalGate: Typically gated for winter beyond a lower point on the road; check NPS road-conditions page for current mile-by-mile status.

climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate typical of the North Cascades crest: heavy orographic precipitation, and wet, heavy snow producing high avalanche danger that can persist on the Cache Col approach into early summer. Clear, warm days are common in late July and August, but rain, fog, or even snow flurries can arrive with little warning at any point in summer.

emergency.notes: Call 911; Skagit County Sheriff's Office coordinates search and rescue for the west-side North Cascades National Park approach.
emergency.county: Skagit (west-side approach via Cascade River Road); the summit itself sits on the Skagit-Chelan county line.
emergency.nearestHospital: Skagit Valley Hospital, Mount Vernon (~49 miles / ~1 hr drive from Marblemount) or Cascade Valley Hospital, Arlington - both Skagit Regional Health facilities.

crowds.peakTraffic: Rarely climbed; overshadowed by the much busier Boston Basin/Cascade Pass corridor (Sahale, Boston Peak, Forbidden Peak) which absorbs most traffic in this part of North Cascades National Park
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low traffic — probably well under a handful of parties per season

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong off-trail/cross-country fitness for the approach over Cache Col to a camp at Kool-Aid Lake, plus a full scramble day on summit day
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight pack (camp gear + basic scramble kit) on the approach; lighter day pack for the summit push

partner_requirements.approachTime: Multi-day trip: roughly a full day off-trail to establish camp at Kool-Aid Lake, then about 3-3.5 hrs round trip from camp to the summit via the south ridge
requiredSkills: Class 3-4 scrambling on loose/blocky rock
Steep snow travel and self-arrest for lingering early-season snow patches
Off-trail route-finding and navigation
Comfortable with sustained exposure and no fixed protection
Basic wilderness/self-rescue judgment given the remote location
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced scrambler comfortable with sustained, unroped Class 3-4 terrain on loose rock; given the remote, low-traffic setting, prior North Cascades alpine scrambling experience and solid self-rescue judgment are strongly recommended

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, with August typically offering the most consistent dry-rock conditions

July.reason: Early July can still hold lingering snow on the ridge and in gullies (steep snow early); conditions firm up and improve toward mid-to-late July

August.reason: Best overall window - firm morning snow largely melted out, dry rock, and the most stable summer weather

September.reason: Cooler and often stable, but shorter days and increasing chance of early-season snow or storms later in the month

weather.typical: Cool alpine climate with cold nights and moderate summer days; there is afternoon cloud buildup, and the exposed ridge amplifies wind and temperature swings
weather.probability: Afternoon weather/cloud buildup is a known hazard on this route; treat cell-driven afternoon storms as a real possibility, especially later in the season

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained, unroped Class 3-4 exposure on loose blocky rock; loose rock, lingering snow and route-finding mean a fall or slip on the steeper sections or on early-season snow could result in a serious, hard-to-reach injury given how little-traveled this route is
seasonal_hazards.crevasses: The South Ridge climbing itself is on blocky ridge/scramble terrain, but the standard approach crosses the Cache Glacier to reach Cache Col — crevasses can open by late summer, and roping up is recommended unless the party is comfortable soloing the crossing.

gaps: The on-file route name 'South Ridge' could not be independently confirmed against Beckey's Cascade Alpine Guide; documented sources describe a Class 3 scramble on the peak's upper slopes from a Kool-Aid Lake camp and a separate South Couloir ski-mountaineering line - these may be the same feature described differently or genuinely distinct routes.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of Cascade River Road (~3,660 ft)

approach_variants.name: Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake, then the col between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road — the upper gravel section is gated and often does not open until late June or July — follow the well-graded Cascade Pass trail 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft. The last reliable trailside water is at the creek crossings low down, so fill up before the switchbacks.

At the pass leave the maintained tread for the climbers' path heading south-southeast, a rising traverse across snow or heather on Mixup Peak's flanks to the base of the CACHE GLACIER near 6,000 ft. Ascend moderate glacier and snow slopes to CACHE COL at about 6,900 ft. From the col, descend and traverse south-southeast about a mile over loose rock and heather benches to KOOL-AID LAKE at about 6,120 ft — the standard camp for this side of the Ptarmigan Traverse and the only dependable water in the basin.

From camp the peak is a side trip: up toward the south flank, across a band of steep snow around 7,100 ft, then broken granite slabs to the ridge. About a mile and 1,400-1,500 ft above camp, roughly an hour to an hour and a half for a fit party.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September; the Cache Col approach commonly holds firm snow into early July and wants an axe and crampons even after the peak itself is snow-free
hazards: Crevasses and snow bridges on the Cache Glacier approach to Cache Col
Icy, steep snow on the Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake descent, worse refrozen in the early morning or late in the day
A band of steep snow around 7,100 ft that wants an axe and crampons even mid-summer
Loose rock and multiple similar-looking gully lines on the granite benches — the main route-finding crux
Short but exposed moves along the summit ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE IS THE COL BETWEEN MAGIC MOUNTAIN AND HURRY-UP PEAK, gained from the Kool-Aid Lake basin, and the col is the last unambiguous feature of the day. Above it the route is route-finding rather than following a line: parties report several viable gully options through the granite benches and not all of them match the published description. SO THE TEST THAT MATTERS IS AT THE TOP, NOT THE BOTTOM, AND IT IS A COUNTABLE ONE. YOU WILL REACH A FALSE SUMMIT. FROM IT YOU MUST DROP ABOUT 80 FT INTO A DIRTY GULLY ON THE RIGHT-HAND (EAST) SIDE, then follow class 3-4 broken ledges that CORKSCREW AROUND THE EAST SIDE of the summit block, and the last 50 ft gains the true top. IF YOU HAVE NOT LOST 80 FT INTO A GULLY, THE HIGH POINT YOU ARE STANDING ON IS THE FALSE SUMMIT. THAT DESCEND-THEN-CORKSCREW SEQUENCE IS THE ROUTE'S SIGNATURE. A summit reached directly off the ridge crest with no drop and no wrap-around is the wrong one. ON THE WAY UP, THE STEEP SNOW BAND AROUND 7,100 FT IS THE POSITION CHECK: it sits between camp and the slabs, it is there most of the summer, and it is why you carry an axe on a class 3 scramble. If you gained the ridge without crossing snow, look again at where you left the basin. AND DO NOT CONFUSE THE COL WITH CACHE COL. Cache Col at about 6,900 ft is on the approach, between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak, and it is where you cross the glacier. The Magic-Hurry-up col is on the far side of Kool-Aid Lake and is where this climb starts. Two cols, a mile and a descent apart. The peak is also recorded under the names Ess Mountain and S Mountain, so a source describing 'the saddle between Magic and S Mountains' is describing this same col.

climbing_route.label: Steep snow band on the south/southwest flank
climbing_route.notes: From camp, head up toward Hurry-up Peak's south/southwest flank, crossing a band of steep snow around 7,100 ft — carry an axe/crampons even mid-summer.

climbing_route.label: Broken granite slabs to the south ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: Gain broken granite slabs and the south ridge crest. Route-finding on the granite benches is the main crux; parties report multiple viable gully lines, not all matching the published description exactly.

climbing_route.label: South ridge crest and upper gully system
climbing_route.notes: Follow the crest/upper gully system with sustained Class 2-3 scrambling and a couple of exposed but short moves along the summit ridge to the 7,821 ft top — about 1 mile and 1,400-1,500 ft above camp, roughly 1-1.5 hours for a fit party.

backups.overview: La Bohn Peak (6,585 ft) is a granite summit at the head of Necklace Valley in the eastern Alpine Lakes Wilderness, rising directly west of La Bohn Gap — a broad, tarn-dotted saddle around 5,900 ft between the peak and Mount Hinman (7,492 ft, 1.7 mi east). The standard line follows a climbers' path west from the gap up the ridge and face above La Bohn Lakes, gaining a final ~1,000 ft of Class 2 (occasional Class 3) talus and rock to the summit. It's rarely climbed on its own — most parties tag it as a half-day add-on from a Necklace Valley or Dutch Miller Gap-Williams Lake-Chain Lakes backpack, often paired with Mount Hinman.
backups.beta: From a camp at La Bohn Lakes or La Bohn Gap, climbers ascend talus on the west/southwest side of the peak. Parties describe crossing to a false summit just short of the true top, with roughly the final 1/8 mile being a walk along the summit ridge. The line is entirely off-trail Class 2-3 talus with no technical climbing required in summer conditions.
backups.turnaround: Given the length of the approach (20+ miles round trip from the trailhead) and off-trail talus terrain, set a firm turnaround time that leaves ample daylight to redescend the valley trail before dark, and be prepared to bail from the summit slopes if fog or weather moves in and cairns become hard to follow.
backups.face: South/southwest basin slopes above upper Necklace Valley, below La Bohn Gap
backups.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
backups.descent: Reverse the east ridge/face back down to La Bohn Gap, staying well back from the cliff band that drops away on the north side of the summit block and taking care on loose talus; from the gap, reverse the boot path down the La Bohn Creek drainage into upper Necklace Valley to regain the maintained Necklace Valley Trail.
obj_haz: loose talus and scree
lingering snowfields/ice in the approach gully into August
long remote off-trail approach with serious route-finding
afternoon thunderstorms on exposed ridges and slopes
