waypoints.name: East Fork Foss River / Necklace Valley Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk; trail follows an old railroad grade along the East Fork Foss River.

waypoints.name: East Fork Foss River crossing
waypoints.note: Log/boulder-hop ford of the East Fork Foss River with no bridge; can be a difficult, cold crossing at high water or early season.
waypoints.directions: The first five miles are the flattest of the route — barely 600 ft of gain along the river through old-growth forest, past established camps, with a spur path near mile 4 dropping to the water. Save your legs here, because everything above the crossing is steep.

waypoints.name: Jade Lake
waypoints.note: First and largest of the Necklace Valley 'gem' lakes, reached after a steep 2,400 ft climb in 3 miles above the river crossing; established campsites and reliable water, but campfires are banned above 4,000 ft in the wilderness.
waypoints.directions: Immediately past the river the trail turns steep and stays that way, gaining roughly 2,400 ft in three miles over large boulders and tree roots on rugged, minimally maintained tread. This is the crux of the approach for footing and stamina, and it is slow in both directions.

waypoints.name: Scree scramble to La Bohn Lakes
waypoints.note: Steep scree/boulder gully gains roughly 950 ft in half a mile above the valley floor to La Bohn Lakes; the boot path is faint and easy to lose, especially in fog or on lingering snow patches.
waypoints.directions: Continue up-valley past Emerald Lake, where a seasonal stream at the north end is the reliable water, toward Opal and Cloudy Lakes at the head of the valley — the maintained trail effectively ends here and boot paths fan out. From the Opal Lake camp area, pick up the crude unmaintained path climbing beside La Bohn Creek, the outlet stream of the La Bohn Lakes. It is west-facing and unshaded, hot in the afternoon, and there is no dependable water once you leave the valley floor.

waypoints.name: La Bohn Gap
waypoints.note: Broad saddle often called the geographic center of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness; routes toward Mt. Hinman, Iron Cap Mountain, and La Bohn Peak's southwest slopes all branch from here.
waypoints.directions: The path eases at the lowest La Bohn Lake; follow the shore and heather benches north to the upper lake, then make a short talus-and-heather traverse east to the broad saddle. Confirm you are at the right saddle before committing to any slope east of it — USGS maps label the gap roughly two-thirds of a mile southeast of its true position, and the ground east of the wrong gap ends in cliffs above Lake Rowena. Lingering snow can mask the correct line into early summer.

waypoints.name: La Bohn Peak
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 tag-on of roughly 700-1,000 ft from the gap up the southwest slopes/east ridge; broad rocky summit with views of Mt. Hinman, Mt. Daniel, and the Necklace Valley lakes below.

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for this unroped scramble; carry an ice axe and microspikes/light traction for the approach gully and any residual snow patches into mid-summer, plus trekking poles for the steep, loose talus.
what_to_bring: map/compass or GPS track for the unmaintained La Bohn Creek boot path
satellite communicator (no cell coverage beyond US 2)
pro_tips: Base-camp at La Bohn Lakes or upper Necklace Valley and day-trip the summit — it's a quick, worthwhile add-on from the gap.
Pair with Mount Hinman (1.7 mi east) for a two-summit day if conditions and daylight allow.
Filter water at La Bohn Lakes; carry what you need for the final scramble, which is dry.
watch_out: The summit block has a cliff band on its north side — don't wander north off the ridge/face line, especially in fog.
Snow/ice can linger in the summit gully into August in heavier-snow years — carry an ice axe even in mid-summer.
The gap-to-lakes boot path along La Bohn Creek is unmaintained, steep, and easy to lose — note your route for the return.
backups.pro_needs: No technical protection is used on this Class 2-3 talus scramble; carry an ice axe (and know how to self-arrest) if climbing early season while snow lingers near La Bohn Gap.
backups.approach: From the East Fork Foss River Trailhead (~1,650 ft, reached via a signed spur off US 2 near Skykomish), follow the Necklace Valley Trail #1062. The first ~5 miles are easy, gaining only about 600 ft as the trail parallels the East Fork Foss River through old-growth forest, passing established camps and a boot path near mile 4 that drops to the river for water. The trail then crosses the East Fork (log crossing, can be a wet-footed ford or tricky in high water/early season) and turns steep, climbing roughly 2,400 ft in the next 3 miles over large boulders and tree roots on a rugged, minimally maintained tread — the crux of the approach for footing and stamina. This deposits you at Jade Lake (~mile 8, 4,600 ft), the first of the Necklace Valley chain; continue past Emerald Lake (~mile 9, seasonal stream at its north end for water) toward Opal and Cloudy Lakes at the head of the valley under the cliffs of La Bohn Gap, where the maintained trail effectively ends and boot paths fan out. From the Opal Lake camp area, leave the trail and pick up a crude, unmaintained boot path climbing 'La Bohn Creek,' the outlet stream of La Bohn Lakes — a steep, west-facing, often hot and exposed slog with no reliable shade. This path eases at the lowest La Bohn Lake; continue north along the lakeshore/heather benches to the upper lake, then make a short talus/heather traverse east to the broad 5,900-ft saddle of La Bohn Gap (note: USGS maps mislabel the gap roughly 2/3 mile southeast of its true position — verify you're at the correct broad saddle before committing to slopes east of it, which end in a precipitous drop toward Lake Rowena). From the gap, ascend talus and open slopes on the southwest side, staying left (west/south) of the broad west ridge, to gain La Bohn Peak's summit (6,585 ft). An alternative that avoids losing/regaining elevation is to leave the main trail near Tank Lakes and follow the 'Magic Staircase' — a bench around 5,200–5,400 ft on La Bohn Peak's south side — over to Chain Lakes and then up to La Bohn Gap from the south. Total one-way distance to the summit is roughly 9–10 miles from the trailhead with about 5,000 ft of cumulative gain; this is realistically a 2-3 day backpack for most parties rather than a car-to-car push. Water is reliable along the East Fork Foss and at the Necklace Valley lakes but scarce above La Bohn Lakes.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is involved. Descend the same southwest-slope talus and open ground back down to La Bohn Gap, watching footing on loose, occasionally wobbly boulders (parties describe roughly 1,500 ft of piled boulders, some that wobble, on this face). From the gap, reverse the boot path down the steep La Bohn Creek drainage to the La Bohn Lakes and back into Necklace Valley, then rejoin the Necklace Valley Trail #1062 for the long descent back through the boulder/root section to Jade Lake and out along the East Fork Foss River to the trailhead. Parties wanting to avoid re-losing and re-gaining elevation at the gap can instead descend south from the gap to Chain Lakes and take the 'Magic Staircase' bench (~5,200–5,400 ft) back toward Tank Lakes before dropping into Necklace Valley — a reasonable variation but not shorter, mainly smoother underfoot. Key hazards on descent are the same as on ascent in reverse: loose/unstable talus on the peak's flank, potential lingering snow patches on the upper slopes into early summer (which can mask the correct gap location — the true La Bohn Gap is commonly misidentified from the USGS map, and dropping east of the wrong 'gap' leads onto cliffs above Lake Rowena), and the steep, exposed, often-hot boot path down the La Bohn Creek drainage, which is unpleasant and slick if wet. The East Fork Foss River crossing partway down should be treated with the same caution as on the approach.
backups.bail: There is no technical descent to rig; retreat simply means reversing the talus slopes back toward La Bohn Gap/La Bohn Lakes at any point.

pitch_detail.notes: Talus/scree gully ('Waterfall Route') from the upper Necklace Valley basin near Opal Lake up to the shelf/ridge below La Bohn Gap; loose rock, short 3rd/4th-class steps, occasional snow patches.
Boulder and talus ridge walk over a false summit to the true summit, roughly 1/8 mile of exposed scrambling.

itinerary.cal: Self-issue wilderness permits (free) are required at the trailhead year-round; the steep final approach to Jade Lake and the gap can hold snow into July, so most parties go July-September.

days.note: From the East Fork Foss trailhead (~1,650 ft) the Necklace Valley trail is gentle for about 5 miles along the river, then kicks up hard for the final ~2-3 miles, gaining roughly 2,500 ft to Jade Lake (~4,600 ft) — the standard base camp for La Bohn Gap. Most parties treat this as a full but straightforward backpacking day, arriving with time to camp, filter water, and scope the gap.
days.title: Backpack in to Jade Lake / La Bohn Lakes
days.objective: Reach high camp below La Bohn Gap

days.note: Break camp early and day-pack up boulder/talus slopes to La Bohn Gap (~5,900 ft), then follow the east ridge/face on solid rock to the summit block — a short, straightforward scramble with light 3rd/easy 4th-class moves near the top. After tagging the summit, most parties return to camp, pack up, and hike the full distance back to the trailhead the same day, making for a long but very doable second day.

schedule.label: Summit La Bohn Peak

days.objective: Tag La Bohn Peak via La Bohn Gap, then pack out to the trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day / 1-night backpack: ~20 mi round trip with ~5,200 ft of total gain, camping at Jade Lake and day-tripping the short summit scramble from La Bohn Gap before hiking all the way out. Very fit parties occasionally push the whole thing car-to-car in one long day (~9-10 hrs), but most parties overnight at Jade/La Bohn Lakes given the long, steep approach.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass required to park at the trailhead ($5/day or $30/annual).
access.rules: No campfires in Necklace Valley; dogs must be leashed; maximum group size 12; no bikes, stock, or motorized use (Wilderness).
access.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the East Fork Foss River trailhead register, required for day and overnight use May 15–Oct 31.
access.closures: Foss River Road (FR 68) has intermittent daytime delays/short closures posted mid-July through fall 2026 for powerline trenching work — check Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts before driving up.
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Skykomish Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required at developed trailheads.

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry your copy.

road.name: Foss River Road (FR 68)
road.status: Gravel, rough with potholes; passable to most passenger cars but high-clearance/AWD recommended. The Forest Service's Skykomish District road-damage alert of June 30, 2026 reports road damage high on Foss River Road (FR 68) that prevents access to the top of the road; it gives no milepost and no end date. Skykomish Ranger District: (360) 677-2414.
road.driveNote: 4.1–4.2 mi from US 2 (0.5 mi east of the Skykomish Ranger Station) to the East Fork Foss River/Necklace Valley trailhead (~1,600–1,650 ft); the last mile can hold snow into early summer.
road.seasonalGate: No seasonal gate, but intermittent daytime closures/delays are posted for FR 68 from mid-July through fall 2026 for powerline trenching — check the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts page before driving up.

climate.typical: Cool, changeable Cascades alpine weather; the gap and lakes basin commonly hold snow into July, and afternoon thunderstorms/humid buildups are common in late summer.

bySeason.fall: Good, often clear conditions into September and early October; nights are cold and the first snow can arrive by mid-October.
bySeason.spring: Lower Necklace Valley (to Jade/Emerald Lakes) is typically snow-free by June, but the gap, summit gully, and La Bohn Creek boot path usually still hold significant snow — expect an ice axe and possibly traction.
bySeason.summer: Late July through September is the reliable snow-free window for the summit scramble; trip reports cluster in August.
bySeason.winter: Not a realistic winter objective — deep unbroken snow on the long Necklace Valley approach and avalanche terrain above the gap.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Stevens Pass zone (avalanche/shoulder-season) and NWS King County Cascades forecast zone.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable to absent along the Necklace Valley trail and at La Bohn Gap/Lakes — the last reliable signal is generally near US 2. Carry a satellite communicator or PLB.
emergency.rangerStation: Skykomish Ranger District, Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — (360) 677-2414, 74920 NE Stevens Pass Hwy, Skykomish, WA 98288
emergency.nearestHospital: EvergreenHealth Monroe (ER), 14701 179th Ave SE, Monroe, WA — roughly 30 mi / ~45 min via US 2 west; far closer than Snoqualmie Valley Hospital, which requires a long cross-corridor drive from this trailhead.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: King County Sheriff's Office non-emergency: 206-296-3311 (coordinates King County Search & Rescue); call 911 for active emergencies.

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends in August, often as a side-summit from a Necklace Valley backpacking trip or paired with Mount Hinman/La Bohn-Tank loop objectives
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low - likely well under 50 parties tag the summit per season; the Necklace Valley trail below sees heavy backpacker traffic (one August trip report counted ~20 backpacking groups to Emerald Lake) but reporters note almost no one continues past La Bohn Gap to the peak itself

fitnessSpec.hiking: 9+ miles one-way to La Bohn Gap with roughly 4,000+ ft of gain via the Necklace Valley trail; most parties camp in the valley and day-trip the peak, so plan for a multi-day-fitness itinerary rather than a single big day
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/backpacking weight (tent, food, bear canister) for the approach; light day pack for the summit push from camp

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - typically a 2-3 day itinerary (hike in, summit day, hike out); a single-push day climb is possible for very fit parties but uncommon given ~18+ miles round trip
requiredSkills: Off-trail navigation on talus and heather
Comfort with loose scree/rock underfoot
Early-season snow travel and basic self-arrest awareness if attempting before the slopes fully melt out
Backcountry camping competence (most parties base out of Necklace Valley or La Bohn Gap)
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate scrambler - comfortable with sustained Class 2-3 talus/heather terrain, off-trail route-finding above La Bohn Gap, and a long multi-day-caliber approach; not a beginner's first scramble given the mileage

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through September, with August the prime month

July.reason: Early July still carries lingering snow patches on the slopes; conditions firm up and become good by mid-to-late month, matching the season start of mid-July

June.reason: Approach and southwest slopes still largely snow-covered; spring snow cover with avalanche risk on the slopes

August.reason: Best window - dry talus and heather, most reliable conditions

September.reason: Continues the dry-talus summer window; early-month conditions remain solid, with increasing chance of early snow toward month's end

weather.typical: Maritime Cascade weather - clearest and driest mid-to-late summer, with the southwest-facing slopes shedding snow earlier than shaded aspects
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are possible in Aug on exposed alpine slopes near the gap; otherwise summer weather is generally stable

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Low-to-moderate consequence: sustained Class 2-3 talus and scree with loose rock underfoot, plus residual early-season snow on the slopes that can mask footing or create slip potential above the gap; no sustained cliff-band exposure on this route

avalanche.zone: West Slopes Central Cascades (NWAC) - approximate; this peak sits between the Stevens Pass and Snoqualmie Pass forecast areas and has no dedicated NWAC zone or specific forecast product

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; this is a talus/heather scramble route, not a glaciated approach

gaps: No confirmed GPS track/waypoints for the gap-to-summit scramble line
Standalone car-to-car round-trip mileage/elevation gain not consistently documented across sources
First-ascent history not found
GPS track sourced from public CalTopo map: https://caltopo.com/m/U9F3

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

backups.rope_note: Class 2-3 talus/scree slope approach near Necklace Valley/La Bohn Gap; a couloir ('waterfall route') variant flanks the peak. No technical rope needed under normal summer conditions.
backups.corrections: No route-specific gear beta found; inferred from general La Bohn Peak/Gap approach descriptions.

approach_variants.name: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Creek to the gap
approach_variants.notes: The first five miles of the Necklace Valley Trail are nearly flat along the river; save your legs, because everything above the log crossing of the East Fork Foss is steep. Roughly 2,400 ft of gain in three miles over large boulders and tree roots on rugged tread brings you to Jade Lake, then it is up-valley past Emerald toward Opal and Cloudy Lakes where the maintained trail effectively ends. From the Opal Lake camps pick up the crude path climbing beside La Bohn Creek — west-facing, unshaded and hot in the afternoon — to the lowest La Bohn Lake, then follow the shore and heather benches north to the upper lake.
hazards: Roughly 1,500 ft of piled boulders on the peak's flank, many of which wobble
Steep, unshaded and slick-when-wet boot path up the La Bohn Creek drainage
Foot-log crossing of the East Fork Foss at high snowmelt
Snow lingering on the upper slopes that masks the correct saddle
Cliffs above Lake Rowena on the ground east of the wrong gap
approach_variants.baseFinding: The identification problem here is the gap itself, and the map is against you: published mapping labels La Bohn Gap roughly two-thirds of a mile southeast of where it actually sits, and the slopes east of that false gap end in a precipitous drop toward Lake Rowena. Verify before you commit to any slope east of a saddle. The true gap is a broad, tarn-dotted saddle at about 5,900 ft, reached by a short talus-and-heather traverse EAST from the upper La Bohn Lake; it is genuinely broad and open, with Mount Hinman filling the view across it and La Bohn Peak's talus rising directly to the west. Lingering snow can hide the correct line into early summer, which is exactly when parties pick the wrong saddle. From the right gap the climbing is straightforward: talus and open slopes on the southwest side, staying left — west and south — of the broad west ridge for the last thousand feet or so. The crest carries a false summit a short way short of the true top, with the final eighth of a mile a walk along the summit ridge.

climbing_route.label: Southwest slopes from La Bohn Gap
climbing_route.notes: From the broad 5,900-ft saddle of La Bohn Gap, ascend talus and open slopes on the southwest side, staying left (west/south) of the broad west ridge, to gain the 6,585 ft summit. Route-finding trap at the gap: USGS maps mislabel it roughly 2/3 mile southeast of its true position, so verify you are at the correct broad saddle before committing to slopes east of it, which end in a precipitous drop toward Lake Rowena. Water is scarce above La Bohn Lakes.

bivy.name: Necklace Valley — Jade, Emerald and Opal Lakes
bivy.notes: The main basecamp for LA BOHN PEAK, which stands directly at the head of this valley, and the first night of the standard west-side approach to MOUNT HINMAN. Drive the Foss River road off Highway 2 a short way east of Skykomish and turn into the Necklace Valley trailhead about four miles up. The trail is famously two-faced: the first five miles along the East Fork Foss gain only about 600 ft through regenerated second growth and go quickly, then the trail crosses the river and climbs roughly 2,400 ft in the next three miles to break out at Jade Lake around 4,600 ft. Emerald is a quarter mile further, Opal about 4,790 ft above that, with Ilswoot, Locket, Jewel and Cloudy scattered on either side. A weathered memorial cabin sits in the meadow just above Emerald; it is a landmark and a piece of the valley's mining history, not a shelter to plan on. From Opal or Emerald the route to La Bohn Gap climbs east under the cliffs, so Jade is fractionally further from the gap but Emerald and Opal put you closest to the day's work. Two honest caveats. The Foss River road has been under construction with weekday delays of about half an hour through the summer, and damage higher on the road has at times cut off the upper end, so allow slack and check before committing to a dawn start. And this valley is very popular for its own sake — a midweek trip is far more pleasant than a Saturday, and the steep middle section is genuinely unpleasant under a heavy climbing pack in the heat.
bivy.water: All four lakes, plus the creek linking them. Reliable the whole season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size limited to twelve including stock. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the range, which puts every lake in the valley under a fire ban — carry a stove and do not build rings.
bivy.capacity: Sites are spread across four separate lake basins rather than concentrated, so the valley absorbs a lot of parties — several groups at Jade, several more around Emerald and Opal, and quieter singles at Ilswoot, Locket and Jewel off to the sides. On a summer weekend the popular shorelines are full by mid-afternoon.

bivy.name: La Bohn Lakes, La Bohn Gap and the Chain Lakes benches
bivy.notes: The high camp for LA BOHN PEAK and the launching point for the west route on MOUNT HINMAN, and the single most useful piece of ground in this zone for a climber. La Bohn Gap is a broad boulder-covered saddle at roughly 6,000 ft on the crest between the Foss and Snoqualmie drainages, with the tarns of the La Bohn Lakes scattered on the benches around it and the Chain Lakes sitting lower at about 5,515 ft in the gully on the south side of La Bohn Peak. From Necklace Valley the climb to the lakes goes either up to the gap itself or by a steeper line beside the waterfall; both are straightforward in summer and both hold snow into July. La Bohn Peak is a short class 2 walk west from the gap. For Hinman the ground continues east and then north, half a mile of easy going to gain the gap area and then a long open ascent to the summit — worth knowing that the Hinman Glacier shown on older maps has essentially gone, so what you will actually cross is a shrinking snowfield with the moat and loose-rock problems that come with that, and conditions vary enormously year to year. The gap is also the hinge of the whole area on foot: north drops into Necklace Valley, south drops toward Dutch Miller Gap and the upper Middle Fork Snoqualmie, and the view takes in Bald Eagle, Silver Eagle and Big Heart Lake off to the west. Camping here is committing. It is fully exposed, the weather arrives without warning, and a bad night in the gap is a real one — carry proper shelter or drop back to the Necklace lakes.
bivy.water: The La Bohn tarns and the Chain Lakes below the gap on the south side, plus lingering snowmelt into midsummer. Late in a dry season the smaller tarns can drop and turn silty; check rather than assume.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, picked up at whichever trailhead you start from. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. Campfires prohibited outright — everything here is well above the 4,000 ft fire-ban line and there is no wood to burn anyway. Camp on rock or bare gravel, not on the heather, which takes decades to recover at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small, exposed pitches on granite benches and heather shelves between the tarns — realistically two or three tents in the good spots, more if you are willing to sleep on rock. There is no sheltered ground.

bivy.name: Money Creek and Miller River campgrounds, Foss River roadhead
bivy.notes: The valley-bottom staging option for every Foss River objective, and worth a line of its own because of what the road has been doing. The Foss River road leaves Highway 2 just east of Skykomish and has been running weekday construction delays of about half an hour through the summer, with damage further up that has at times cut off the top of the road, while the West Fork Foss spur has been impassable to vehicles and adding a two-and-a-half-mile road walk. All of that argues for sleeping close to the highway the night before rather than driving out in the dark and discovering the situation at 5 a.m. Both campgrounds sit off the old highway just west of milepost 46 — one on the South Fork Skykomish in old growth, the other a mile or two up the Miller River road — and both are twenty minutes or so from either Foss trailhead. This is the practical first night for a party heading to Necklace Valley for LA BOHN PEAK or MOUNT HINMAN, or up the West Fork for BALD EAGLE PEAK. Open roughly late May through September; outside that, it is roadside pull-outs and your own judgement.
bivy.water: Piped or hand-pumped drinking water on site, with the South Fork Skykomish and the Miller River beside them. No treating required.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fees, and reservations for most sites. No wilderness permit needed at this elevation — pick that up at the trailhead the next morning. Campfires are allowed in the provided rings when there is no seasonal fire ban in force, which is the last time you will see one on any of these trips.
bivy.capacity: Money Creek has around twenty-five sites, a couple of them first-come; Miller River is a group camp of about fifteen sites with a gathering area. Both take vehicles and both fill on summer weekends, so reserve where you can.

bivy.name: Jade Lake

backups.name: West Ridge / Southwest Gully
gear: ice axe (needed for the trail's north side and approach gullies into early-mid July)
crampons (the steep snowfield traverse below Kitling Peak can hold hard snow well into summer)
30m rope or a few slings if you prefer to rappel the crux chockstone in the summit gully (a fixed sling has been reported there)
hazards: loose, blocky rock along the ridge crest and summit gullies — rockfall risk to any party below
steep, hard snow in the approach gullies and on the Ragged Ridge traverse below Kitling Peak, often lingering into July
exposed Class 4 traverse around the north side of a false summit block just below the true summit
complex, cliffy gully/rib maze on the final summit pyramid — parties repeatedly report getting cliffed out without a GPX track or route photos
long, remote, very exposed ridge traverse with few bail options and high exposure to afternoon thunderstorms
backups.overview: Mesahchie Peak (8,795 ft) is the highest of four Bulger List summits on Ragged Ridge, 0.25 mi east of Katsuk Peak, between the Fisher Creek and Thunder Creek drainages in North Cascades National Park. First climbed in 1966. It's often cited as one of the hardest non-technical Bulgers on the list: the standard lines need no rope or glacier travel, but loose, blocky rock, a confusing gully/rib maze on the summit pyramid, and a long, exposed cross-country traverse of the Ragged Ridge crest from Easy Pass make route-finding and scrambling skill the real crux. Trip reports commonly note 'there's nothing easy about Easy Pass.'
backups.beta: Grade: Class 3/4 scramble on rocky terrain. Route description: From Mesahchie Col, cross talus to base of first obvious gully leading up west ridge. Initial section steep class 3/4 at bottom, broadens into gentler gully passing cairns. At 8,100 ft, descend 100 feet to enter south-side Class 3 gully with beige rock. Climb gully until it steepens, locate notch on left side, climb Class 4 deep cut traverse into second gully leading to ridge crest. Hazards: Extremely loose rock (every handhold requires testing), narrow ridge with significant exposure at summit. Required skills: Rock scrambling Class 3/4, exposure comfort. First ascent: 1966. Peak elevation: 8,795 feet (2,681 m), highest in Ragged Ridge.
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.descent: From the summit, reverse the ascending gully/rib system to the ~8,050 ft ridge shoulder below the summit pyramid, downclimbing the crux Class 4 chockstone gully (a fixed rappel sling has been reported at this spot for parties who prefer to rappel it) and re-crossing the exposed traverse around the north side of the false summit block. Many parties avoid reversing the same terrain by ascending one ridge (e.g., the East Ridge) and descending the other (West Ridge/Southwest Gully), looping back down through forest to the Fisher Creek Trail before returning to Easy Pass. Watch for lingering steep, hard snow in the descent gullies, especially before August.
obj_haz: rockfall from loose blocky terrain on the ridge and summit gullies
sun-softened or hard-frozen snow on the approach traverse and gullies depending on time of day/season
afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the long, open ridge crest with few retreat options

waypoints.name: Easy Pass / Fisher Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: On SR-20 near milepost 151, ~10-car lot with pit toilet; Northwest Forest Pass required to park.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Easy Pass/Fisher Creek Trailhead on SR-20, a marked pullout near milepost 151 about five miles west of Rainy Pass at roughly 3,700 feet elevation. The lot holds about ten cars, has a pit toilet and no water, and a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park. Overnight camping requires a backcountry permit, reserved in advance through Recreation.gov or picked up as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

waypoints.name: Easy Pass
waypoints.note: Trail crests the Forest Service/North Cascades NP boundary here; views of Mt. Logan and Fisher Peak before the trail switchbacks down into Fisher Basin.
waypoints.directions: The Easy Pass Trail climbs steadily through forest and then open meadow and talus, gaining about 2,800 ft over three and a half miles; a fit party takes an hour and a half to two hours. Streams are reliable lower down but there is none at the pass itself, so fill up before the last switchbacks.

waypoints.name: Fisher Camp
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp (3 tent sites, privy) in the Fisher Creek valley with water from Fisher Creek just downhill; used as the jump-off point to leave the trail for Mesahchie's south side.
waypoints.directions: From the pass the trail switchbacks down the far side, losing roughly 1,400 ft over three miles into the Fisher Creek valley. Every foot of that has to be climbed again at the end of the trip — budget around six hours summit-to-car and do not judge the exit by how fast this descent goes.

waypoints.name: Off-trail turnoff above Fisher Camp
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Fisher Creek Trail roughly a half-mile past Fisher Camp and head upslope along the stream draining Mesahchie's southeast/south basin.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the Fisher Creek Trail for roughly another half mile past the camp, continuing gently downstream, until you reach a grassy, flower-filled glade. Nothing marks the departure and the maintained trail carries on past it, so it is worth fixing on a track; this is the last built tread of the day.

waypoints.name: 8,050 ft ridge shoulder
waypoints.note: Flat spot on the ridge at the base of the summit pyramid where the south rib meets the southwest gully system; descend a few feet south to enter the climbing gully.
waypoints.directions: Head cross-country and uphill along the drainage above the trail. Around 6,500 ft the line crosses a waterfall on an easy bench — the last reliable water, and the one real hazard on the approach, since it is slick and worse after rain or with snow still around. Above it, work up a mix of scree, talus, grass benches and low-angle blocky rock, threading short cliff bands and steep heather to a shoulder near 6,700-6,800 ft with flat bivy ground, then up the ridge crest itself, where a few Class 4 moves are needed to get established, onto gentler but loose cairned terrain. Everything above Fisher Creek is unmarked and parties do get cliffed out on this flank, so carry a GPX track or route photos rather than working from a description.

waypoints.name: Chockstone notch (crux gully)
waypoints.note: Rap-sling and cairn-marked gully narrows here; a Class 4 move past a chockstone in a notch gains the final summit ridge — very loose rock, test every hold.
waypoints.directions: Drop south off the shoulder to enter the first obvious gully on the southwest side, identifiable by its beige rock. It is steep Class 3-4 where it starts, then broadens and eases once a string of cairns appears. Follow it up until it steepens again and look left for the notch.

waypoints.name: Summit ridge crest
waypoints.note: Narrow crest with a series of small false points leading to the true summit; exposed scrambling on both sides.
waypoints.directions: The Class 4 move past the chockstone leads into a deep-cut traverse and a second gully, which runs up to the crest. The rock through here is genuinely rotten — test every hold, and keep the party out from under each other, because anything knocked loose funnels straight down the gully.

waypoints.name: Mesahchie Peak
waypoints.note: True summit of Ragged Ridge's highest point; panoramic views of Mt. Logan, Goode, and the Fisher Creek/Thunder Creek drainages.
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest over a series of small false points. One of them is turned by an exposed Class 4 traverse around its north side, the most committing move on the route; confirm the holds and your retreat before starting across. Past it the ridge is moderate but narrow, dropping away on both sides, to the top.

sectionBreakdown.note: From camp, gear up light and climb the Southwest Gully system to the summit, downclimbing the same Class 3-4 terrain to return to camp. Many parties tag nearby Katsuk Peak (0.25 mi…

pro_tips: A fixed rappel sling and a large cairn mark the top of the crux chockstone gully — a useful way-finding checkpoint on both ascent and descent.
Many parties ascend one ridge (commonly the East Ridge) and descend the other (West Ridge/Southwest Gully) to make a loop back to the Fisher Creek Trail instead of reversing the same terrain.
Katsuk Peak is only 0.25 mi west of the summit and is frequently tagged on the same trip.
watch_out: The summit pyramid's gully/rib network is genuinely confusing — several parties have gotten cliffed out; carry route photos or a GPX track rather than relying on the general description.
The false-summit Class 4 traverse around the north side is 'wildly exposed' per multiple trip reports — don't commit without confirming the holds and turnaround options.
Hard, steep snow below Kitling Peak on the ridge traverse can persist into July even in an average year.
backups.pro_needs: Generally unroped scramble; a short rope and minimal protection useful for the exposed class 4 step in marginal conditions.
backups.approach: Start at the Easy Pass/Fisher Creek Trailhead on SR-20 (marked pullout near milepost 151, about 5 miles west of Rainy Pass, elevation ~3,700 ft; room for roughly 10 cars, pit toilet, no water at the lot). Follow the Easy Pass Trail, which climbs steadily through forest and then open meadows/talus, gaining roughly 2,800 ft over about 3.6 miles to Easy Pass (~6,500 ft); budget 1.5-2 hours at a good pace. There are reliable streams along the lower trail but none right at the pass, so top off water before cresting. From Easy Pass, drop about 1,400-1,500 ft on the Fisher Creek Trail into the Fisher Creek valley, passing Fisher Camp (~5,100 ft) and continuing downstream roughly another half mile to a grassy, flower-filled glade below Mesahchie's west/southwest flank - this is the key junction where you leave the maintained trail. Head cross-country and uphill, aiming for the drainage that comes down off Mesahchie's basin; around 6,500 ft the route crosses a waterfall on an easy bench (last reliable water before the ridge, and the one real ford/hazard on the approach - can be slick and is worse early season or after rain). Above the crossing, ascend a mix of scree, talus, grass benches and low-angle blocky rock, with steep heather slopes and short cliff bands requiring some routefinding, to a shoulder around 6,700-6,800 ft below the west ridge - a common bivy/high-camp site with flat tent spots. From here, work up the ridge crest (some class 4 moves getting established) to gentler but loose, cairned terrain leading to a col with a good bivy site. From the col, cross talus to the base of the first obvious gully leading up the southwest/west ridge - steep class 3/4 at its bottom, then broadening and easing after a string of cairns - and follow it to the ridge crest, then the exposed but moderate ridgecrest to the summit. Trailhead to the col/high-camp shoulder typically takes 4-4.5 hours for a fit party; the whole approach is loose and unmarked above Fisher Creek, so GPS or a photo of the route is worth having. Total one-way distance/gain to the summit run around 12 km and 4,900 ft of the route's overall 24.1 km / 7,480 ft round trip.
backups.descent_text: Standard descent is to reverse the ascent line: downclimb the ridgecrest and southwest gully back to the col, cross the talus to the ~6,700 ft shoulder/bivy site, then pick back down through the cliff bands and heather slopes to the cross-country entry point near the waterfall crossing and back onto the Fisher Creek Trail, before climbing back over Easy Pass and dropping to the trailhead. There is no mandatory rappelling - this is a class 3-4 scramble route and most parties downclimb the entire way - but an old rap sling sits on the bench at the top of the class 4 chockstone gully, and parties uncomfortable downclimbing that chockstone step sometimes back it off with a single-rope rappel (one rope length, roughly 30-50 ft, off the existing tat/natural block anchor - bring your own rap gear and consider backing up old slings, as their age/condition is unknown) rather than downclimbing it. The heather and slab sections lower down get notably treacherous when wet (parties describe lichen/moss-covered rock and multiple slips/falls in rain), and the waterfall crossing and loose talus/scree throughout are the main ongoing hazards. Summit-to-trailhead descent time is typically around 6 hours for a fit party (about 2 hours summit to high camp, remainder back to the car).
backups.bail: Retreat down the ascent gully; no easier alternative descent.

itinerary.cal: Overnight camping on Ragged Ridge is inside North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness) and requires a backcountry permit (quota via recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center); the route is typically snow-free and most climbed July-September.

days.note: Hike the maintained Easy Pass Trail to the pass, then leave the trail for cross-country ridge travel west along the Ragged Ridge crest, sidehilling below Point 7,690, crossing the 7,450 ft saddle south of Kitling Peak, and scrambling over Cub Peak (Class 3) before dropping to a flat camp spot on Mesahchie's shoulder. Route-finding on loose rock and heather benches is the crux of the day, not the elevation gain.

Many parties tag nearby Katsuk Peak (0.25 mi west) on the same push. After breaking camp, retrace Day 1's ridge traverse and trail back to the car, making for a long second day.

itinerary.totalNote: A remote 2-day scramble (~15 mi round trip, ~7,480 ft cumulative gain) with a high camp on Ragged Ridge below Mesahchie's south/east shoulder; very fit parties instead push it car-to-car in one very long (12+ hr) day.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 fee for an overnight wilderness permit (youth 15 and under free); a Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful interagency pass is separately required for trailhead parking on SR-20.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Stay on trail, snow, or rock in the fragile subalpine terrain near the pass; no camping at Easy Pass itself; pets are prohibited throughout the national park; bear canisters are required (and loaned free) for some backcountry camps.
access.permit: Mandatory NPS wilderness permit for any overnight stay: $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee, youth 15 and under free. Reserve in advance on Recreation.gov (watch the mandatory safety/rules video, then email noca_wilderness@nps.gov up to 3 days before the trip) or get a walk-up permit in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount (about 40% of permits are held for walk-ups). No camping is allowed at Easy Pass or in the surrounding meadows; nearest designated camps are Fisher Camp (~2 mi past the pass) and Cosho Camp (~6 mi along Fisher Creek). Day climbs with no overnight stay do not require a permit.
access.closures: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes every winter due to avalanche hazard through the Rainy/Washington Pass corridor, typically from early December until sometime between late May and late June depending on snowpack (it opened as late as June 25 in 2026). The Easy Pass/Fisher Creek trailhead at milepost 151 is unreachable by car until the highway reopens.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (National Park Service)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP wilderness permit — quota, fee
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov; permits for Cascade River Road trailheads must be picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

road.name: North Cascades Highway (State Route 20)
road.status: Seasonal — gated closed in winter/spring due to avalanche hazard through Rainy and Washington Passes.
road.driveNote: Trailhead is 32 mi east of Newhalem and about 5 mi west of Rainy Pass, on the south side of SR-20 at milepost 151; parking requires a Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass.
road.seasonalGate: Typically closed early December through late May or June depending on snowpack (reopened as late as June 25 in 2026); Easy Pass Trailhead (MP 151) is inaccessible by car until the gates open.

climate.typical: Marine-influenced alpine climate with a heavy winter snowpack (the highway itself closes for avalanche hazard) and a short, generally reliable dry window from roughly late July through September. Afternoon thunderstorms and fast-moving weather are common on the exposed ridge crest in summer.

bySeason.fall: Larches turn gold in the high basins by late September/early October; days shorten and storm frequency increases.
bySeason.summer: Prime climbing window; expect residual snow on north-facing gullies and the Kitling Peak traverse into early-mid July, generally snow-free and driest by August.
bySeason.winter: SR-20 is gated closed and the approach is not feasible without extensive ski/snowshoe travel and serious avalanche exposure.

emergency.notes: This is a remote, multi-hour cross-country evacuation off the Ragged Ridge crest with unreliable cell coverage; a satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) is strongly advised. Serious trauma cases from this area are typically airlifted (Airlift Northwest or military SAR) directly to Harborview Medical Center, Seattle's Level I trauma center, rather than driven out.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Road, Marblemount, WA 98267 (open mid-May to mid-October); (360) 854-7245.
emergency.nearestHospital: Skagit Valley Hospital (Level III trauma center), 300 Hospital Pkwy, Mount Vernon, WA — roughly 60-65 miles / 1.5+ hrs drive from the Easy Pass trailhead.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911; after-hours SAR coordination via Skagit County Sheriff (360) 336-9450, or NPS Communications Center after-hours (360) 873-4590 ext. 37.

crowds.peakTraffic: If any, late July through August once approach gullies clear of snow and Easy Pass trail is fully melted out; essentially empty on weekdays and in shoulder months
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very low — likely well under 20 parties per season; no route-specific numeric logs found, this is a rough estimate based on remoteness and reported solitude

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong, multi-day fitness: long off-trail approach over Easy Pass to a high camp (~6,700 ft) on Mesahchie's south shoulder before a full summit day on exposed terrain
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/multi-day pack (typically 2-3 day trip with camp at Fisher Camp or high camp) — expect roughly 30-40+ lb with camping gear, water, and scrambling kit

partner_requirements.approachTime: Multi-day approach: Easy Pass trail to Fisher Camp (~5,100 ft) then up to a high camp on Mesahchie's south shoulder (~6,700 ft); typically climbed as a 2-3 day trip rather than a single push
requiredSkills: Route-finding on complex, unmarked ridge/gully terrain
Comfort with sustained exposure on loose Class 3-4 rock
Basic snow travel / self-arrest for early-season snow lingering in approach gullies
Off-trail navigation (map/compass/GPS) — no maintained trail beyond Easy Pass
Rockfall awareness and party spacing in loose gullies
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine scrambler comfortable with sustained, committing Class 3-4 terrain, loose/blocky rock, and cross-country route-finding on a remote unmaintained ridge — not appropriate for a scrambling novice's first outing.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September; late July through August is the most reliable stretch once approach gullies have shed snow

July.reason: Early-to-mid July gullies may still hold snow; conditions steadily improve and by late July this becomes a solid window.

June.reason: Approach basins are still snow-covered and in avalanche terrain this early in the season; not the intended window for this scramble.

August.reason: Prime scrambling window — gullies typically clear and weather is most stable, aside from afternoon thunderstorm risk.

September.reason: Still within the best-season; stable but shorter days and increasing chance of early-season storms.

weather.typical: Alpine North Cascades weather; rapid changes possible — the North Cascades are known for fast-moving fronts that can turn a clear morning into poor visibility on exposed ridge terrain.
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a noted hazard here; combined with an early-dawn recommended start, this points to a strong pattern of building afternoon convection in summer that parties should beat by climbing early.

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High-consequence: sustained Class 3-4 climbing on loose, blocky rock along a committing ridge/gully system; a slip or rockfall from another party could cause a serious fall or strike a climber below.

avalanche.zone: No NWAC zone precisely covers Ragged Ridge/Easy Pass terrain; the nearest reference is the Washington Pass zone, and in any case NWAC issues forecasts only while SR-20 is open in winter/spring, so it has limited relevance to this route's actual (summer) climbing season

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - this route (West Ridge/Southwest Gully) stays on rock/gully terrain and does not cross glaciers; note the peak does have a small glacier/icefall on its north side (used by the separate Mesahchie Icefall Couloir route), which is not part of this route.

gaps: No single surveyed/official prominence figure was found; secondary sources disagree (2,235 ft per Wikipedia/NGS-derived data vs ~2,255 ft per a Peakbagger search snippet) — used the Wikipedia figure as internally consistent with the listed elevation.
Exact first-ascent date beyond the year (1966) and party names not established from available sources.
Approach/gain/distance stats are drawn from trip reports of a common East-Ridge-up/West-Ridge-down loop, not a single out-and-back on this specific route, so treat gain_ft/dist_km as approximate.
No trip reports newer than a few years old were reviewed, so current gully/snow conditions should be confirmed with a recent report before a trip.

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

backups.rope_note: The West Ridge gully is steep Class 3/4 at its base, broadens above cairns, then a narrower branch has a Class 4 chockstone; near the ridge crest climbers cross an exposed slab before a crux ~150 ft Class 4 blocky headwall to the false summit. Some parties carry a short rope/handline for the chockstone and headwall crux.
rack: Short rope/handline for the crux chockstone and headwall

approach_variants.name: Easy Pass into Fisher Creek, then the south basin
approach_variants.notes: From the marked pullout on SR-20 near milepost 151 the Easy Pass Trail climbs steadily through forest and then open meadow and talus to the pass; streams are reliable low down and there is none at the pass, so fill up before the last switchbacks. From the pass the trail switchbacks down the far side into the Fisher Creek valley, past Fisher Camp, and continues gently downstream for roughly another half mile to a grassy, flower-filled glade. Nothing marks the departure and the maintained trail carries on past it, so it is worth fixing on a track — this is the last built tread of the day. Head cross-country and uphill along the drainage that comes down off the peak's basin. Around 6,500 ft the line crosses a waterfall on an easy bench, the last reliable water and the one real hazard low down, since it is slick and worse after rain. Above it, work up scree, talus, grass benches and low-angle blocky rock, threading short cliff bands and steep heather to a shoulder near 6,700 to 6,800 ft with flat bivy ground, then up the ridge crest itself, where a few Class 4 moves get you established, onto gentler but loose cairned terrain leading to the col.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September. Snow lingers in the approach gullies and on the ridge traverse into July, and the heather and slab lower down turn treacherous when wet.
hazards: genuinely rotten rock in the summit gullies — every hold needs testing and anything knocked loose funnels down the gully onto the party
the cliffy gully-and-rib maze on the summit pyramid, where parties repeatedly get cliffed out without a track or route photos
an exposed Class 4 traverse around the north side of a false summit block just below the top
the waterfall crossing at 6,500 ft, slick and worse after rain or with snow still around
lichen- and moss-covered rock lower down that becomes very slippery when wet
a long, exposed ridge with few bail options and real exposure to afternoon thunderstorms
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ROCK CHANGES COLOUR AT THE START, AND THAT IS THE TEST. The base of the climbing is a flat spot on the ridge at about 8,050 ft where the south rib meets the gully system at the foot of the summit pyramid. From that flat spot you do not climb — you step DOWN a few feet to the south, on your left, to enter the first gully. The correct gully is unmistakably BEIGE, noticeably paler than the darker rock of the ridge you walked up, and it is steep Class 3 to 4 where it starts before broadening and easing once a string of cairns appears. Follow it until it steepens again and look left for a notch: a chockstone is jammed at the top of it and pulling past that chockstone is the Class 4 move that gains a deep-cut traverse into a second gully. Immediately above the chockstone you should arrive on a flat bench carrying an old rappel sling and a large cairn — if you have climbed a gully and found no bench, no sling and no cairn, you are in the wrong one. Two other ways to know you are wrong: if the gully rock is the same colour as the ridge, and if you started climbing upward from the flat spot instead of dropping a few feet south into it first.

climbing_route.label: West ridge crest to the col
climbing_route.notes: From the 6,700-6,800 ft shoulder, work up the ridge crest — some class 4 moves getting established — to gentler but loose, cairned terrain leading to a col with a good bivy site.

climbing_route.label: First gully on the southwest/west ridge
climbing_route.notes: From the col, cross talus to the base of the first obvious gully leading up the southwest/west ridge: steep class 3/4 at its bottom, then broadening and easing after a string of cairns; follow it to the ridge crest. Terrain here is loose and unmarked.

climbing_route.label: Ridgecrest to the summit
climbing_route.notes: The exposed but moderate ridgecrest leads to the summit.

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
bivy.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
bivy.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp

backups.name: Standard Scramble
backups.fa: Sam Heller, 1940 (first ascent of the peak, via this easiest Class 3 line)
gear: ice axe (useful through June/early July for the Headlee Pass chute and any lingering snow near the summit)
helmet (rockfall is common in the loose Headlee Pass chute)
sturdy boots with good ankle support
hazards: notorious rockfall chute immediately below Headlee Pass — helmet strongly recommended
difficult ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish ~0.5 mi from the trailhead; seasonal log crossings often washed out, especially during high runoff
lingering steep snow in the Headlee Pass gully and on north-facing terrain into July
