backups.overview: Morning Star Peak (6,020 ft) sits above Headlee Pass and the Sunrise Mine basin between Sperry and Del Campo Peaks, in the Mountain Loop Highway corridor of the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District). The standard route leaves the Sunrise Mine Trail about half a mile in, before the South Fork Stillaguamish crossing, and climbs the brushy river valley and snow-covered slabs to a notch in the southeast ridge, then a steep gully to the south ridge and the summit. The South Ridge scramble requires comfort on steep rock and snow and is tougher than the Class 2-3 label alone suggests, especially in early season. Route-finding takes some care, and the snow-covered slabs below the notch are the route's main avalanche concern.
backups.beta: The Standard Scramble represents the basic approach to Morning Star Peak's 6,020 ft summit. Multiple scramble options exist on the peak, including the South Ridge and Northwest Face routes, both of which involve Class 3 scrambling with sections of steep rock and snow.
backups.turnaround: Turn around if snow slopes are firm without an axe or weather closes in.
backups.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
backups.comms: Cell service is unreliable in the Stillaguamish River Valley and absent above ~4,000 feet. Assume no service; rely on satellite devices (Garmin inReach, PLB) for emergency communication.
backups.descent: Reverse the scramble toward Headlee Pass / Sunrise Mine Trail.
obj_haz: steep snow/ice in gully and notch outside summer
loose rock on upper ledges
off-trail route-finding through talus/brush
short class 4 step on the NW variant

sectionBreakdown.note: Standard scramble from the Sunrise Mine Trailhead: ford the South Fork Stillaguamish, climb to Headlee Pass, then traverse cairned talus and heather benches below the Mile High But…

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rack; ice axe useful early season for snow in the basin.
what_to_bring: Green Trails Mountain Loop Highway No. 111SX map
Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee
pro_tips: Start early, both to beat other parties into the loose Headlee Pass chute and to keep daylight margin for the descent
Carry an ice axe even in July in high-snow years — the chute below Headlee Pass holds snow longest
Green Trails 'Mountain Loop Highway No. 111SX' is the standard paper map for this approach
watch_out: rockfall in the Headlee Pass chute — go early and space out from other parties
high/unbridged river ford during spring snowmelt
afternoon thunderstorms are common in the North Cascades in summer — start early
backups.approach: From the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of FR-4065 off the Mountain Loop Highway), follow the Sunrise Mine Trail (Trail #707) about half a mile. Just before the trail crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish River, leave it for a faint abandoned path on the river's east side, or take the line of least resistance along that side. The path soon fades into slide alder, brush and rock debris; fording the river to dodge the brush is hazardous in high runoff, especially in late spring and early summer. Work up the valley past a house-sized boulder near 3,100 ft, then either cross the river and climb a ridge ramp southwest to the upper basin (about 4,000 ft), or continue to a broad basin at about 3,700 ft and climb the steep gully (or the slabs to its right) directly east of it, leaving it to the right where that is easy. Climb snow-covered slabs to a notch in Morning Star's southeast ridge at about 5,600 ft; these slabs are the route's main avalanche concern. The round trip is roughly 5.5-6 miles with 3,700-4,200 ft of gain. The steep gully is often icy when snow-filled, so helmet, ice axe and crampons are standard early in the season; early-season snow makes this a basic alpine climb rather than a scramble.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb — reverse the ascent line, there is no rappelling on the standard route (0 rappels). From the 6,020 ft summit, descend on or near the south ridge to the broad gully, downclimb it into the southeast basin, traverse back below the cliffs and climb about 200 ft through trees to the notch in the southeast ridge. The gully (icy in early/mid-season) is often easier to face in and downclimb than to descend facing out, and crampons make the icy sections much smoother; groups should stay tight and avoid stacking directly above one another. From the notch, descend the snow-covered slabs (watch for avalanche conditions) and the gully or ridge ramp back into the South Fork Stillaguamish valley, then retrace the brushy east-side path to the Sunrise Mine Trail and the trailhead.
backups.bail: Descend to the basin and trail.

pitch_detail.notes: Follow the Sunrise Mine Trail about half a mile. Just before it crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish, leave it for a faint abandoned path on the river's east side. The path comes and goes and soon vanishes into slide alder and brush, worst around 2,700 ft. Fording the river to dodge the brush is not safe when the water is high.

Keep working up the east side of the valley past a house-sized boulder near 3,000–3,100 ft. One option crosses the river here and climbs a ridge ramp southwest to an upper basin at 4,000 ft, which is brushier. The other follows the river to the broad basin at about 3,700 ft below Del Campo's north face. In spring this ground is piled with hard, lumpy avalanche debris shed off the slabs.

From the 3,700-ft basin turn sharply right up the steep gully directly east, or the slabs on its right. Leave it to the right once that is easy. At a headwall near 4,400 ft either climb straight up or go around through the trees, which is the easier line on snow and on the way down. The gully often holds snow into early summer, with water running down its middle.

Climb the slabs east to a notch in Morning Star's southeast ridge at about 5,600 ft. The summit comes into view on this flatter ground. These slabs hold snow well into the season and are the route's main avalanche concern. Close to the notch the snow can be icy under fresh snow, so put crampons on before it steepens.

From the notch drop roughly 100–200 ft through trees into the southeast basin (about 5,400 ft). Traverse right below the cliffs to the first broad gully and climb it to the south ridge about 250 ft below the summit. Filled with snow, the gully runs near 45° and is often icy, so crampons are standard. When the snow is bad, the rocks on its right are an alternative, but they are exposed.

Climb north on or near the south ridge over the last 200–250 ft of steep ground to the 6,020-ft summit. Early in the day the west-facing slope below the top can stay icy, so mix rock, heather and snow to avoid the iced patches. Descend the same way, taking particular care in the gully below.

itinerary.cal: Sunrise Mine Trailhead requires a NW Forest Pass; the trail is typically snow-free and brushy June through October.

days.note: Standard scramble from the Sunrise Mine Trailhead: ford the South Fork Stillaguamish, climb to Headlee Pass, then traverse cairned talus and heather benches below the Mile High Buttress before a short scramble gully/ridge to the summit. Descent reverses the same line.
days.title: Car-to-car scramble via Headlee Pass

schedule.label: Leave trailhead
schedule.detail: Ford the South Fork Stillaguamish at 0.5 mi; can be a difficult crossing after rain.

schedule.label: Reach Headlee Pass (4,600')
schedule.detail: 2.7 mi and 2,400 ft in, between Sperry and Morning Star Peaks.

schedule.label: Leave the pass trail, traverse talus/heather
schedule.detail: Cairned route northeast toward the Mile High Buttress.

schedule.label: Summit Morning Star Peak
schedule.detail: Final scramble gully/ridge right of the buttress.

schedule.label: Begin descent
schedule.detail: Reverse the scramble to Headlee Pass / Sunrise Mine Trail.

days.objective: Summit Morning Star Peak (6,020')

itinerary.totalNote: A long single day: about 9 hrs car-to-car, 3,800 ft gain over roughly 5.4 mi round trip via Headlee Pass.

access.fees: $5/vehicle day-use fee or $30 annual site pass at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead; Northwest Forest Pass and Interagency (America the Beautiful) passes are honored. Washington's Discover Pass is NOT accepted here.
access.rules: Standard Leave No Trace practice. This approach is outside the Glacier Peak Wilderness, so that wilderness's group-size and campfire-elevation rules do not apply.
access.permit: No wilderness permit or self-issue permit required for day trips.
access.closures: Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065) and the trail have no formal gate but are typically snow-covered and impassable until roughly June; the South Fork Stillaguamish ford near the trailhead can become impassable during high runoff.
access.seasonal: Mountain Loop Highway has a seasonal gate closure (Deer Creek–Bedal, ~14 mi), typically Nov–mid/late May.
access.landManager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Darrington Ranger District (administered from Verlot Public Service Center)
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District); the peak and much of the approach lie within or adjacent to WA DNR's Morning Star Natural Resources Conservation Area, not Glacier Peak Wilderness.
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Mountain Loop Highway trailheads (e.g. Sunrise Mine TH for Vesper Peak) — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass (or equivalent day-use fee) required for trailhead parking

overnight_permit.what: No overnight permit required outside the wilderness
overnight_permit.where: Park with a Northwest Forest Pass. Routes entering the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness need the free self-issue permit from the trailhead register.

road.name: Sunrise Mine Road (Forest Road 4065)
road.status: Narrow gravel road, rough in spots but passable to most passenger cars in dry conditions
road.driveNote: From Verlot Public Service Center, drive 17.1 mi east on the paved Mountain Loop Highway, then turn right onto FR 4065 and continue 2.2 mi to its end at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (~2,350 ft).
road.seasonalGate: No permanent gate; road and trail typically aren't clear of snow until June — check Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts before driving out.

climate.typical: Wet, west-slope North Cascades marine climate with heavy winter snowpack and a relatively narrow reliable snow-free window at elevation.

bySeason.fall: Good conditions can persist into early October; watch for early-season snow after storms and shrinking daylight for the descent.
bySeason.spring: Deep, unstable snow lingers in the Headlee Pass gully and on north aspects into June; the river ford runs high with snowmelt.
bySeason.summer: Best window, roughly July-September; trail and scramble terrain typically snow-free by mid-to-late July.
bySeason.winter: Road and trail generally inaccessible; the Headlee Pass chute is avalanche terrain.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable to nonexistent from the trailhead through Headlee Pass. The river ford near the trailhead and the loose chute below Headlee Pass are the most commonly reported hazard sites on this approach.
emergency.rangerStation: Verlot Public Service Center, 33515 Mountain Loop Highway, Granite Falls, WA 98252 — (360) 691-7791 (seasonal hours, Fri-Mon 8am-noon & 12:30-4pm; closed Tue-Thu)
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Valley Hospital (Arlington, WA) — Level IV Emergency Department, the closest facility to the Mountain Loop Highway corridor; Providence Regional Medical Center Everett — Level II trauma center — for serious/major trauma
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 — Snohomish County Sheriff's Office dispatches Snohomish County Volunteer Search & Rescue (SCVSAR) for backcountry incidents

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends July-September; drawn mostly by WA peak-bagging (Bulger list) parties and climbers using the same Sunrise Mine Trail/Headlee Pass approach as the much more popular Vesper Peak and Vesper Lake day hike, but Morning Star itself sees a fraction of that traffic since it requires leaving the trail into the basin
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Roughly a dozen to a few dozen parties per season (rough estimate) - one party in 2007 described only a single other car at the trailhead

fitnessSpec.hiking: Full day out (9 hrs total) with significant elevation gain on trail followed by steep, loose off-trail terrain to Headlee Pass and into the Sunrise Mine basin
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day-pack, roughly 15-25 lbs (water, layers, helmet, basic scramble gear) - no technical rack needed

partner_requirements.approachTime: Roughly 5 hrs one-way to the summit, within a 9-hr round trip from a 6:00 AM start
requiredSkills: off-trail routefinding into the basin
steep loose talus and heather scrambling
judgment around the Headlee Pass chute, which is notorious for rockfall
comfort with exposure near the summit block
early-season snow/glissade judgment when the basin is still snow-filled
turnaround discipline given afternoon weather buildup
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate scrambler - comfortable leaving an established trail for unmarked off-trail routefinding and sustained Class 2-3 talus/heather scrambling; not a beginner objective

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September (July-September); July is prime once the basin clears of snow

July.reason: Prime scramble season; talus and heather are typically snow-free by this point

June.reason: The basin typically holds snow into early summer ('snow-filled basin' in spring); early-season snow above Headlee Pass adds glissade/post-hole hazard and obscures the talus route

August.reason: Most reliable dry footing on talus/heather; prime scramble season

October.reason: Outside the best-season window; early snow can return above Headlee Pass and Sunrise Mine Road access becomes less reliable

September.reason: Early fall is good; still within the best season window but shortening days and higher chance of an early cold snap

weather.typical: Maritime Cascades weather the basin can still be holding snow into early summer, transitioning to dry talus/heather conditions through the July-September window and turning snowbound again once the road closes for winter
weather.probability: 'afternoon weather' - convective buildups are common in the alpine on summer afternoons, so an early (06:00) start and summit-before-midday plan is advised

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Class 2-3 scrambling; exposure and fall consequence concentrate at the steep, loose Headlee Pass chute (notorious for rockfall onto parties below) and near the summit block, where exposure is the hazard - a slip on loose talus could produce a serious fall, though this is not sustained technical climbing

avalanche.zone: West Slopes Central (NWAC) covers the Mountain Loop Highway/Sunrise Mine area, but this is a dry-season (Jul-Sep) scramble outside NWAC's formal winter forecast window, so no meaningful avalanche advisory applies during the climbing season

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; this is a talus-and-heather scramble, not glaciated terrain

gaps: precise round-trip mileage/elevation-gain for the summit itself (beyond the Vesper Lake trail figures) not independently confirmed
GPS track sourced from public CalTopo map: https://caltopo.com/m/VUQF9

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (~2,340 ft) at the end of FR-4065 off the Mountain Loop Highway, via Trail #707

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail over Headlee Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the Sunrise Mine trailhead, take the trail the whole way. The first mile crosses two unbridged creeks — a log crossing, a root crossing and a more substantial ford — which need real caution in early season or after rain. Beyond them the trail climbs steadily through forest and then tightens into ever-sharper switchbacks up a narrow rocky couloir. The last quarter mile below the pass is the notorious part: steep, with tread periodically wrecked by snow and rockfall and a genuine risk from rock kicked down by parties above. Unlike the three rock routes on this peak, do NOT leave the trail at the switchback lower down.
approach_variants.season: July to September. Snow lingers in the pass gully and on north-facing ground into July, and an ice axe is worth carrying until it has gone.
hazards: Notorious rockfall chute immediately below the pass — a helmet is worth wearing on the trail here, not just above it
Difficult ford about half a mile from the trailhead; seasonal log crossings are often washed out in high runoff
Lingering steep snow in the pass gully and on north-facing terrain into July
Loose talus and heather sidehilling above the pass with only sparse cairns
A steep gully partway up the scramble is often icy; parties commonly move onto the rock rib to its right to avoid it
approach_variants.baseFinding: The scrambling starts at HEADLEE PASS itself — the notch where the trail finally tops out of the rockfall chute and the ground opens northward. The test that you are at the pass and not at a false top inside the chute is water: the outlet stream just beyond the pass runs strong for most of the season and is the last reliable water of the day, so if there is no stream on the far side you have not topped out yet. From the pass, leave the maintained tread and work north along and below the peak's south ridge over talus and heather benches. Cairns mark parts of the line and stop entirely higher up, so the real check is that the ground steepens continuously into rock and gully terrain rather than easing off. Negative marker: if you have left the trail lower down on open talus, following cairns northeast toward a rock tower, you are on the climbers' traverse to the towers north of the peak and you are heading for a bolted rock route, not the summit scramble.

climbing_route.label: South Fork Stillaguamish valley
climbing_route.notes: Leave the Sunrise Mine Trail about half a mile in, just before it crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish, and work up the east side of the valley through brush, slide alder and rock debris past a house-sized boulder near 3,100 ft. Either cross the river and climb a ridge ramp southwest to the upper basin (about 4,000 ft), or continue to the broad basin near 3,700 ft and climb the steep gully, or the slabs to its right, directly east.

climbing_route.label: Slabs to the southeast-ridge notch (~5,600 ft)
climbing_route.notes: Climb snow-covered slabs to the notch in Morning Star's southeast ridge. These slabs hold snow well into the season and are the route's main avalanche concern.

climbing_route.label: Gully and south ridge to the summit (6,020 ft)
climbing_route.notes: From the notch drop about 200 ft through trees into the southeast basin, traverse right below the cliffs to the first broad gully, and climb it to the south ridge about 250 ft below the summit. Finish on or near the south ridge. The gully is steep and often icy when snow-filled; helmet, ice axe and crampons are standard early in the season.

bivy.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
bivy.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
bivy.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
bivy.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

bivy.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
bivy.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
bivy.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

backups.name: Southeast Route
backups.fa: July 1897, John Charlton and Albert H. Sylvester
gear: Light rock rack: a few small-to-medium cams and nuts plus slings for the chimney crux
60m rope for glacier travel and short rappels
Mountain bike (optional, speeds the closed-roadbed approach from Dingford Creek)
hazards: Crevasses on the Overcoat Glacier, especially as snow bridges thin later in summer
Steep moats where the glacier pulls away from the rock late in the season
Loose rock in the summit chimney and on the class 3 slabs to its right
Exposed class 4 (occasionally low 5th-class) climbing on the final summit block
Long, brushy approach with downed trees and rocks hidden under thimbleberry on the old Dutch Miller Gap trailbed
Heavy mosquitoes at valley camps (e.g., Bears Breast tarns) in early-mid summer
backups.overview: Overcoat Peak (7,432 ft) is the rugged, glacier-draped satellite summit immediately northwest of taller Chimney Rock, both crowning the ridge above the head of the Overcoat Glacier in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. It was named by USGS surveyor Albert H. Sylvester after he left his coat on the summit during a 1897 survey trip, an outing also considered the peak's first ascent. Overcoat sees far fewer visits than its taller neighbor because of the long, brushy approach up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley and the glacier travel required just to reach the base of the climbing. The true summit sits atop a steep roughly 400-foot rock block rising above the surrounding terrain on all sides, demanding sustained class 4 (occasionally low 5th-class) climbing no matter which side is used.
backups.beta: Approach via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River trail to Dutch Miller Gap, then bushwhack to Overcoat Lake basecamp and contour to the Overcoat Glacier. Ascend the glacier, navigate crevasses and moats, then climb the exposed fourth class rock on the northeast side of the summit pyramid. Crampons and ice tools are essential. Descent is via downclimbing and rappels to return to the glacier.
backups.turnaround: Given the long approach and glacier/rock climbing above 6,000 ft, set a hard summit turnaround (e.g., early-to-mid afternoon) so the party can safely re-cross the glacier and negotiate the brushy descent to camp in daylight; afternoon thunderstorm buildup and softening snow bridges are the main reasons to bail early.
backups.rappels: 2 rappels on a 60m rope down the damp dihedral, back to the top of the Overcoat Glacier
backups.face: Southeast side of the peak (the side facing Chimney Rock), above the Overcoat Glacier
backups.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
backups.descent: Most parties reverse the ascent ledges/chimney and re-cross the Overcoat Glacier back to camp. At least one documented descent instead exits via heather ledges and a dihedral on the peak's east side, finishing with two full rope-length rappels back to the glacier.
obj_haz: crevasses on the Overcoat Glacier
moats at the glacier margins
steep snow requiring axe and crampons
loose/exposed class 3-4 rock near the summit

waypoints.name: Dingford Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Standard access point via FR-56/Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road; no day-use fee is currently charged at this specific trailhead (per USFS), though a free self-issue wilderness permit is required beyond it for Alpine Lakes Wilderness travel, and the road washout beyond this point means biking or hiking the closed roadbed toward Dutch Miller Gap.
waypoints.directions: FR-56 up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie to the lot is heavily potholed and rutted; parties in low-clearance cars routinely park short and walk the last stretch, which adds to an already long day.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Lake
waypoints.note: Standard high camp for the route, roughly 10 mi in via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail/old roadbed then a steep, unmaintained forested slog above a river ford near the old Dutch Miller Gap Trail; seldom-visited alpine lake below the Overcoat Glacier basin.
waypoints.directions: The continuation of the road past the gate is roughly 7-8 miles of old roadbed to Hardscrabble Horse Camp, and most parties bike it rather than walk it. Beyond that the Dutch Miller Gap Trail runs east along the north bank; the tread is reasonable but summer thimbleberry buries the rocks underfoot. Leave the trail about a mile before it swings toward Williams Lake and ford the river: it can run thigh-to-waist deep, and it is colder and higher on the way back than it was in the morning.

waypoints.name: Rock benches above Overcoat Glacier
waypoints.note: Higher alternate camp on open benches used to shorten summit day; this bivy option sits at roughly 6,600 ft.
waypoints.directions: Above the ford the ground climbs steeply through brush into a rocky corridor of waterfalls and steep faces before opening onto snow and benches. Snow lingers here well past midsummer. The awkward part is a sloping rock step partway up, which is markedly harder to downclimb than to climb and is worth noting for the return.

waypoints.name: Notch on Overcoat Peak's north ridge (Overcoat Col)
waypoints.note: Contour east from camp to this notch to gain the upper Overcoat Glacier; a col of the same name and elevation (~6,800 ft) sits beneath Chimney Rock's east face.
waypoints.directions: Only a couple of hundred feet of net gain, but it is a rising traverse over benches and old snow rather than a walk. The glacier starts immediately on the far side, so rope up and fit crampons at the notch rather than after stepping onto it.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the glacier's lower snowfields toward the peak's southeast side; expect deep crevasses and weak, undermined snow bridges on this rapidly retreating glacier.
waypoints.directions: Drop onto the upper glacier from the notch and work toward the peak's southeast side. Most parties time this route for the tail end of summer, when the crevasses are open and visible and the rock above is clear of snow; earlier in the season the bridges are the thing that will catch you out.

waypoints.name: Snow finger to east face
waypoints.note: Find the snow finger leading off the glacier onto the east face here, then pick up the Class 3-4 ledges and heathery gully toward the summit block.
waypoints.directions: The finger rises off the top of the glacier and is steep enough that crampons and a second tool are the norm. A crevasse commonly cuts it partway up and has to be turned. Near the dark towers at its top, move off snow onto rock and round the corner east to reach the ledge system.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Peak
waypoints.note: True summit; the final ~400 vertical ft is a Class 4/low-5.0 heathery gully leading to an angled chimney, with a small summit register.
waypoints.directions: The gully has solid holds but a few tall steps force committing, exposed moves, and most parties pitch it out on small cams and nuts in mediocre rock rather than soloing it. Sort the descent before you commit: the damp dihedral below is normally rappelled twice, not downclimbed.

backups.detailed_rack: Ice axe and crampons for the glacier approach (rope up for crevasse hazard); helmet; a few small-to-medium cams and nuts with slings for the summit chimney; a 30m+ rope doubles as glacier rope and rappel line if descending the east-side dihedral (two rope-length rappels reported).
what_to_bring: Helmet, ice axe, crampons for glacier travel
Light rock rack (small-medium cams/nuts, slings) for the chimney crux
Satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) — little to no cell coverage along the approach
Water treatment and bug protection for camp
pro_tips: A mountain bike can save real time on the ~7-10 mile closed-roadbed section between Dingford Creek Trailhead and Hardscrabble Horse Camp
Camp at Overcoat Lake or the rock benches above the Overcoat Glacier (~6,600 ft) to split the long approach into two days and climb the peak light on summit day
The class 3 slabs right of the summit chimney avoid the crux move but are looser — useful as a bail-out or alternate line
Only attempt the upper ledges in snow-free conditions; lingering snow there adds real risk beyond the rock difficulty
watch_out: Loose rock in and around the summit chimney
Thin, softening glacier snow bridges by late summer
Hidden rocks and downed trees on the abandoned Dutch Miller Gap trail corridor
Heavy mosquitoes at Bears Breast tarns and other valley camps
backups.pro_needs: Light rack (small-to-medium cams/nuts) for the class 4 chimney, plus a standard glacier travel kit (axe, crampons, rope) for the Overcoat Glacier approach.
backups.best_season: Late July into August is the classic window: approach brush has dried and the glacier still offers reasonably solid, crevasse-bridged travel. A documented 2024 ascent succeeded in mid-July, though with lingering snow patches on the summit ledges adding difficulty. By September the glacier is more broken and bare, so rope up and scout crevasses carefully; this is not sensible as a pre-July objective given the long, brushy, low-elevation approach.
backups.approach: From the Dingford Creek Trailhead (end of FR 56, Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road), the fastest approach uses the gated continuation of the road as a mountain-bike/hike-in: roughly 7-8 miles of old roadbed (NF-5620) to Hardscrabble Horse Camp near the old Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead, saving significant time over walking it. From there, follow the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River / Dutch Miller Gap Trail (Trail 1030) east along the north bank of the river for several more miles — the tread here is in reasonable shape with minimal blowdown, passing dispersed camps and, in season, overgrown thimbleberry brush that obscures footing on the lower tread. Roughly 13-14 miles in from the trailhead (about a mile before the trail crosses toward Williams Lake/Dutch Miller Gap proper), leave the trail and ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River — a real ford, potentially thigh-to-waist deep and cold with snowmelt, so time it for lower water and expect wet feet. On the far side, climb steep, brushy forest into the rocky defile some parties call the 'Valley of the Chiefs,' a roughly two-mile corridor that gains the bench below Overcoat Peak. Continuous snowfields typically begin around 4,600 ft; above about 6,600 ft the route alternates between rock and snow, with one sloping, exposed rock step that requires care to downclimb onto steep snow. A common camp is on rock slabs/benches around 6,600 ft directly overlooking the Overcoat Glacier, roughly 100 ft below the glacier's toe. Total trailhead-to-camp distance is on the order of 15-16 miles with 5,000+ ft of gain; this is a serious, mostly off-trail approach through wilderness terrain (Alpine Lakes Wilderness) with real route-finding, so a GPS track or careful map work for the Valley of the Chiefs and glacier-bench section is worthwhile. From camp, traverse west across the mellow lower-angle part of the Overcoat Glacier to reach the base of a snow finger on the peak's north/east side that leads to the summit rock.
backups.descent_text: Reverse the ascent for most parties: from the summit, downclimb the Class 3-4 gully/ledge system on the peak's east side back toward the snow finger and glacier. Where the ledges pinch down at a dihedral feature (a damp, water-streaked corner reported by climbers), most parties do NOT free-downclimb the full corner — instead, build two rappels (roughly full 30m/60m-rope-length pitches) down the dihedral to regain the glacier below. Anchors are natural (slung horns, chockstones, or gear placements) rather than fixed bolts/chains — this is an alpine line with no fixed hardware, so carry a small rack and cordage for anchor-building and expect to leave gear (or plan to down-lead/simul on lower-angle sections to save equipment). A single 60m rope handles both rappels; parties without a 60m would need to break it into more, shorter rappels. Some parties instead find they can downclimb the full chimney/ledge system without rappelling if conditions and confidence allow (reversing the ascent by downclimbing is the lower-commitment option), but the two-rappel dihedral descent is the more commonly reported method, especially when the rock is wet or holds are snow-covered. Below the glacier, retrace the approach: descend the Valley of the Chiefs (or, as at least one party has done, an alternate line down the main Overcoat drainage through open trees to avoid waterfall-forming cliffs lower down), re-ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie, and rejoin the Dutch Miller Gap Trail back to Hardscrabble Horse Camp and the bike/hike-out to Dingford Creek Trailhead. Watch for loose rock in the gully/dihedral and for the river ford being higher/colder in the afternoon on hot days from glacier/snowmelt runoff.
backups.bail: If the chimney feels wet, loose, or above the party's comfort level, retreat via the looser class 3 slabs to climber's right rather than forcing the direct crux; on the glacier, turn back if crevasse bridges look thin, visibility drops, or the party lacks rope/crevasse-rescue gear.

pitch_detail.notes: Cross or circle the Overcoat Glacier from high camp to the notch/col between Chimney Rock and Overcoat Peak; rope and crampons typically used.
Shed glacier gear at the col and step directly onto the south ridge; rock is loose for roughly the first 20 feet.
A ledge traverses the west side of the south ridge with real exposure; rock is generally sound but looser than elsewhere on the route — test holds carefully.
Final short scramble/climbing moves to the true summit.

itinerary.cal: Best climbed roughly July-September when the approach road/trail are passable and the snow finger above the glacier is still climbable with crampons; a self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead.

days.note: Bike the old roadbed and Dutch Miller Gap Trail corridor from Dingford Creek, ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie, then push up through brush, talus and the 'Valley of the Chiefs' benches to camp near Overcoat Lake/glacier. It's a long, grinding approach day with little technical difficulty but a lot of vertical and bushwhacking.

days.objective: Reach high camp on rock benches above the Overcoat Glacier (~6,600 ft)

days.note: Cross the glacier and climb steep snow to the base of the summit rock, then finish on exposed 4th-class ledges and a gully to the 7,432 ft summit; reverse via two rappels back to the glacier. Rather than return to the same camp, most parties then break camp and hike out toward Bears Breast Tarns the same afternoon to shorten the exit.

schedule.detail: Cross glacier flats toward the SE side of the peak.

schedule.label: Snow finger
schedule.detail: Crampons/ice tools up a ~500 ft rising traverse of steep snow.

schedule.label: Transition to rock
schedule.detail: Alternate rock/snow above 6,600 ft; downclimb a sloping rock crux.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Exposed 4th-class (low 5th in spots) moves up the final gully to 7,432 ft.

schedule.label: Descent begins
schedule.detail: Two rappels back down to the glacier.

schedule.label: Break camp, hike out
schedule.detail: Retrace to Dutch Miller Gap Trail and continue to Bears Breast Tarns camp (~4,400 ft).

days.objective: Climb the SE ledges/chimney to the summit, then move camp toward the exit

days.note: An optional short side trip to Williams Lake, then a straightforward but long hike back down the Middle Fork corridor to the horse camp, followed by a quick downhill bike ride to the car.
days.title: Exit to trailhead
days.objective: Hike and bike back to the Dingford Creek Trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A remote 3-day/2-night trip: ~40 miles round trip and ~6,000 ft net gain, with the crux being the exposed 4th-class summit block and a steep snow finger above the Overcoat Glacier; a few very fit parties have done it car-to-car in ~15 hrs during good spring ski-mountaineering conditions, but that is a fast-party exception, not the standard plan.

access.fees: No day-use fee currently posted at the Dingford Creek Trailhead itself; carry a Northwest Forest Pass/interagency pass in case requirements change.
access.notes: The west side of Alpine Lakes Wilderness — jointly managed with Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest holding the western portion these peaks sit in (trailheads themselves may be administered by either forest).
access.rules: Standard Alpine Lakes Wilderness regulations apply (group size limits, Leave No Trace camping); check current forest orders on campfire restrictions before the trip.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit required at the trailhead for both day and overnight use within the Alpine Lakes Wilderness.
access.closures: Forest Road 56 (Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road) is prone to washouts, particularly near the Taylor River bend, and the old Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead further up-valley is no longer reachable by vehicle. Call the Snoqualmie Ranger District, North Bend Office, (425) 888-1421, for current road status before driving.

access.land_manager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Snoqualmie Ranger District) — Alpine Lakes Wilderness

overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry your copy.

road.name: Forest Road 56 (Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road)
road.status: Rough, pothole-prone gravel; high-clearance vehicle recommended; periodically closed by washouts
road.driveNote: Roughly 12-18 miles from North Bend to the Dingford Creek Trailhead; call the Snoqualmie Ranger District North Bend Office (425-888-1421) for current status before driving
road.seasonalGate: Not gated on a fixed seasonal schedule, but washout closures can occur at any time of year — check current alerts

climate.typical: Alpine, glacier-influenced climate; expect a mix of sun, wind, and fast-moving Cascades weather even in midsummer, with snow lingering on the Overcoat Glacier and approach benches into July.

bySeason.fall: Early fall can bring stable weather but a more broken/bare glacier surface with wider crevasses — rope up and scout carefully; not recommended once fall snow starts sticking.
bySeason.spring: Heavy Cascades snowpack typically buries the approach trail and glacier in continuous snow into June or later — feasible terrain for ski mountaineering lines but not for this rock route.
bySeason.summer: July-September is the standard window. By late July/August the approach trail has dried out and the glacier still offers reasonably solid, well-bridged travel; a 2024 trip climbed the route in mid-July with lingering snow patches on the approach ledges adding difficulty.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective; the Middle Fork Snoqualmie access road is not maintained for winter travel and the approach is unreasonably long under full snow cover.

emergency.notes: This is a remote, multi-day wilderness approach with little to no cell coverage along most of the route; a satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) is strongly advised given the glacier travel and technical summit block.
emergency.rangerStation: Snoqualmie Ranger District, North Bend Office, 902 SE North Bend Way, North Bend, WA — (425) 888-1421
emergency.nearestHospital: Snoqualmie Valley Hospital (Snoqualmie, WA) for initial/urgent care; serious trauma is typically transported or flown to Harborview Medical Center in Seattle, the region's Level I trauma center.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: King County Sheriff's Office / Search and Rescue — call 911 for emergencies; non-emergency line (206) 296-3311.

crowds.peakTraffic: Late July-August weekends, often the same parties climbing Chimney Rock via the shared Overcoat Glacier approach
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Roughly a handful to a dozen parties per season - unlike its more famous neighbor Chimney Rock (which draws Mountaineers/club trip parties), Overcoat Peak is usually tagged as a side-summit add-on rather than a standalone objective

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strenuous off-trail approach through the Alpine Lakes Wilderness with significant elevation gain; typically done as a long day or overnight backpack, not a quick outing
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Moderate-heavy - overnight/glacier kit (rope, crampons, ice axe, crevasse rescue gear) plus a rock rack for the summit block

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - multi-hour off-trail approach up to and across the Overcoat Glacier; many parties do this as an overnight trip rather than a car-to-car day
requiredSkills: Glacier travel and basic crevasse rescue (Overcoat Glacier crossing on approach)
Off-trail routefinding through wilderness terrain with no maintained trail to the summit
Exposed 4th-class/low 5th-class scrambling on slabs and ledges
Comfort with loose rock and an exposed summit block
Self-arrest and crampon use on the glacier approach
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate alpine scrambler/climber - needs prior glacier travel experience plus comfort on exposed, loose 4th-class-to-low-5th-class rock

July.reason: Route opens up in late July per the season window, but lingering snowfields and a more filled-in (harder to read) Overcoat Glacier can complicate crevasse crossing early in the month

August.reason: Matches the best-season - glacier approach typically most stable and rock driest for the southeast slabs/ledges and summit block

September.reason: Still within the season window; rock stays dry but days shorten and early-season snow can arrive late in the month, plus the glacier becomes more broken and icier as the season progresses

weather.typical: Typical dry Washington Cascades summer alpine weather during the July-September window: warm, mostly stable days with cooler nights at elevation
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms and pop-up convection are a recognized summer hazard in the Cascades and can affect exposed sections like the summit block; check forecasts before committing to the glacier crossing and summit block

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Significant fall exposure on the summit block and on the slabs/ledges gained above the Overcoat Glacier on the southeast side; a slip on the exposed summit block or approach ledges would be a high-consequence fall

avalanche.zone: NWAC Stevens Pass zone (approximate - covers the broader Alpine Lakes Wilderness corridor; no zone is drawn specifically around Overcoat Peak)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Overcoat Glacier crossing on approach has real crevasse hazard; crossing is generally most straightforward in compact-snow conditions early in the season and becomes more broken/icy with visible crevasses as summer progresses toward September

gaps: No confirmed pitch count or exact rappel anchor details

rappel_detail.notes: First of two near-full-rope-length rappels down the damp, water-streaked dihedral where the descent ledges pinch out; no fixed hardware - build anchors from a small rack and expect to leave gear.
rappel_detail.anchor: natural anchor (slung horn / chockstone / gear placement)

rappel_detail.notes: Second rappel continuing down the dihedral to regain the Overcoat Glacier below; a single 60m rope handles both, shorter ropes would require breaking this into more rappels.
rappel_detail.anchor: natural anchor (slung horn / chockstone / gear placement)

backups.rappel_count_note: Two rappels of roughly 30m each, which is what a single 60m rope doubled reaches — this is the commonly reported method where the descent ledges pinch out at the damp dihedral. Some parties downclimb the full chimney/ledge system instead when conditions allow. Anchors are natural (slung horns, chockstones, gear) with no fixed hardware, so carry cordage and expect to leave gear. A shorter rope means more rappels, not longer ones.

approach_variants.name: Dingford Creek, bike the closed road, then ford the Middle Fork under the big cliff
approach_variants.notes: From I-90 exit 34 go north, then right onto SE Middle Fork Road, FR 56, and follow it about twelve miles to the Taylor River junction. Bear right onto FR 5620 and continue to the Dingford Creek trailhead at roughly 1,500 ft. FR 56 is notorious for potholes and ruts and high clearance is genuinely useful; the stretch beyond the gate is reported to be in better shape than the public road. FR 5620 is decommissioned beyond Dingford Creek. The closed stretch to the old Dutch Miller Gap trailhead and Hardscrabble Horse Camp is given as seven, eight or ten miles, so do not plan on a precise number. A bike is universally recommended and cuts hours off both ends. Beyond the road, parties use three genuinely different lines, none of them confirmed by another, so read all three before choosing. The most specific of them fords the Middle Fork on a visual cue rather than a mileage: walk roughly four miles of trail until you can SEE the large cliff rising above the south side of the river at the foot of Overcoat. Push through about ten minutes of alder, ford there, and you land on the talus field at the base of those cliffs. Further north-east the alder gets much thicker. A second line crosses about a mile before the Dutch Miller Gap trail proper and climbs steep forest to camp at Overcoat Lake. A third crosses the river on rocks, climbs steep brushy ground into a two-mile rocky corridor sometimes called the Valley of the Chiefs, meets continuous snow around 4,600 ft, and goes over a pass at about 6,140 ft. On the traverse toward camp, one party's correction: they climbed to the ridge and then realised the line stays LOWER, and had to drop back to find the sloping rock crux and downclimb to the snow. A durable warning about the road rather than the mountain: the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road has a long-standing reputation for unsavoury activity, including gunfire, and at least one regular visitor reports it on every trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The river ford is the timing constraint — thigh deep in the morning has been recorded as waist deep on the same day by evening
hazards: A real ford of the Middle Fork Snoqualmie, thigh to waist deep and colder in the afternoon than the morning
Dense slide alder on both banks, worse to the north-east of the standard crossing
Moats around the margin of the Overcoat Glacier
Crevasses part way up the snow finger
Poor protection and loose rock on the summit pyramid
A long decommissioned road walk or ride at both ends of the day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The snow finger is not visible until you are underneath it, so do not try to identify it from camp or from the glacier below.

The sequence that works: reach the Overcoat Glacier, make a long rising traverse of five hundred feet or so to the top of the mild glacier, and only then does the steep snow finger show itself, with dark towers standing above it.

THE DARK TOWERS ARE THE TRANSITION. You leave snow for rock at their foot, then round the corner EAST and the glacier reappears below you. From there it is steep gully climbing on solid holds with a few exposed steps over tall blocks to the summit.

The consistent fact across every published account, and the one to steer by: the summit pyramid is gained on its EAST or NORTH-EAST side. Nobody describes climbing it from the south-east. If you are working around to the south side of the block looking for a way up, you have gone the wrong way round.

Grade opinions on that finish run from Class 3 to low fifth, and parties have pitched it out in two short pitches with a few small cams and nuts, with one rappel and some downclimbing to get back to the top of the snow finger. Expect thin protection and poor rock rather than a scramble.

Moats around the glacier margin and crevasses part way up the snow finger are the two things that most often force a detour here, and both were reported as more awkward than expected by parties who had read otherwise.

climbing_route.label: Snow finger off the Overcoat Glacier
climbing_route.notes: A steep snow finger rises off the glacier toward the summit rock and is the feature the route is known for. It starts as a low-angle ramp and steepens continuously, and parties have wanted a second tool near the top; crevasses cut across it partway up and are the main hazard on this section. In late season the transition from glacier ice to the snow finger and again from snow to rock opens into moats, so expect the exit onto rock to be the awkward part of the day.

climbing_route.label: Heathery slot to the notch
climbing_route.notes: Leave the snow and round the corner onto rock, then scramble a reddish, heather-filled slot set against the mountainside for roughly two thirds of its length before stepping out left (west) onto exposed rock. Route-finding here is the trap on the peak: the obvious south-to-north angled gully that looks like it leads straight to the summit blocks is not the route, and parties who follow it end up under steep, unclimbable terrain. Holds in the correct line are reported solid, but the position is exposed.

climbing_route.label: Angled chimney to the saddle
climbing_route.notes: An angled chimney — overhanging wall on the left above slabby rock on the right — leads to the saddle between the south peak and the true summit. This is stemming and opposition on friction rather than crack climbing, so dry boots and hands make a real difference and it is markedly harder wet. A rope and harnesses already carried for the glacier are worth using here; parties describe it as the section where an inexperienced scrambler gets into trouble.

climbing_route.label: Summit block
climbing_route.notes: The final block stands roughly 400 vertical ft above the surrounding terrain and is steep on every side, so at least class 4 and arguably low 5th is unavoidable to reach the top. Climb the steep gully above the saddle on generally good holds with a few exposed moves over tall steps to gain a roomy summit. Summit rocks have been described as wobbly — test everything, and be aware that anyone below is directly in the fall line. Descent is normally a downclimb through a dihedral and heather ledges followed by two full-length rappels back to the glacier, so bring enough rope and slings to build anchors.

bivy.name: Overcoat Lake
Rock benches above Overcoat Glacier
Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

backups.name: East Ridge
gear: Light rock rack plus a few slings
Single 30-40 m rope covers the technical sections and the Balanced Rock; the stored West Ridge descent needs two ropes for its final ~50 m double-rope rappel to the west notch
hazards: Loose blocky rock along the ridge crest
Afternoon thunderstorms common July-August
Exposed, unprotected 3rd/4th-class sections
backups.overview: The East Ridge is the easier of Sherpa's two south-side ridge routes: broad blocky terrain and sandy benches at Class 3-4 with only brief low-5th-class steps, passing directly beneath the Sherpa Balanced Rock obelisk before finishing at the true summit. Because it's less sustained than the West Ridge, most parties descend via the West Ridge rather than reversing this line.
backups.beta: From a basin camp around 6,800 ft, follow the east ridge toward the summit; cairns and fixed slings/webbing along the ridge aid route-finding. The route passes around the balanced rock from the north side, which can involve a sketchy traverse over snow or wet rock in early season. The balanced-rock move itself is a shoulder-stand or rope-throw over a pedestal point to gain its east side, then bolt-protected friction climbing to the top, rated 5.7, with a rappel bolt atop.
backups.turnaround: Set an early-afternoon turnaround. If progress over the towers is slow or weather builds, retreat by rappel rather than committing to the upper ridge.
backups.rock_grade: Class 3-4 (short 5th-class moves possible near the Balanced Rock traverse)
backups.rappels: Descend the West Ridge rap line: 2 single-rope rappels, a scramble, another single, then a double-rope rappel to the west notch (4 total; ~3 combined on two ropes). Parties heading for the South Gully often take only the first 2 and downclimb
backups.face: South/East side, via the Sherpa-Argonaut (south) basin
backups.permit: Free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead covers both day and overnight trips. Longs Pass and the Ingalls Creek basin lie outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery or quota permit applies.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the Ingalls Creek/Longs Pass basins; the summit ridge may get intermittent signal. A satellite communicator is recommended for this remote wilderness approach.
backups.descent: Descend the west ridge, rappelling the summit block, then the approach slopes.
obj_haz: loose rock
exposed ridge traverse
snow/ice on the Balanced Rock traverse early season

waypoints.name: Esmeralda Basin / Ingalls Way Trailhead (North Fork Teanaway Rd, FR-9737) via Longs Pass
waypoints.note: Shared trailhead for Longs Pass Trail and Esmeralda Basin/Ingalls Way Trail; route drops from Longs Pass into Ingalls Creek drainage before climbing to Sherpa's east basin.
waypoints.directions: Drive the North Fork Teanaway Road (FR-9737) to its end at the Esmeralda Basin / Ingalls Way trailhead. This is the shared lot for the Longs Pass Trail and the Esmeralda Basin / Ingalls Way Trail, and it is the same trailhead the West Ridge uses; for the East Ridge you want the Longs Pass Trail (FST 1391), which goes over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and down to Ingalls Creek. Plan on late June through September, once that Longs Pass and Ingalls Creek approach is snow-free.

backups.detailed_rack: A single rack of cams to 2 inches, a set of nuts, plenty of slings for horns, about 8 alpine draws, and a 60m rope for the steps and rappels.
pro_tips: Climb the East Ridge and descend the West Ridge for a traverse.
Sling horns to move fast and protect.
Pre-plan rappel stations for retreat.
Watch the exposed crest for building weather.

Balanced Rock is a separate ~20-ft obelisk about 100 yards from Sherpa's true summit, not the summit itself — tagging its top requires a shoulder-stand onto the obelisk's east-side pedestal, then a few 5.7 friction moves past an old fixed piton (rappel bolt atop). It's an optional bonus, not required to reach the true summit.
watch_out: Old, sun-bleached fixed slings and a single piton protect the 5.7 Balanced Rock move - inspect before weighting
Route-finding around the Balanced Rock is confusing in poor visibility
Descent is not a reversal of the ascent - know the West Ridge rappels before you commit
backups.pro_needs: The crest offers good crack and horn protection on steeper steps, with run-out moderate sections between. Carry enough slings to protect efficiently over the towers.
backups.best_season: Mid-July through September; the north-facing approach gully can hold snow into early July.
backups.approach: Access is the same Esmeralda Basin/Longs Pass Trailhead used for the West Ridge: follow the Longs Pass Trail (FST 1391) over Longs Pass (~6,200 ft) and down to Ingalls Creek Trail, crossing Ingalls Creek and continuing on the climbers' boot path up into the Sherpa-Argonaut basin (see West Ridge approach for that shared section). From the basin, rather than aiming for the West Ridge notch, angle climber's-left (east), traversing a grassy slope and ascending a talus/scree gully to reach the prominent notch at roughly 8,000 ft, about 600 vertical feet below and east of the true summit. Gain the ridge crest about 100 ft above (east of) the notch via class 2 terrain. This line is longer and more circuitous through loose talus than the direct West Ridge approach, and picking the correct gully/notch is the main route-finding crux; a 50m rope is worth carrying from here since the route above uses fixed rappel slings at several obstacles.
backups.descent_text: Most parties do not reverse the East Ridge; the accepted descent is to finish near the summit, traverse to the top of the West Ridge, and go down using the West Ridge's established rappel line (two single-rope rappels past the crux, a short scramble, another single, then a double-rope rappel to the west notch - see the West Ridge descent for full detail) before dropping back to the basin and Ingalls Creek. Some parties do reverse the East Ridge directly, especially when combining the climb with the nearby Balanced Rock feature: this involves downclimbing/rappelling a vertical chimney using chained-together fixed rappel slings, then a rappel down a steep gully to an exposed slab, then another rappel after crossing the slab, finishing with class 3 downclimbing to the 8,000-ft notch. Expect roughly 2-4 short single-rope rappels off existing (sometimes weathered) fixed slings and chains rather than full ropelength raps; a 50m rope was reported as sufficient. Back up any suspect fixed anchors with your own gear. From the notch/basin, reverse the approach: descend to Ingalls Creek Trail, cross the creek, and climb back over Longs Pass to the trailhead.
backups.bail: Rappels off horns and blocks allow retreat from several points on the ridge, giving a reasonable escape, though the long walk out remains regardless.

pitch_detail.notes: Gain the east ridge crest above the 8,000 ft notch and climb the first blocky steps on sound granite; mostly class 3-4 with occasional low-5th moves.
A steeper tower of solid granite just below the Sherpa Balanced Rock obelisk provides the technical crux - a short crack/corner move rated 5.7.
Continue over and around a series of towers along the crest, passing directly beneath the Balanced Rock feature; route-finding among blocks is the main challenge here.
Moderate, more broken climbing across sandy benches toward the base of the summit block.
Short final pitch up the summit pinnacle to the true summit; most parties then traverse to the West Ridge for the descent rather than reversing this route.

itinerary.cal: Best late June through September once the Longs Pass/Ingalls Creek approach is snow-free.

days.note: Same Longs Pass approach as the West Ridge, but continue along the Ingalls Creek Trail past the Beverly-Turnpike junction and climb into the basin below Sherpa's east side for a treeline bivy.

Descend via the West Ridge side with a rappel off the summit block, then hike back out over Longs Pass. Many parties do this all in one long day, but some split the hike-out into a third day.

July.reason: Warming and drying, though early-month snow/wet rock on north-facing steps can slow the harder pitches

August.reason: Most reliable dry conditions for the sustained 5.7 climbing and long summit day

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Higher sustained exposure than the West Ridge: a full day of roped travel across towers and steps with limited retreat, loose blocks on the towers, and a long, involved rappel/downclimb exit

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel on this ridge route
