backups.rappel_count_note: Both stored numbers were right about different things: the 2 is the partial descent to the South Gully, the 4 stations are the full West Ridge line to the west notch. A published West Ridge description gives two single-rope rappels from the top leading to a scramble, then another single-rope rappel followed by a final double-rope rappel, and notes some single rappels can be combined into doubles with difficult pulls. Most parties do not reverse the East Ridge.

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass, then east to the 8,000 ft notch
approach_variants.notes:
The approach shares everything with the West Ridge as far as the basin: Longs Pass Trail from the Esmeralda trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft, down to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft, ford, east on the Ingalls Creek Trail to the Beverly-Turnpike junction, then off-trail up the rib and into the basin beneath Sherpa.

From the basin the two routes diverge. Instead of heading for the West Ridge notch, angle climber's LEFT — east — traversing a grassy slope and then climbing a talus and scree gully toward the notch east of the summit.

This is longer and more circuitous through loose talus than the direct West Ridge line, and picking the right gully is the main problem. There is another level of basin higher and southwest of the summit; ending up in it means you have gone the wrong way. Carry a 50m rope from the notch, since the route above uses fixed slings at several obstacles.
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep; the north-facing approach gully holds snow into early July
hazards: Loose talus and scree in the approach gully
Route-finding: the higher basin southwest of the summit is the overshoot trap
Snow lingering in the north-facing gully into early July
Ingalls Creek ford and the long brushy off-trail section, same as the West Ridge
Fixed slings on the route and on the descent are weathered — carry replacement cord
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The target is a notch at roughly 8,000 ft, EAST of the true summit and about 600 vertical feet below it. Gaining the ridge crest itself happens about 100 ft ABOVE (east of) that notch, on class 2 ground — so the notch is a waypoint, and the crest is gained just past it, not in it.

From the basin the gully leading to it is the obvious one heading up toward that saddle east of the summit, and trip reports confirm that the gully that looks right from below IS the right one. The failure mode is overshooting rather than picking the wrong-looking line: parties climb too far and end up in the higher basin to the southwest of the summit.

The orientation check: at the notch the summit should be UP and to your WEST, roughly 600 ft above you. If the summit is above and east, or if you are level with the summit, you are in the wrong saddle.

Sherpa's Balanced Rock sits on the summit ridge and is visible from below — it is the West Ridge's landmark, not this route's start, but it tells you where the summit ridge runs and therefore which way to count from.

Most parties do not reverse this ridge. The accepted descent finishes near the summit, traverses to the top of the West Ridge, and uses that route's rappel line — so plan to end the day on the other side of the peak from where you started climbing.

bivy.name: Sherpa south basin camp
bivy.notes: Sitting a couple of thousand feet above the Ingalls Creek trail in the cirque south of Sherpa, this is where a party wanting a reasonable summit day on the East or West Ridge sleeps. Getting here means leaving the valley trail and grinding up open slopes and gullies with no path to speak of, so the climb from the creek is the crux of the day rather than the ridge. The payoff is that the East Ridge start is an easy morning from here instead of a pre-dawn thrash. It is also the natural base for the Northeast Couloir on Sherpa Balanced Rock, which is reached by continuing up the basin to the notch east of the balanced block. Ground is a mix of scree and low heather and level spots take some hunting; the basin is open and catches wind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams draining the basin are reliable into midsummer and thin out by September; late-season parties should fill on the way up from Ingalls Creek rather than assume
bivy.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, outside the Enchantment Permit Area. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, no lottery, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda. No campfires at this elevation, and pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than on the meadow.
bivy.capacity: A small number of established spots on gravel and heather benches; two parties is comfortable, three is crowded

bivy.name: Table Rock bivy, upper Sherpa basin
bivy.notes: A large flat block high in the basin below Sherpa's south side, used by parties who want the East Ridge to start within minutes of waking rather than an hour and a half above camp. From here the route climbs a broad gully trending north-northeast to gain the crest east of the balanced rock, then follows blocks and sandy benches west past the block to the summit. It is exposed, windy and cold compared with the basin camp a thousand feet lower, and whether the extra height is worth carrying water up for is a real judgement call rather than an obvious yes. Anyone attempting Sherpa Balanced Rock's Northeast Couloir gets the most from this position, since the couloir tops out close by. Leave no trace of a platform; the rock is bare and the ground around it is fragile.
bivy.water: None dependable. Snow patches persist into midsummer and can be melted, but treat it as a dry bivy and carry water up from the basin below.
bivy.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, no Enchantment lottery involved. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda if you came over Longs Pass. No fires, and nothing here to build one with.
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat rock; this is a perch rather than a campsite, and there is nothing else level nearby

bivy.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
bivy.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
bivy.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
bivy.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
bivy.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

backups.name: Southwest Scramble
backups.fa: Forrest Farr and Art Winder, 1933 (first ascent of the peak)
backups.aspect: SW (basin/approach) transitioning to N on the final tower traverse
backups.season: July through the first significant snowfall of autumn (typically into October); expect lingering snow into early August in shaded sections
gear: Small alpine rock rack (a few cams and stoppers) for building anchors on the summit crack/ledge traverse
30-60m rope for a hand line on the exposed ledge and a short rappel off the summit crux
Ice axe and crampons — worth carrying even into August for lingering snow in the basin and summit gully
hazards: Loose, blocky rock on the talus approach and summit ridge with rockfall risk to parties below
Lingering snow/ice in the basin and summit gully into early August
Extreme remoteness — a multi-day evacuation or helicopter rescue should be assumed for any serious injury
Exposed Class 4 ledge traverse just below the summit with real fall consequences
Seasonal trail washouts and stream crossings on the Bridge Creek/Stehekin approach
backups.overview: Storm King is a rugged, remote satellite peak just southwest of Mount Goode in North Cascades National Park's Stephen Mather Wilderness, and one of Washington's 'Bulger List' 100 highest summits. It has no easy access from any direction — approaches run roughly 13 to 20+ miles one-way via Thunder Creek, Cascade Pass/Park Creek Pass, or the Stehekin/Park Creek corridor, making it one of the farthest Top-100 peaks in the state from a trailhead. Most parties combine it with Mount Goode (Northeast Buttress or Southwest Couloir) from a shared high camp. The summit looks straight across upper Park Creek at Buckner, Logan, and Goode.
backups.beta: Approach the peak from Park Creek campground by ascending a loose talus slope, bearing left toward a cirque below the towers. Route-finding requires staying on the correct gully (right-side route preferred over left). Traverse a ledge across the backside of the southern tower with Class 3-4 moves and occasional exposure. Navigate a slight overhang with a squeeze-through section (Class 3), then traverse the summit tower's backside to a small spur. Final approach involves either climbing a 15-foot Class 4 solid face or wrapping around the left side on Class 3 blocks to reach the summit register. Slings are in place near the summit for rappel anchors.
backups.turnaround: Descend from the notch before the summit pitch if weather deteriorates, rope systems fail, or party members become fatigued. Descent to Park Creek campground in daylight to avoid navigating loose talus in darkness.
backups.rappels: Normally downclimbed; at most one optional rappel off fixed slings near the summit back to the north-side ledge. Carry a 60 m rope for it
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
backups.comms: No cell service in the North Cascades backcountry. Satellite communicators (e.g., Garmin InReach, personal locator beacons) are strongly recommended for emergencies. Weather changes rapidly; consider filing a float plan with rangers at Stehekin.
backups.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.
obj_haz: rockfall/loose blocks
lingering snow and ice on the basin and ledge traverse into early August
exposed, unprotected ledge traverse
route-finding among several similar-looking summit towers

waypoints.name: Colonial Creek Campground Trailhead
waypoints.note: Drive-to trailhead in Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, just past milepost 130; the Thunder Creek Trail leaves from the south end of the campground near the amphitheater. The alternative southern start is by boat to Stehekin and shuttle to High Bridge, then up the Park Creek Trail.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 (the North Cascades Highway) to the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead, the start of the most commonly used approach into this basin. From there the Thunder Creek Trail — an easy, mostly forested stock and hiker trail — climbs only about 600 feet over its first 13 miles up-valley. Two alternate approaches reach the same high basin: a steeper, more direct line over McAlester Pass and down Rainbow Creek, also starting from SR-20, or a southern approach by boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp, then up the Park Creek Trail. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required, and if you're using the Stehekin ferry or shuttle, both run on a limited schedule — typically mid-June through September — so check timetables and reserve the permit before planning dates.

waypoints.name: Skagit Queen Camp
waypoints.note: Established camp near old Skagit Queen mine workings where the trail steepens into switchbacks; reliable creek water, common first- or second-night stop.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Thunder Creek Trail south from the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 — an easy, mostly-forested stock/hiker trail with only about 600 ft of gain — roughly 13 miles up-valley, passing McAllister Camp near mile 6 and Junction Camp near mile 9.5.

waypoints.name: Park Creek Pass
waypoints.note: Trail high point in the notch between Mt. Logan and Mt. Buckner; camping is prohibited at the pass itself to protect fragile meadows, so continue on or camp just below it.
waypoints.directions: Continue up-valley past Thunder Basin Camp around mile 16.5, then pick up the signed Park Creek Pass Trail junction a couple of miles beyond; it switchbacks up through meadows to the pass.

waypoints.name: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
waypoints.note: Flat, grassy camp on a small NE/SW-trending rib south of Storm King with a nearby water source; leave the maintained trail here and go cross-country toward the peak.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and traverse cross-country west/southwest across snow and talus, favouring climber's left, toward the basin under Storm King's east and west towers. Carry an ice axe and consider crampons into August for lingering snow on this traverse, and take care not to drift off-line in poor visibility.

waypoints.name: Talus cirque beneath the towers
waypoints.note: About a mile of loose talus/scree past the rib camp brings you into the cirque directly under Storm King's west and east towers; take the path of least resistance up the scree.
waypoints.directions: About a mile of loose talus and scree past the rib camp, bearing right toward the cirque; cairns mark a Class 2-3 climber's trail and the line is the path of least resistance up the scree.

waypoints.name: North-side exposed ledge traverse
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 ledge system traversing the backside of the summit towers, including a slight overhang requiring a squeeze-under move; most parties fix a line here.
waypoints.directions: From the cirque, ascend the long, very loose talus/scree slope on the path of least resistance toward the southwest gully system below the summit rocks, staying right of the horn-shaped rock gully at about 8,000 ft to be in the correct gully. This slope is the approach's main hazard — helmets on and space the party out for rockfall and unstable footing. Around 70 ft of Class 3 scrambling reaches the notch, and it is the right-most of the notches in the summit rocks; cross to the north side of it to gain the ledge.

waypoints.name: Summit crux crack
waypoints.note: 15-foot crack (Class 4 to low 5th) leads to the fixed rappel anchor used for the descent; rope up or belay through this section.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the ledge roughly 70 ft across the backside of the tower — two or three Class 4 moves, full exposure, and a squeeze under a slight overhang; many parties fix a line. The ledge widens and holds loose rock, so move carefully, then continue across the summit tower's backside to the small spur at the foot of the crack.

waypoints.name: Storm King summit
waypoints.directions: Climb the 15-ft solid Class 4 face crack, or wrap around its left side on easier Class 3 blocks; both reach the register and the fixed rappel slings. A final short Class 3 pitch tops out. Two points above 8,520 ft sit east of the triangulated 8,515 ft subsummit — the easternmost is the true high point.

backups.detailed_rack: No rock gear required for the scramble.
what_to_bring: Bear canister or NPS-approved food storage for the multi-day approach
Satellite communicator (InReach or similar) given the lack of cell coverage
Water treatment for camps along Thunder/Park/Bridge Creek
pro_tips: Many parties combine Storm King with Mount Goode (NE Buttress or SW Couloir) from the same high camp, since the approaches overlap
The Thunder Creek approach is longest but avoids ferry/floatplane scheduling; the Stehekin/Park Creek approach is shortest but ties your trip to the Lake Chelan boat schedule
Biking the Stehekin road/PCT reroute from High Bridge can save real time when the trail is bike-legal — check current NPS trail conditions before counting on it
Check the NPS North Cascades climbing-conditions blog before you go for current beta on snow line and washouts
watch_out: This is a 3-day trip even for fit parties given the approach length — don't plan it as a single long day
The crux ledge/crack near the summit is short but exposed; most parties fix a line rather than solo it
Camping is banned at Park Creek Pass itself — plan your camp at Thunder Basin, Park Creek, or the high basin instead
Cell service is unreliable to nonexistent for the entire approach and climb
backups.pro_needs: A scramble with one short technical crux rather than a multi-pitch rock route — a few small cams/stoppers and slings are enough to rig a hand line on the ledge traverse and the summit rappel.
backups.best_season: Late July through September is the reliable window. Snow often lingers in the basin above ~7,400 ft into early August, so carry an ice axe (and consider crampons) even for a nominally dry climb. The route generally stays climbable until the first real snows of autumn, typically early-to-mid October, but shorter days and colder nights make late-season attempts riskier given the 3-day approach.
backups.approach: Storm King sits at the head of Thunder Creek in the North Cascades and is one of the range's most remote 'Bulger/Top 100' summits — a three-day car-to-car trip is the norm, and three separate trailhead approaches converge on the same high basin below Mount Goode's south side. The most common line is the Thunder Creek approach: from the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20, follow the Thunder Creek Trail (an easy, mostly-forested stock/hiker trail) about 13 miles with only ~600 ft of gain to the McAllister Creek confluence — McAllister Camp (~mile 6) is a common night-one camp. Continue past Junction Camp (~mile 9.5) and Skagit Queen Camp (~mile 13.5) to Thunder Basin Camp (~mile 16.5), then pick up the signed Park Creek Pass Trail junction a couple miles beyond and follow it up through meadows to Park Creek Pass. Two alternate approaches reach the same basin: a steeper, more direct line over McAlester Pass and down Rainbow Creek from SR-20 (camp at Rainbow Lake, ~9 mi and 2,700 ft of gain), or a southern approach via boat/shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp, then up the Park Creek Trail to Park Creek Pass from the south. From Park Creek Pass, leave the maintained trail and traverse cross-country west/southwest across snow and talus (favor climber's left) for roughly a mile to reach the cirque below Storm King's east and west towers — an ice axe and even crampons are worth carrying into August for lingering snow on this traverse, and it's easy to drift off-line in poor visibility. From the cirque, ascend a long, very loose talus/scree slope on the path of least resistance toward the southwest gully system below the summit rocks; this slope is the approach's main hazard — expect rockfall onto parties below and unstable footing, so helmet up here and space out.
backups.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent line. From the notch/crack area just below the true summit, most parties downclimb the ~15-ft crux crack and the exposed Class 4 ledge just below it. Some instead rappel off the fixed slings (in-situ tat/webbing — inspect it and back it up before committing) back to the ledge on the north side; even with a 60 m rope, expect to downclimb some Class 3 terrain. From the ledge, cross back through the right-most notch and descend the loose talus and scree slope to the cirque. From the base of the talus, reverse the cross-country traverse east back to Park Creek Pass and the maintained trail system, then descend via whichever of the three approach trails (Thunder Creek, McAlester Pass/Rainbow Creek, or Park Creek/Stehekin) matches your itinerary. Loose rock is the dominant descent hazard from the summit all the way down through the talus — keep helmets on and parties tight until well below the scree.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward down the southwest talus/scree back to camp from anywhere below the summit ridge; the only technical step to reverse is the short crux ledge/crack near the top, which most parties down-climb or rappel rather than commit to unroped.

pitch_detail.notes: 1-2 miles of loose talus slopes from Park Creek campground/base cirque. Ascend right-bearing toward cirque. Path of least resistance; cairns mark climber's trail. ~1000 ft elevation gain. Expect loose rock and rockfall hazard. Take ice axe and crampons for any remaining snow patches (common into August).

Traverse ledge across backside of southern tower (~70 feet). Fairly exposed; 2-3 Class 4 moves on ledge. Squeeze under slight overhang (Class 3). Some parties set up fixed line. Ledge widens and contains loose rock; move carefully.
pitch_detail.pitch: South tower ledge traverse and squeeze

pitch_detail.notes: Traverse summit tower's backside to small spur. Ascend a 15-foot solid Class 4 face crack, or wrap around left side on Class 3 blocks (easier). Fixed anchors (slings) present near summit for rappel. Either climb the solid Class 4 crack or traverse Class 3 blocks; both lead to register and rappel slings. Short but sustained exposure.
pitch_detail.pitch: Summit tower access and final crack

itinerary.cal: North Cascades NP wilderness permits and the Stehekin shuttle bus/ferry both run on limited schedules (typically mid-June through September); reserve the permit and check ferry/shuttle timetables before planning dates.

days.note: Take the Lady of the Lake ferry (or Chelan Seaplanes) up Lake Chelan to Stehekin Landing, then the NPS shuttle bus 11 miles to High Bridge (not hiked). From High Bridge, follow the road/Old Wagon Trail bypass to Bridge Creek Camp, continue to Park Creek campground, then up the Park Creek Pass Trail to Two Mile Camp (~3,400 ft). A permit is required to camp in North Cascades NP / Lake Chelan NRA.
days.title: Boat + hike-in to Two Mile Camp
days.objective: Reach Two Mile Camp on the Park Creek Pass Trail

days.note: Continue up the Park Creek Pass Trail about 2 miles, then leave the trail around 4,100 ft at a large washout and climb diagonally climber's-left through heather, meadows and game trails. Terrain steepens and turns rocky near 6,500 ft; cairns then mark a Class 2-3 climber's trail up to the basin below Goode at 7,400 ft, a strenuous full day with an overnight pack. This basin (or the rib just south of it) is the standard high camp for both Storm King and Goode.
days.title: Push to high basin camp below Storm King
days.objective: Establish high camp in the basin below Goode/Storm King (~7,400-7,500 ft)

days.note: From high camp, cross the cirque beneath the west and east towers on very loose talus, staying right of the horn-shaped-rock gully at ~8,000 ft for the correct gully. A short Class 3 scramble to a notch, a 15 ft crack (Class 4/low 5th), and a final Class 3 pitch reach the summit. Fit parties reverse the route back to camp, break camp, and hike all the way out to High Bridge/Stehekin for the shuttle and boat the same day; less aggressive parties add a 4th day to hike out.
days.title: Summit day and full descent to trailhead

schedule.label: Alpine start from high camp
schedule.detail: Day pack; leave overnight gear staged at camp.

schedule.label: Enter the summit cirque
schedule.detail: Loose talus below the west/east towers; identify the correct gully, avoiding the horn-rock gully.

schedule.label: Class 3 to the notch
schedule.detail: ~70 ft of scrambling to reach the summit notch.

schedule.label: Crux crack and final scramble
schedule.detail: 15 ft crack (Class 4/low 5th), then Class 3 to the true summit.

schedule.label: Summit (8,565 ft)
schedule.detail: Views of Goode, Logan, and Buckner; begin descent soon after.

schedule.label: Back at high camp, break camp
schedule.detail: Pack up and begin the long hike out toward High Bridge/Stehekin.

days.objective: Climb Storm King, then break camp and hike all the way out

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day, roughly 33-mile round-trip trip: two days of approach (boat/shuttle plus a strenuous climb to a ~7,400 ft high camp below Goode), a technical Class 3-4 scramble to the 8,565 ft summit, and a long descent all the way to the trailhead on day 3. Very fit, fast parties occasionally compress this to 2 days; less aggressive parties sometimes split the hike-out into a 4th day.

access.fees: Backcountry camping fee is $10/person plus a one-time $6 non-refundable reservation fee, charged mid-May through early October; no charge outside that window and none for youth 15 and under. There is no park entrance fee for North Cascades NP.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: A backcountry permit is required for any overnight stay in the park; get it at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount ((360) 854-7245) or the Golden West Visitor Center in Stehekin. About 60% of sites are reservable in advance on Recreation.gov; the remaining ~40% are walk-up only, issued in person up to 24 hours ahead.
access.closures: Camping is prohibited at Park Creek Pass itself to protect fragile alpine turf — plan to camp at Thunder Basin, Park Creek, or the high basin instead. Trail washouts have periodically hit the Bridge Creek/North Fork corridor near Stehekin, sometimes requiring a bike-and-hike detour around damaged sections — check current NPS trail conditions before relying on that approach. A major December 2025 atmospheric-river flood also severely damaged Stehekin's Company Creek Road, power, and wastewater infrastructure, disrupting North Cascades Lodge services and the Stehekin shuttle/ferry into the 2026 season; an interim road repair was completed in June 2026 but services remain limited — check the NPS Stehekin Flood Response Update page before planning the Stehekin/Park Creek approach. Thunder Creek Fire: North Cascades National Park's fire-closure list (updated September 14, 2026; no end date given) closes the Thunder Creek Trail from the Fisher Creek Trail junction to Park Creek Pass for the Thunder Creek Fire, along with Junction Camp, Skagit Queen Camp and Thunder Basin Camp (hiker and stock sites), and prohibits cross-country travel from the closed trail. The Thunder Creek approach cannot be used past the Fisher Creek junction while this stands. The same list also closes the Stehekin Valley Road from Stehekin Valley Ranch to High Bridge, the High Bridge area, and the Pacific Crest Trail from the park boundary to Bridge Creek Camp for the Sisi Fire, so the Stehekin/High Bridge approach is closed as well. North Cascades National Park: (360) 854-7200.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Complex, Stephen Mather Wilderness (National Park Service).
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: No day-use pass; a paid/reserved backcountry permit is required for any overnight stay (see fees).

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit — quota reservation or walk-up
overnight_permit.where: Reserve a night-by-night itinerary online via Recreation.gov during the early-access lottery, or get a walk-up permit in person (about 40% of sites) at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount up to 24 hours ahead.

road.name: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to Colonial Creek CG, or Cascade River Road to the Cascade Pass Trailhead, or the Lake Chelan ferry/floatplane to Stehekin, depending on approach chosen.
road.status: SR-20 is paved; Cascade River Road is gravel beyond the pavement's end and has had early-season washout closures in some years; Stehekin has no outside road access at all — it's reached only by the Lake Chelan passenger ferry, floatplane, or a very long trail.
road.driveNote: For the Thunder Creek approach, the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead is on SR-20 about 24 miles east of Marblemount, just past milepost 130.
road.seasonalGate: SR-20 over Washington/Rainy Pass typically closes for winter (roughly mid-November through April, weather dependent); Cascade River Road usually opens later in spring than the highway.

climate.fall: First significant snowfalls typically end the climbing season by October.
climate.summer: Climbable July through the first snows of autumn; the Stehekin valley bottom can be hot and dry while snow still lingers above roughly 7,400 ft into early August.
climate.typical: Mixed maritime/continental North Cascades weather — Storm King sits near the crest between the wetter west-side drainages and the drier Stehekin/Lake Chelan side, so conditions vary with the approach chosen. Weather windows can be short; afternoon thunderstorms and sudden fog are possible even in mid-summer.

bySeason.fall: Early-to-mid October usually brings the first snows that end the season for the year; shorter days add pressure to the 3-day itinerary.
bySeason.summer: July-September is normally the driest, most stable window, though snow can linger in the basin and summit gully above ~7,400 ft into early August, calling for an ice axe and sometimes crampons.

emergency.notes: Given the remoteness, assume self-rescue or an NPS/SAR helicopter evacuation for serious injuries — cell coverage is unreliable to absent throughout the approach and basin. Carry a satellite communicator and leave a trip plan with the Wilderness Information Center.
emergency.county: Chelan County (South Unit of the North Cascades National Park Complex, near the Skagit County line).
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount — (360) 854-7245; or Golden West Visitor Center, Stehekin.
emergency.nearestHospital: No hospital is close — this is roughly a 3-day approach from any trailhead. Via the Stehekin side, Lake Chelan Health (Chelan, WA) is nearest, reachable only by boat/floatplane from Stehekin. Via the Marblemount/SR-20 side, Skagit Valley Hospital (Mount Vernon, ~50 mi from Marblemount) is the nearest full-service ER.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Chelan County Sheriff's Office non-emergency (509) 667-6851; dial 911 for emergencies.

lists: Washington Bulgers (100 Highest Peaks) — tied for #51

crowds.peakTraffic: Late July through August weekends, driven mostly by parties already camped near Park Creek Pass for Goode's NE Buttress or SW Couloir who tack on Storm King
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low - a handful to roughly a dozen parties per season; Storm King is almost always climbed as an add-on to a Mount Goode trip rather than as a standalone objective, so pure Storm King traffic is sparse

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong - must be able to sustain a long, rugged multi-day backpacking approach through North Cascades National Park (Park Creek Pass area) with significant elevation gain before even starting the scramble
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Heavy overnight/mountaineering load (ice axe, crampons, camping gear, multi-day food) - typically 35-45+ lbs on the approach

partner_requirements.approachTime: Multi-day approach - typically 1-2 days in to a camp near Park Creek Pass (or combined with the Goode approach) before a long summit day; not feasible as a single-day car-to-car trip for most parties
requiredSkills: Class 4 scrambling on loose/blocky rock
route-finding in benches/gullies with limited beta
self-arrest and basic snow travel (ice axe/crampons for lingering snow, even into August)
backcountry/off-trail navigation
comfort with unroped exposure near the summit
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate-to-advanced alpine scrambler/climber comfortable with sustained Class 3-4 terrain, loose rock, and remote North Cascades wilderness travel; not a beginner objective given the multi-day approach and route-finding demands

July.reason: Snow-filled gullies and lingering snowpack are still common early-to-mid month; ice axe/crampons recommended; conditions improve steadily as the month progresses

August.reason: Driest, most stable window with the least residual snow in the gullies and benches - the best month for the southwest flank scramble

September.reason: Rock is dry and stable but days are shorter and early-season snow/weather can arrive late in the month, especially at this 8500+ ft elevation

weather.typical: Typical dry-season North Cascades alpine weather in the best-season window - warm, sunny days with cool nights at elevation; lingering snow in shaded gullies persists into July
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms/showers are possible in the North Cascades in summer, as on most Cascade alpine objectives, though not called out specifically in existing sources for this route

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Class 4 summit exposure over loose rock - a slip near the top of the route or in the exposed gullies could result in a serious fall; compounded by the route's remoteness (North Cascades NP / Lake Chelan NRA backcountry), which extends any rescue timeline significantly

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route; falls outside NWAC's operational forecast season (NWAC issues zone forecasts roughly Nov-Apr) and this remote North Cascades NP cross-country area is not one of NWAC's named zones

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; route stays on benches, gullies, and blocky rock

gaps: Round-trip mileage/elevation gain vary substantially by chosen approach (roughly 13-25+ mi, 5,000-7,000+ ft) and weren't consolidated into one authoritative figure
Crux rating is cited only as 'Class 4 to low Class 5' in secondary online sources (Mountaineers.org route page); not cross-checked against Beckey's Cascade Alpine Guide directly
Primary route pages (Mountaineers.org, SummitPost) returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch — information here is drawn from search-result excerpts of those pages plus trip reports
No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

backups.corrections: Storm King's exact summit elevation is disputed across sources and could not be pinned to one authoritative figure. 8,346 ft is cited by some peak lists; SummitPost notes that 8,515 ft (the figure used in most trip-report titles, adopted here as highPointFt) is technically a triangulated subsummit, and that the true highpoint is one of two unnamed tops east of it exceeding 8,520 ft; listsofjohn.com separately lists 8,564 ft. No single figure could be confirmed as definitive after cross-checking available sources. 2026-08-05: loss_ft corrected from 2200 to 6300 — matches this row's own itinerary day-sum (300+100+5900) and is consistent with gain_ft (6800) for this out-and-back route.
backups.rappel_count_note: Most parties downclimb this rather than rappel, though slings near the summit show some do rappel it. If you use it, a single rappel off the east side returns you to the ledge on the north side, and even with a 60 m rope expect to downclimb some class 3 terrain.

approach_variants.name: The shared Goode approach to 7,400 ft, then the talus cirque and the right-most notch
approach_variants.notes:
Storm King sits at the head of Thunder Creek and is one of the range's most remote summits — a three-day car-to-car trip is the norm, and three separate trailhead approaches converge on the same high basin below Goode's south side.

The most common is Thunder Creek: from Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, the Thunder Creek trail roughly 13 miles with little gain to the McAllister Creek confluence, past Junction, Skagit Queen and Thunder Basin camps, then the Park Creek Pass trail junction and the switchbacks to PARK CREEK PASS. Alternatives are McAlester Pass and Rainbow Creek from SR-20, or a boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp then the Park Creek trail from the south. From Stehekin the boot path starts on the north side of a large whitish-rock washout about two miles up the trail, five minutes further into the woods.

From Park Creek Pass, leave the maintained trail and traverse cross-country west-southwest across snow and talus, favouring climber's left, roughly a mile to the cirque below Storm King's east and west towers. A rib camp around 7,450 ft with nearby water is the usual base.

From the cirque, a long and very loose talus and scree slope leads up toward the southwest gully system. Helmet on and space out — that slope is the approach's main hazard.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September; snow often lingers in the basin above about 7,400 ft into early August, so carry an axe and consider crampons even for a nominally dry climb
hazards: Loose blocky rock on the talus approach and the summit ridge, with rockfall onto parties below
Lingering snow and ice in the basin and the summit gully into early August, and bullet-hard patches
An exposed class 4 ledge traverse just below the summit with real fall consequences
In-situ slings at the crux that are aging tat and need backing up before they are weighted
Extreme remoteness — assume a multi-day evacuation or a helicopter for any serious injury
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO KNOW ABOUT THIS APPROACH IS THAT BELOW 7,400 FT IT IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM GOODE MOUNTAIN'S. The same trail, the same basin, the same cairned climber's path. A party in fog below that elevation cannot tell from the ground which peak's route it is on. The split happens above it, where this route trends toward the towers while Goode's continue toward the glacier or Black Tooth Notch.

THE COUNTING TEST IS THE NOTCH, AND THE WORD IS RIGHT-MOST. There are several notches in the summit rocks; the route crosses at the RIGHT-MOST one. Most of the way up to it is loose scree and talus, which is what makes the notch worth confirming rather than guessing.

CROSS TO THE NORTH SIDE OF THAT NOTCH AND THE GROUND CHANGES CHARACTER COMPLETELY: a fun ledge traverse on the BACKSIDE of the tower, roughly 70 ft, with two or three class 4 moves and full exposure. IF YOU HAVE NOT CROSSED TO THE NORTH SIDE, YOU HAVE NOT FOUND THE LEDGE TRAVERSE, and there is no version of this route that goes up the front.

CONFIRM ON THE LEDGE: it includes a SQUEEZE UNDER A SLIGHT OVERHANG, and there are IN-SITU SLINGS at the crux left by earlier parties. A squeeze move plus old tat is the strongest positive confirmation on the climb — though the tat is aging and is not to be trusted with body weight without backup.

THE LAST MOVE IS A CHOICE, NOT A CRUX: a 15-ft solid class 4 face crack, or a wrap around its LEFT side on class 3 blocks. Both reach the register and the rappel slings.

AND KNOW WHICH TOP YOU WANT: two 8,520-ft-plus points sit east of a triangulated 8,515 ft subsummit, and the EASTERNMOST is the true high point.

bivy.name: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
Neve Camp
bivy.notes: Under two miles from the Colonial Creek trailhead on flat valley trail, this is the camp that exists to absorb a late arrival rather than to stage a climb. Parties driving over from the west side after work can sleep here and still be at Junction by early afternoon the next day. It is deep forest with no views, and the bugs are heavy through midsummer. Nothing about it is alpine, which is exactly its function on a corridor where the climbing is fifteen or more miles in.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek runs beside the camp and is reliable all season.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round. Issued at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, or emailed in advance against a reservation. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through recreation.gov (spring lottery, then a general on-sale in late April); the rest is held for walk-up and can only be claimed the day before or day of your start.
bivy.capacity: Small forested camp, reported at roughly five tent spots, spread out enough that parties are not on top of each other. Confirm the count and per-site party limit when the permit is issued.

bivy.name: Junction Camp
bivy.notes: About ten miles in, this is where the trail finally gives something back after a long forest walk, with the Boston Glacier visible through a gap in the trees. It is the natural first or second night for parties heading to Mount Logan, and the standard stopping point on the way back out from a high camp. The trail to Fisher Basin and Easy Pass leaves from here, so it also works as a hinge for loop itineraries. The climb up gains roughly a thousand feet in a bit over two miles and is the first real work of the approach.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek is the source and is dependable, but the camp sits on a bench well above it, so water means a descent and a climb back with full bottles. Arrive with enough to cook on if you get in late.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the rest of the corridor. Fire rings and a privy are present here, unlike the cross-country zones higher up — but confirm current fire restrictions on the permit rather than assuming the rings mean fires are legal.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites, one tucked away and more private than the others. A separate stock camp sits nearby. The quota is small enough that a weekend party without a reservation should have a fallback in mind.

bivy.name: Skagit Queen Camp
bivy.notes: Roughly thirteen miles up the valley, reached after a steep mile of climbing through silver fir, and the last creekside camp before the trail commits to the headwaters. Remains of early twentieth-century mining work sit just beyond the camp. The bridge over Thunder Creek in this stretch was rebuilt in recent years, but high water in the side creeks earlier in the season is still worth asking about at the permit desk.
bivy.water: Directly on Thunder Creek, reliable through the season.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. The quota applies to the specific camp and night, so an itinerary that slips a day needs the permit amended rather than ignored.
bivy.capacity: Small hiker camp, a handful of sites. Treat capacity as tight and reserve if your schedule cannot flex by a day.

bivy.name: Thunder Basin Hiker Camp
bivy.notes: The staging camp for Booker, Storm King and Buckner from the west, and for parties continuing over the pass toward Stehekin. It sits in meadows and small trees with roughly a thousand feet of climbing still to reach the pass, and it is reliably buggy in warm weather. Because the pass is closed to camping, groups wanting to be higher have to leave the designated system entirely and take a cross-country zone permit instead. Snow lingers in the basin and on the pass well into summer, and how long is the single most variable thing about timing a trip here.
bivy.water: Creek water at the camp, dependable through the normal climbing season. Sources higher toward the pass thin out as the snow goes.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED AT PARK CREEK PASS ITSELF, so this is the last legal designated camp on the west approach. A portable food canister is recommended and black bears are active in the basin; canisters can be borrowed at the permit offices.
bivy.capacity: Small subalpine hiker camp near seventeen miles in; a separate stock camp sits about a mile lower and requires fording Thunder Creek. Sites are few, and this is the most contested camp in the corridor because everyone headed for the pass wants it.

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

backups.name: South Face / Standard Route
hazards: Loose, blocky rock and occasional rockfall on the approach ledges and scramble sections
Significant exposure on unroped Class 3-4 terrain below/around the technical pitches
Snow and ice lingering on Aasgard Pass and the approach into July, requiring an ice axe (crampons in early season)
Afternoon thunderstorms are common July-August — start early and be off the summit by early afternoon
No reliable water source between Colchuck Lake and the summit
Sparse, hard-to-find gear placements on the first roped pitch
backups.overview: Witches Tower is the distinct granite pinnacle at the west end of the Enchantments, about 0.4 mi east-southeast of Dragontail Peak (its nearest higher neighbor) and dividing remnants of the Snow Creek Glacier between Little Annapurna and Dragontail. It's a compact, airy summit block commonly tacked on to an Aasgard Pass day, or linked with Colchuck Peak, Dragontail Peak, and Little Annapurna as part of the classic Enchantments traverse.
backups.beta: This route approaches from the south after descending Aasgard Pass into the Upper Enchantments. Navigate south and southwest toward the tower's base, ascending toward the white granitic wall. Find a ledge to traverse around the east side of the tower, then scramble large black granite blocks to reach the summit. A 4-foot slot requires a jump to access the true summit. The route is exposed and requires careful footwork, especially on descent.
backups.turnaround: Maintain safety margins for your skill level on exposure and descending terrain. Turn around if weather deteriorates, if party members are exhausted, or if descending daylight appears insufficient. The exposed ledge traverse and descent scree present objective hazards that demand clear visibility and stable conditions. Never continue descending if visibility drops or afternoon storms develop.
backups.permit: Enchantment permit area: overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need the free self-issued day-use permit at the trailhead.
backups.comms: No cellular service in the Enchantments basin or valleys. Cell coverage may be available at the Lake Stuart-Colchuck Lake trailhead. Satellite phones or personal locator beacons (PLBs) recommended for overnight trips.
backups.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb or make a short single-rope rappel (fixed slings are sometimes found at the base of the tower) back to the col/notch, then retrace the approach back over Aasgard Pass to Colchuck Lake. The down-scramble of Aasgard Pass is loose and exposed — take care on the scree/talus, especially with any residual snow.
obj_haz: rockfall on Aasgard Pass
steep snow on the pass/approach in early season
exposure on the final scramble to the summit

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk; NW Forest Pass or $5 day-use fee required, and parking on FR 7601 often fills before sunrise in summer.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits at the end of Eightmile Road (FR 7601) off Icicle Creek Road, at about 3,400 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass or $5 day-use fee is required, and you self-issue a wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk. Parking along FR 7601 often fills before sunrise in summer, so plan on an early arrival.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake Trail split
waypoints.note: Signed fork where the Colchuck Lake Trail branches left off the Stuart Lake Trail (right continues to Lake Stuart).

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water and the last established camps before Aasgard Pass; overnight stays require an Enchantment Permit Area reservation May 15-Oct 31.

waypoints.name: Aasgard Pass
waypoints.note: Top of the roughly 2,200 ft scree/talus grind from the lake's south shore; loose, steep class 2-3 terrain that frequently holds snow into July.

waypoints.name: Brynhild (Isolation) Lake, west shore
waypoints.note: Largest of the Upper Enchantment lakes; skirt along its west shore and contour behind it toward the pinnacle rather than dropping to the outlet.

waypoints.name: Notch/col southwest of the tower
waypoints.note: Gained by a short class 4 step with loose rock and real exposure; the route's crux 5.5 move on the South Face begins just above here.

waypoints.name: Witches Tower
waypoints.note: Granite pinnacle dividing Snow Creek Glacier from Little Annapurna; descend via a short single-rope rappel or downclimb back through the same notch.

pro_tips: Tack onto a Dragontail or upper Enchantments day
Mind the afternoon weather

afternoon thunderstorms

backups.pro_needs: Minimal; a few placements on the granite.
backups.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (Mountaineer Creek Trail #1599, elev. ~3,400 ft; Northwest Forest Pass required) at the end of Icicle Creek/Eightmile Road (FR 7601), follow the trail steadily uphill through forest along Mountaineer Creek. At about 2.5 miles, bear left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail (the right fork continues to Lake Stuart). Continue climbing, crossing a boulder-strewn section near the outlet, to reach Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) at roughly mile 4, having gained about 2,000-2,100 ft — this is the last reliable water source before Aasgard Pass. Pick up the rough climbers' path along the lake's east/south shore (boulder-hopping in places) to its south end, then begin the well-known Aasgard Pass climb: an unrelenting, loose boot-track/goat-trail ascent of roughly 2,200 ft in under a mile to the 7,750-7,800 ft pass. This is the crux of the approach — footing is loose scree and talus lower down, the gully sections can be wet or icy, and snow commonly lingers into July, making an ice axe (and sometimes crampons/self-arrest practice) advisable; it is also a well-documented spot for slips given the sustained steepness and long runout. From the pass, work south to southwest across talus (and often a residual snow patch) toward the base of Dragontail Peak's east side, angling for the notch/col just below and east of Witches Tower's distinctive summit spire — the pinnacle that divides the upper Snow Creek Glacier basin between Little Annapurna and Dragontail. All told, trailhead to the base of the tower is on the order of 6.5-7 miles one-way with roughly 4,700-4,900 ft of gain (consistent with the ~14-mile, ~5,400 ft round-trip car-to-car days reported by parties who do this as a single push). There is significant exposure on the final approach scramble to the col, and the Enchantments are prone to fast-building afternoon thunderstorms in summer, so an early start is standard practice.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the south face scramble back to the notch/col below the true summit — Class 3 terrain with one short Class 4 section near the top. Multiple parties report finding rappel slings wrapped around a horn/block just below the summit, used to bypass the single 5.5 step-up/short face move that guards the final scramble to the top (the route also involves jumping a 4-ft summit slot). That is 1 rappel: parties not comfortable downclimbing the 5.5 move typically rig one short rappel (roughly 40-60 ft — easily covered on a single strand or on half of a doubled 60m rope) from a natural sling anchor on the summit block down onto the upper south face, then downclimb/scramble the remaining Class 2-3 ground to the col. There are no bolts reported on this route; anchors are natural (slung horn/block) and should be inspected or backed up, as sling material left by previous parties can be sun-weathered. Note also a short but airy step across a gap on an exposed ledge encountered by at least one party partway down the face — straightforward when dry but worth caution if wet or icy. From the col, reverse the approach line: descend the scree/goat-trail gully roughly 2,200 ft back to Aasgard Pass (plunge-stepping or glissading any snow with an ice axe in hand), then continue down through Aasgard Pass to Colchuck Lake and out via the Colchuck Lake Trail/Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the trailhead. No additional rappels are needed below the col — the rest of the descent is a hike/scramble walk-off.
backups.bail: The short route reverses easily with a single rappel.

pitch_detail.notes: Clean granite face and corner off the scramble base — the short technical crux of this quick summit add-on.
Easier moves past a 4-ft summit slot to the top; parties sometimes find rappel slings wrapped on a horn just below the summit for the way down.

itinerary.cal: Aasgard Pass and the traverse into the Enchantment Basin hold firm, often icy snow well into July, so most parties carry an ice axe even in mid-summer and target July-September for the driest, most straightforward footing.

days.note: From the Stuart/Colchuck Lake trailhead (3,540 ft), hike 4 miles to Colchuck Lake, then grind up the notoriously steep, loose 2,200 ft Aasgard Pass headwall into the Enchantment Basin. Traverse past Brynhild Lake to the col behind the tower, scramble class 3-4 blocks (with a short class 5 step on some lines) to the summit, then reverse the entire route back to the car — expect a full dawn-to-dark day.
days.title: Car-to-car: Colchuck Lake, Aasgard Pass, South Face

schedule.label: Leave trailhead
schedule.detail: Stuart/Colchuck Lake TH, 3,400 ft; start in the dark to buy time for the long day.

schedule.label: Reach Colchuck Lake
schedule.detail: ~4 miles and 2,000 ft in; refill water before the pass.

schedule.label: Top out Aasgard Pass
schedule.detail: The steep, loose 2,200 ft headwall is the day's crux effort; snow/ice axe often needed even in summer.

schedule.label: Traverse to the col behind the tower
schedule.detail: Past Brynhild Lake and around the base of the tower to the notch.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Class 3-4 scrambling on solid granite blocks; a short class 5 chimney/step on some lines.

schedule.label: Back at the trailhead
schedule.detail: Headlamps typically needed for the final miles out.

days.objective: Summit Witches Tower via the South Face/standard scramble route and return to the trailhead same day

itinerary.totalNote: A very long single day, not an overnight: ~14 mi round trip with ~5,400 ft of gain, typically a dawn-to-after-dark car-to-car push via Colchuck Lake and Aasgard Pass.

access.fees: $6 non-refundable lottery application fee; $5 per person per day for successful overnight permits (May 15-Oct 31).
access.notes: 2026 lottery application window Feb 15–Mar 1 (results after Mar 17, accept/pay by Mar 31). ~25% of overnight slots also released as a walk-up daily lottery the day before entry. Season requiring the overnight permit: May 15–Oct 31. A single-day ascent with no camp inside the boundary never needs the lottery.
access.rules: Dogs and pack animals are prohibited throughout the Enchantment Permit core zone; camping is restricted to permitted zones/sites.
access.permit: Overnight travel anywhere in the Enchantment Permit Area (which covers Witches Tower) requires a permit May 15-Oct 31, allocated via the Recreation.gov advance lottery (opens mid-to-late Feb for ~2 weeks) or the daily walk-up geofence lottery (apply online the day before entry). Day climbers must self-issue a free day-use permit at the trailhead.
access.closures: FR 7601 access road closed to vehicles mid-fall through spring; dogs are prohibited on the Stuart/Colchuck Lake trails and within the Enchantment Permit Area
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Leavenworth Ranger District (Enchantment Permit Area, Alpine Lakes Wilderness)
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — Alpine Lakes Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Stuart Lake, Eightmile, and Snow Lakes trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (overnight permit holders get a covering parking pass instead).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass required to park at Stuart Lake Trailhead

overnight_permit.what: Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit (lottery, not free) May 15 to Oct 31; self-issue at the trailhead the rest of the year
overnight_permit.where: Apply in the February advance lottery or the daily lottery on Recreation.gov. The permit names one zone (Core, Colchuck, Snow Lakes, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline) and you camp only there, except a Core permit, which covers every zone.

road.name: Icicle Creek Road (FR 7601) to Stuart Lake Trailhead
road.status: Paved then gravel Forest Service road, generally passenger-car accessible in summer
road.driveNote: From US-2 in Leavenworth, follow Icicle Creek Road about 8.7 miles to the Stuart Lake Trailhead (~3,400 ft).
road.seasonalGate: FR 7601 is closed to vehicles mid-fall through spring

climate.fall: Stable weather windows can occur into October, but nights are cold and snow can arrive quickly.
climate.spring: Basin and approach slopes typically still snow-covered into June/early July.
climate.summer: Jul-Sep is the main season; watch for building afternoon cumulus and thunderstorms.
climate.winter: Fully snowed-in and avalanche-prone; the access road (FR 7601) itself is gated.
climate.typical: East-slope Cascades rain-shadow climate: hot, dry summer days (often 75-85F at the trailhead) with cool nights above 8,000 ft; wind and sudden weather shifts are common on the exposed summit block.

bySeason.fall: September usually brings the most stable weather but shorter daylight and a chance of early snow.
bySeason.spring: Aasgard Pass and the approach typically hold snow/ice into late June or later, turning the climb into a steep snow ascent requiring axe and crampons.
bySeason.summer: July-August is prime season, but afternoon thunderstorms build regularly — start early.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible; deep snow and avalanche terrain on the approach.

emergency.notes: Chelan County SAR responded to roughly 31 backcountry calls in the Enchantments/Colchuck Lake area in 2025 alone, including at least one helicopter hoist rescue near Aasgard Pass — a reminder of how remote and exposed this approach is.
emergency.rangerStation: Leavenworth Ranger District, 600 Sherbourne St, Leavenworth, WA 98826 — (509) 548-2550
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Medical Center, Leavenworth — 24-hr ER with ambulance service, closest facility to the trailhead; serious trauma cases are typically flown to Central Washington Hospital (Wenatchee) or Harborview Medical Center (Seattle).
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Chelan County Sheriff's Office / Chelan County Volunteer Search & Rescue — call 911; cell coverage is unreliable in the Enchantments basin, so a satellite messenger (inReach/SPOT) is strongly recommended.

crowds.peakTraffic: Mid-July through August, on days when overnight Enchantments zone permit holders (a lottery-limited, capped-quota permit system) detour from Aasgard Pass/Colchuck-Prusik camps to tag the tower as a bonus scramble
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low - likely a few dozen parties per season at most (rough estimate; not found precisely in sources). Witches Tower is a minor side-objective for parties already camped in the upper Enchantments basin near Prusik Peak/Colchuck, not a standalone trailhead destination, so its own traffic is much lower than the Enchantments core hiking corridor.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong all-day alpine fitness - the approach via Colchuck Lake and Aasgard Pass gains roughly 2,200 ft over a short, steep boulder/talus and often snow-covered gully to reach the upper basin, on top of the long Stuart Lake trailhead approach
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light climbing rack only (helmet, harness, a few slings/small rack for the short 5.4 pitch, rope) - most parties are already carrying overnight/backpacking loads since they're camped in the basin, so keep the summit-day kit minimal

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - typically a multi-day trip (overnight Enchantments permit) with 6-9+ hours to reach the upper basin via Colchuck Lake and Aasgard Pass before the short climb itself, which only takes an hour or so once at the base
requiredSkills: exposed 3rd/4th class scrambling
basic rope/belay skills for a short 5.4 pitch
loose rock / choss management
route-finding on a small alpine tower
steep snow/talus travel on the Aasgard Pass approach
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Comfortable on exposed 3rd/4th-class terrain and easy low-5th-class rock (5.4) with a rope and minimal gear; should have prior alpine scrambling or easy multi-pitch rock experience and be at ease with loose rock and airy positions on a summit pinnacle

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, with late July-August the most reliable core window

July.reason: Early-to-mid July can still have residual snow patches on the approach and cooler/wetter rock; conditions improve markedly by mid-July per the best-season

June.reason: Aasgard Pass approach typically still holds significant snow/ice, adding avalanche and steep-snow hazard on top of the tower's exposed rock; not covered by the best-season window

August.reason: Peak dry-rock conditions and the most stable weather window in the Enchantments; matches the best-season core

October.reason: Outside the best-season window; early snowfall and freezing overnight temps at this elevation become likely, and the Enchantments overnight permit season is winding down

September.reason: Generally dry and climbable, but shortening days and increasing chance of early-season snow or cold snaps toward month's end

weather.typical: Typical dry-season Cascades alpine weather during the July-September window; can turn cold and wet quickly outside that window
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a known hazard - build in an early start and be off the tower before storms build

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Significant - loose blocks and exposure on this short but airy pinnacle route; a slip or rockfall on the exposed south face scramble/5.4 section has serious fall consequence given the summit's small, exposed profile

avalanche.zone: NWAC East Central zone (nearest NWAC forecast zone covering the Stuart Range/Leavenworth area; no zone-specific forecast exists for Witches Tower itself)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; the route stays on rock/talus/scramble terrain to the tower's base

gaps: Exact grade/pitch count varies by source between the 'South Face' (Class 3-4 scramble with a short 5th-class step) and the 'West Buttress' (2 roped pitches to 5.4) — guidebook naming for Witches Tower's routes is inconsistent
No confirmed first-ascent history found
No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of FR-7601 off Icicle Creek Road, ~3,400 ft)

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass, then southwest across the Upper Enchantments to the col below the tower
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,400 ft, follow the Stuart Lake Trail south along Mountaineer Creek; at about 2.5 miles bear left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail. Cross Mountaineer Creek on logs and boulders — an awkward wet ford in early-season high water — and climb through forest and a boulder field to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, roughly four miles in. Last reliable water.

Take the climbers' path along the lake's east and south shore through talus to the foot of Aasgard Pass, then up the eroded boot track: roughly 2,200 ft in well under a mile of loose scree and blocks, holding snow and ice into July.

From the pass at about 7,800 ft, work south to southwest across talus — initially as though heading for the snow route on Dragontail's east side — toward the tower, then up snow or Class 2 rock to the col just SOUTHWEST of it.

Figure six and a half to seven miles one way with something like 4,700-4,900 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; earlier the traverse from the pass is a snow crossing and the col wants an axe
hazards: Aasgard Pass: 2,200 ft of loose eroded scree with rockfall from parties above, holding snow into July
Serious exposure on the final approach scramble to the col
A four-foot slot that must be jumped to reach the true summit, with real consequence
Fast-building afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter in the Upper Enchantments
Protection on the 5.5 step can be hard to find
The downclimb off the south face is the crux for most parties
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL SOUTHWEST OF THE TOWER IS THE BASE, AND THE TOWER ITSELF IS THE LANDMARK — a distinct rock pinnacle standing alone at the west end of the Enchantments, dividing the upper basin between Little Annapurna and Dragontail. It is a pinnacle, not a summit on a ridge, so once you are close enough to see anything at all it is unambiguous.

WHICH SIDE OF IT YOU WANT: the SOUTHWEST col. From the col the climbing goes up a sharp ridge for about 100 ft and then traverses a few feet RIGHT onto the south face. If the ground above your col does not narrow into a sharp ridge within the first hundred feet, you are at the wrong notch.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER ROUTES, and it is a clean one because the two cols are on opposite sides:
  - Snow or Class 2 rock up to a col, sharp ridge above, traverse right onto the south face — this route.
  - A col with a STEEP SNOWFIELD to cross before you reach rock — that is the west-side line, and the snowfield is the tell.
  - Working EAST or SOUTHEAST from the pass toward light-coloured rock below Dragontail's south ridge, with no col involved at all — that is the east face line.

ARRIVAL CONFIRMED BY THE SUMMIT ITSELF: the top of this tower is guarded by a four-foot slot you have to jump. If you have scrambled to a high point and there was no slot, you are on a subsidiary block and not on the tower.

GRADE CHECK: the hardest single move on this line is one 5.5 step-up after the Class 4 traverse. Ground that feels harder than that means you missed the traverse right and are climbing the face direct.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.
